div.head: VALUABLE DISCOVERY.
div.p: A VALUABLE DISCOVERY.

Most readers have had some experience of sick rooms, either as patients or attendants. How many such are there who have not felt the weakness or dubility which follows the sickness, more discouracing than even the disease itself? Though the disease may have given way before the timely application of proper remedies, and though, in consequence, no immediate danger is to be apprehended, the slow progress towards convalescence is very disheartening to Patient and attendant alike.

How often do we hear people say :—" Yes. The fever has left bin]. Be is free from ang immediate danger. But he is so weak. If he could only regain strength !" This debilitating effect of fevers and other diseases is indeed a great source of anxiety to medical men as well as to their patients; and anything which would tend directly to shorten the period between the departure of the fever and the complete recovery of strength would be naturally welcomed by both doctors and patients.

This is one of the reasons why Gwylym Evans' Quinine Bitters are so popular,why doctors prescribe it so largely, why chemists selL it so generally, why patients have recourse to it so readily, and why everybody has a good word to say for it. Not only does it attack the disease in its stronghold, not only does it drive the evil from the system, but it gives bark directly the strength of which the system has been deprived by sickness ; it infuses new life into the blood, and the recovery of health and strength, instead of being, as it otherwise would be, discouragingly slow, intermittent, and uncer- tain, becomes, when this excellent medicine is resorted to, encouraginely rapid, regular, and certain. It is, therefore, confidently recommended as an unrivalled tonic medicine,and may be safely used by all who suffer from any form of weakness or debility from whatever cause it may arise.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

A NEGLECTFUL PARENT COMMITTED TO GAOL. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Satur- day, Frederick Roberts was charged with neglecting his son Henry (aged eight years) several times during the put six months. Inspector WAteer, N.S.P.C.C., stated that the defendant resided at 103, Pierpoint-street. The child was in the habit of sleeping out at night, and had been found on doorsteps several times by the witness himself, who had either taken him home or brought him to the Police Station. Witness had ask-d the defendant why he did not look after the child, and he had replied that he did not see what harm there was in a lad sleep- ing out at night. The child was also sent out by his father to beg in the streets. There were six children altogether. On the 16th of June the inspector visited the defendant's house and found it in a dirty and neg- lected condition. Three of the children slept in one bed which was without any covering but a few rags. De- fendant was a clock cleaner by trade,and went about the country doing odd jobs. While he was away the house was left in charge of his eldest daughter(ap,,ed 19).—P.C. Corcoran deposed to having seen the lad slteping out at night. The magistrates committed the defendant to gaol for 14 days hard labour.

GARDEN ROBBERY BY BOYS. At the Warrington Borough Court,on Friday last week, four boys whose ages ranged from 13 to 15 years, were charged with stealing from the garden of Mrs. Eliztbeth Greening, 110, Bewsey-road, on Monday, the 13th inst., a quantity of fruit, viz.: 161bs of pears, value ss. The names of the defendants wer; : John Burton, 5, gdward- street, John Patrick Hind, 101, Pierpoint-street, John Bennett, 120, Pierpoint-street, and Albert Stokes, 77., Pierpoint-street. On being charged with the offence they all pleaded guilty. The Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) in his statement to the magistrates informed them that on the previous Monday, a brickmaker named John Litherland was working in a field close to the complain- ant's house, and he saw the four defendants together, at the back of Mrs. Greening's house. Hind was seen to get a plank and place it against the wall. He proceeded up the plank with a bass in his hand, and got into the gar- den. One of the other defendants had charge of thepla.nk, and theremaining two kept "nix." Hind filled his bass from one or two pear trees with half-grown pears. These were afterwards divided amongst the four defend- ants, Hind keeping the larger share. Lit herland very adroitly approached the lads, and caught Hind, while the others ran away. The police were informed, but the lads were not summoned as their mothers promised to bring them to court that morning. On being charged that morning with stealing the pears, three of the de- fendants pleaded guilty, and the fourth lad said, "I am not guilty of stealing, but I had five of them." There were similar robberies going on in other parts of the town. The lads were ordered to be detained until five o'clock, and the Chairman reprimanded them for their conduct.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. FRIDAY .—Before Alderman Harrison (chairman), Aid. Wright, Councillor Henry Roberts, Dr. Gornall, and Mr. S. Wright. CHARGES OF DESERTING.—John Fudge was charged with being an absentee from the annual training of the Somersetshire Militia this year, and Patrick Duffy was charged with being an absentee from the annual training of the 4th Cheshire Militia this year. Both prisoners were remanded until Monday. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY —William Hancock and Eliza Hancock were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Suez-st. the previous night last week. P.C.'s Robinson Lexham proved the case. The magistrates discharged the prisoners, who promised to leave the town. CRUELTY TO BORSES.—William Arm<trong, 1. Dakin's- yard, was charged with cruelly ill-treating a horse by working it in an unfit state on the 30th July, and Richard Miller, Bridge-foot, was charged with causing the horse to be so ill-treated.—P.C. Smith stated that on the date named he met the defendant Armstrong in charge of a horse and cart in Mersey-st. The horse was very lame on the near foreleg, and he pointed out to the driver that it was unfit for work.—lnspector Luff de- posed to seeing the horse the same night. It was suffer- ing from fever in the feet, and was unfit to work on the hard roads in the town.—Mr. Miller stated that the horse had not been worked since, and it was about to be sold to a farmer, when it would be employed on soft ground. The magistrates fined the defendants in the coats, us. altogether.—Charles Yardwood, Woolston, was charged with cruelly ill-treating a horse by work'ng it in an unfit state, and William Griffiths, Woolston was charged with causing the same to be worked. Mr. Willett. solicitor, Warrington, appeared on behalf of Mr. Griffiths. Inspector Luff stated that on the 31st ult., he was at Market Gate when he saw Yardwood driving a grey mare attached to a trap in which was seated Mr. Griffiths. He watched the horse for some time, and when it stopped he went up to it and examined it. The horse was very lame, and was suffer- ing from a spa Yin. He called the attention of Mr. Griffiths, who was the owner of it, and told him that it was unfit for work. Mr. Griffiths replied that he would not work it again.--Sergeant Taylor gave corroborative evidence.—Mr. Willett stated that the horse had since been sold. The defendants were fined the costs.

SATUBDAY.—Before Mr. J. Burgess (in the chair) and Mr. S. Wright. ASSAULTING A DirrEenve.—Johnßebbington, a soldier, WRS chareed with being drun k and disorderly last Friday, on Bank Quay station and with assaulting John Dipple,a London and North-Western Railway Co.'s detective.— P.C.Monks gave evidence to being called into Bank Quay station to eject the prisoner. He found Bebbington in the custody of the detective and upon attempting to put him out, the prisoner kicked the detective and struck him in the face—The detective deposed. that on the 17th of August the communication enrrl no a train from Man- chester to Warrington was pulled and the train stopped. Immediately the train came to a standstill the prisoner got out. He was drunk and the guard put him into his van, and released him at Warrington. On attempting to pass the barrier at Warrington the prisoner could not find his ticket and was detained till the detective came. *Thedisorderly conduct above referred to then took place. Prisoner was remanded until Monday, se that inquiries as tthis past character could be made. Mmmax.—Before Mr. J. Burgess (chairman), Alderman Harrison, Messrs. T. Birchen, J. W. Hayward, S. Wright. Dipple said the prisoner was noticed while passing the Vulcan, in the train from Manchester to Warrington, to be standing upon the footboard of the train. The signal driver stopped the train,and the prisoner who was drunk was taken into the guards van. When the train arrived at Warrington he got out and went along the line. A porter brought him back, and he then went past the ticket collector's office but did not produce any ticket. He however paid the fair from Manchester to Warrington and was allowed to pass. Witness however told P.C. Monks that he thought that the prisoner was beyond his leave of absence. Upon this the prisoner turned round and struck witness in the face. A struggle ensued and the prisoner was taken to the police station.— The prisoner had a good character in the army and the magistrates accordingly considered that he had received sufficient punishment by being locked up, and dismissed him. THEFT OF EGGS AND Beam—Philip J. Riley, a man unknown to Warrington,was charged with stealing from the shop of Edward Green in Buttermarket-street on Saturday evening, four eggs and half a pound of bacon. The prisoner went into Mr. Green's shop on Saturday night and asked for the eggs and bacon. When served he picked them up and ran off with them along Butter- market-street. Two boys followed him and saw him go into a lodging house in Percival's-fold. Information was then given to P.C. Clarke who went to the house ; and found the prisoner feasting on the eggs and bacon. He was told that he would have to go to the police- station whereupon he loudly protested that be had paid for the eatables. He was however arrested and locked up. When in the court, he appeared to have consider- able knowledge how to conduct his case, for he told the Chief Constable that he must not lead the witnesses and he conducted his cross-examination in most orthodox styles. The magistrates however considered the case amply proved and sent the prisoner to gaol for fourteen days. DRUNE AND DISORDERLY.—Catberine Brown was fined ss. and costs or in default seven days on this charge.

TIIESDAY.—Before Mr. R. Garnett (in the chair) and Dr. T. Starkey Smith. Datnix AND DISORDERLT.—Robert Schoss, a German sailor, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Sankey-at., on Sunday night. He was brandishing a knife and threatening to rise on anybody who approached him. Defendant was conveyed to the Police Station, where he was seen by Mr. Aukland, ' relieving officer,who thought it advisable to take him to the Workhouse, as he was acting like a lunatic. Defend- ant said he had left his vessel at Fleetwood and come by train to Bank Quay, Warrington, where be should have changed for Cardiff. He was drunk when he got out at Warrington, and had no recollection of what he bad done. The magistrates inflicted a penalty of Is., and defendant was taken to the station by a constable and sent on his way to Cardiff.—William Price and John Cooper were each fined ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly in Dolman's-lane on Monday. THEATRICAL LICENCE.—Mr.H. Hoffman, an actor at the Theatre Royal, Scotland-road, applied for a licence, per- mitting his son Dalzie,aged seven years, to act an heroic part in " Mid-Ocean," at the above theatre. The boy's hours would be from 7.30 to 10 o'clock at night. Some amusement was caused by the Chairman asking the ap- plicant if the boy was his own son; to which Mr. Hoff- man replied, "Most decidedly." The application was granted. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASES.—Mr. G. Riley prosecuted in the following cases, for non-attendance at school. John Buckley was charged with not sending his boy Gilbert, aged 13, to school. The defendant was repre- sented by Mr. A. Browne. It appears that the defend- ant wanted the help of his son in his business as a baker, and for that reason bad kept him away from school. During the past few years defendant had resided in several towns (at which the bey had been sent to school) but never long enough for his son to go in for the examinations. The result is that the boy, though well versed in the different school subjects for his age, has not passed,except by sample.the required examinations. An order was made for him to attend school till he was 14 years of age.—Mary Barlow, Howley-lane, was also or- dered to send her child to school.—Thomas Bridge, Win- wick-road, was fined 2s. 6d. ; Michael Dempsey, Fennel- st., ss. ; Charles Higginson,Ellesmere-st., 2s. 6d. ; Thos. Rowlands, Bridge-st., 2s. 6d. Ellen Mellor, Arpley-walk, 2s. 6d. ; and George Smith, West-st., as. 6d.

div.head: TICURSDAY.—Before Alderman T. Sutton.
div.p: TICURSDAY.—Before Alderman T. Sutton.

LYMM PETTY SESSIONS. FRlDAY.—Before Messrs. T. P. Norris (in the chair), A. Watkin Dr. Brabazon and W. Long. MOVING SWINEVITHOUT LICENSE.—David Williamson and James Bolton, were each charged with having moved certain swine from the residence of Mr. Worth- ington, of Rixton Hall, in the County of Lancashire, .to there residences near Warburton Bridge, in Cheshire, without a license ; the former on the 14th July and the latter on the 16th of the same month. P.C. Bebbington deposed to having questioned both defendants about the removal of the swine and they had replied that they did not know of the regulation being in force compelling them to have a license. Adam Robinson, the manager of Mr. Worthington's farm, stated that he had sold three pigs to each of the defendants on the days named. He, also did not know of the licensing regulation.—There was a notice, with reference to the license, posted on Warburton bridge,over which the defendants had to pass, but neither of them had noticed it. A penalty of 10s. and costs was inflicted in each case. BREACH or THE PEACE.—A charge was preferred against two youths—Thomas Moran and Anthony Dono- van—for creating a breach of the peace by fighting in Lymm, on the 29th July. P.C. Sandbach said that on the above-named date he saw the defendants fighting, with their jackets and vests off, in the midst of a large crowd. Re had some diffidulty in parting the combat- ants. The defendants were each bound over t keep the peace for six months in a surety of £lO. They were also fined the costs. A DISORDERLY CIISTODIER.—George Shaw was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Lymm, on the 29th July. The evidence was produced by Sergeant Wynne. There was a further charge of being disorderly on the premises of Thomas Marsh, the landlord of the "Bridge- water Arms," Lynam, on the 28th July.—Mr. Marsh stated that on the night in question the defendant was creating a nuisance on his (witness's) premises by sing- ing and jumping about. Witness did not ask defendant to leave the place, but seized him by the arms and I forcibly ejected him.—The Chairman (Mr. T. P. Norris) 'remarking on this, said that it was lucky for defendant that the landlord had not asked him to go out, because for that reason the bench could not fine him. For the first offence, however, the defendant was fined 10s. and costs. QUARRELSOME Nwornsouns.—George Jameson and Mary Jane Brazendale were charged with having as- saulted and beaten Emmeline Twiss on the 11th ilugust. —Mrs. Twiss, the complainant, stated that on the 11th August, she received information that the male defen- dant was going to wait for her and assault her. The same day while complainant was returning home from her work. she saw Jameson come out of a public house, and on being joined by Mary Brazendale, follow her home. As complainant was going into her house the defendants pushed the door open and tried to pull her back, whereupon the complainant struck the male de- fendant with a chair. Defendants then seized hold of her and pulled her into the road and Mary Brazendale struck her in the face.—Mrs. Elizabeth Mills, a neigh- bour, deposed to seeing Brazendale strike the complain- ant.—The magistrates bound all three over to keep the peace for six months in a surety of £lO and to paylthe costs of the proceedings. AN UNPROVOKED ASSAULT.—James Weeks was charged with assaulting Thomas Hurst on the 12th August, at Heatley, by striking him in the face with his fist. Hurst, the complainant, stated that he lived at Rush Green, Lymm and that on the day in question he came out of the "Farmer's Arms," Heatley, in company with the defendant; each had a dog with him. On getting outside the two dogs commenced fighting, and complain- ant to stop them' pulled defendant's dog away. Immediately he did this Weeks struck him a violent blow in the face with his fist. Complainant did not strike him back.—Abram Wilson, a witnes, deposed to see- ing defendant strike Hurst.—Frederick Gupwell who was present when the assault took place. also gave corroborative evidence.—The defendant said he gave complainant a .push but not a blow. He also stated that Hurst, pulling a shilling out, offered to fight him for half a sovereign; but this was not proved. Defendant was fined 10s. and costs.

A SUSPICIOUS CHLEACTER.—Wm.Brown,no fixed abode, was charged with being a rogue and vagabond. Defendant stated that he had been working at Messrs. Maginn's. He was dismissed on promising to leave the town.

RUNCORN PETIY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. Philip Speakman, C.C., Semi. Taylor, F. J. Norman, and Thomas Handley. THE LICENSE OF THE THEATRE ROYAL.—MT. Henry William Caddick, licensee of the Theatre Royal, Runcorn, made an application for the renewal of his license authorizing the performance of stage plays at the Theatre Royal. Runcorn. In answer to the deputy magistrates' clerk (Mr. Frank Johnson) the applicant said that this was his fourth annual application since he had been the manager of the building.—Superintendent Atherton, in reply to the magistrates, stated that the theatre was in a satisfactory state, and there were ample means of egress in case of fire.—Messrs. Fredk. Coward, and Thomas Whitfield were the sworn sureties of the applicant. —The renewal was granted. MAINTENANCE ORDER.—George Jones, waterman, of 44, Gilbert-street, was summoned to show cause why he should not contribute towards the maintenance of his two sons, named Samuel and George, at present in the Boltorelndustrial School, and aged eight and ten years respectively.—Superintendent Atherton stated that he had been authorized to take these proceedings and pro- duced the authority. The defendant was well able and satisfied to contribute is. 6d. per week towards the maintenance of each of his two boys, and he (the super- intendent) asked the magistrates to make an order to that effect ag,ainet defendant. Be would also ask for costs.—No objection to such an order being lodged by the defendant, the Bench granted the request. They also allowed the costs of the pro ceedings, amounting to 19s. 6cl. CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—Messrs. John and George Percival, farmers of Parkside Farm, Aston, were sum- moned for causing a horse to be cruelly illtreated by allowing it to be worked when in an unfit state on the 11th inst. ; and Charles Logan, labourer, in their employ was charged with cruelly illtreating the same by working it.—Mr. George Percival, who appeared on behalf of his brother and himself, denied the charge. Logan likewise pleaded not guilty.—P.C. Richardson stated that at 2.30 p.m. on Saturday. the 11th inst., the defendant Logan was taken into custody for being drunk whilstin charge of a horse and cart. When witness was afterwards tak- ing the horse and cart to the Wilson's Hotel he discovered 'that the animal was suffering from a wound on its back, apparently caused by the rubbing of a strap, which had been fastened underneath the saddle, instead of being taken over it. Blood was issuing from the wound, and the horse seemed to he in great pain in consequence. When he spoke to Logan about the wound, he replied. "Yes, it has been there for three days." He added that the horse was nevertheless quite right, because Mr. John Percival had seen him take the animal out of the stable that morning.—Corroborative evidence having been tendered, Superintendent Atherton remarked that he had also seen the horse alluded to. The wound at the time was being made worse by a strap which had first of all been carelessly thrown over the saddle and then brought underneath it. From all appearances the wound was about two days old.—George Percival stated that when he saw the animal on the night,previous to the defendant going out with it on the 11th inst there was no wound such as the one described by the constable. There had been an old wound on its back some months ago, but that had healed up. His brother and himself were very careful not to allow their horses to be worked when unfit, as they were both aware that the value of a horse was depreciated thereby. Consequently, it was the practice of one of them to inspect the horses every evening.—Logan said that whilst he was proceeding down Surrey-street, Runcorn, on the afternoon of the 11th inst. the saddle-strap came to pieces and he was bound to fasten it in.the way described by the superin- tendent and the other witnesses. He did not know, at the time, that it would interfere with the old wound. which had healed up.—The case against the employers of Logan was dismissed, and the last-named defendant was fined ss. and costs. RIDING WITHOUT RElNS.—William Wilson of 6, Light- foot's Square, was summoned for riding a cart in Hal- ton-toad, Runcorn, on the 15th inst. without having proper control of his horse by means of reins.—P.C. Richardson deposed to seeing the defendant sitting on one of the cart shafts whilst the horse was proceeding along the thoroughfare named above.—Fined ss. includ- ing costs. "IN CLOVER" BUT Nov AGREEABLY SO.—William Nicholls, Church-st., was charged with stealing a quan- tity of clover valued 6d. from a field owned by Henry Ackeriey on the 15th inst at Runcorn.—Prosecutor testi- fied to passing along Norman-road, Runcorn, at about 3.30 on Wednesday afternoon, the 15th, and finding the defendant in his field gathering a quantity of clover. When spoken to,defendant replied to witness "I am not doing any harm." Prosecutor told him he was damag- ing his clover and would have to answer for the offence at the court-house on the following Monday. Replying to the Superintendent prosecutor said he had recently lost a considerable amount of clover from his fields, and it was with a view to stopping these petty larcenies that he had proceeded against the present defendant. He had complained to the police about the same matter, and he understood that constables had been stationed near the spot for the purpose of securing offenders. At the time he found the defendant, the latter was putting the clover into a bag.—Superintendent AthertOn observed that the defendant had procured the clover for certain persons' rabbits and was given beer in return.—Fined Is. and 9s. costs.

div.head: NEW CATHOLIC SCHOOL CHAPEL AT
div.p: NEW CATHOLIC SCHOOL CHAPEL AT
ST. _HELENS.

HISTORICAL REMINISCENCES. On Sunday afternoon the Very Rev. Dean Walms- ley performed the ceremony of blessing the founda- tion stone of a new school chapel, which is being erected by the Catholics of the district at Thatto Heath, St.Helens. Amongst those present were the Revs. Father Pewell, Father Kenny, and Father Welsby, and Councillor James Burchall. J.P. The site of the building is in Ffeath-st.,and adjoins Scholes-lane. It will consist of a one-storey building,containing a large room 721 t. by 22ft., a class-room 221 ft. square, with proper appointments and ante-rooms. The large room will be divided by a screen. A chancel will be formed so that services may be held, but on week" days, while school is being held, it will be shut off. It is intended to use the building for boys only for the present,the smaller school in Elephant-lane being kept for the girls of the district. The cost will be ab,*ut £l,OOO. Messrs. Synott and Powell, of Liverpool, are the architects, and Mr. James Pilkington, of *Rainford, is the contractor.—The Rev. Dean Walmsley said the object of a school was higher and did greater work than any other public in- stitution, as it was intended to cultivate and train the highest faculties of children. In a Catholic school they did more than train the intellect, they formed the man- ners of children, and taught them good Christian be- haviour—how to live aright and do right. That new building was the beginning of a new Catholic mission in the neighbourhood.--The Rev.FatherKenny said through stress of circumstances they had no church in the dis- trict, but he was glad they had made a start that day, and they hoped in time to improve upon it by the charitable subscriptions of the people.—The Rev. Father Powell then gave a historical sketch of Catholicism in that neighbourhood. He said there was formerly a mission called " The Scholes " not far from that spot. It was begun in 1728 by the Rev. Wm. Molyneux, who in 1752 became Viscount Molyneux. He was not only a priest but a lord, and in 1752 became entitled to the lordly property of Croxteth Hall. He car- ried on at the Scholes until March, 1759, when he died at the ave of seventy-four years, and was buried' in Sef- ton Chapel. It was reported that between 1728 and 1759 he had a congregation of 300 gmwn-up. people. He was succeeded in the estate by his nephew, Charles William, who abandoned his religion, being terribly frightened by his wife, and was rewarded by George 111. with the title of Earl of Sefton. The priest who suc- ceeded the Rev. Wm. Molyneux (the viscount) was in many respects a greater man, and had a wonderful career. His name was Thomas Weldon, and he was a soldier,having served in continental wars and taken part in a number of battles near the Rhine. He was present on his horse when the Commander-in-Chief, Marshal Duke of Berwick, had his head taken off with a cannon ball. Weldon afterwards left the army and came to Eng- land, where he studied as a priest. It was recorded of him that when he lived at the Scholes he always kept his sword hung over the head of his bed. He was the last priest in Lancashire arrested for being a priest. Those were days when there was a heavy fine (£100) for saying mass,and the informant got the fine. A beggar in Elephant-lane brought Weldon before Mr. Hughes, of Sherdlev Hall, but Mr. Hughes was a gentleman, and said, "Mr. Weldon is a quiet and agreeable neighbour," and he refused to order the fine to DO paid. Father Wel- don died in 1786 at the age of eighty-one years, and was buried in Old Windleshaw Abbey. After him came the Rev. Peter Wesby, but he died in 1788, and he was also buried in Windleshaw. Then came the Rev. Nich@las Sewell, who founded Portico Chapel, a mile away, and there services had since been held. it had now been decided to have a new place at Thatto Heath, where the population had rapidly increased. He appealed for sup- port in aid of the building, and placed £5 in the offer- tory. The cost had to be defrayed by voluntary sub- scriptions, and nearly the whole of it had yet to be raised.

div.head: DETONATOR ACCIDENT AT ST.
div.p: DETONATOR ACCIDENT AT ST.
HELENS. A BOY SERIOUSLY INJURED.

Daniel Painter, aged thirteen, son of John Painter, a collier living at 116, Parr Stocks-road, St. Helens, found a detonator in a. field at the back of the house on Satur- day. and, not knowing its dangerous nature, he sent another boy for a hammer, intending to open it and see what it contained. As soon as the detonator was struck, it exploded, and the boy's right eye and left hand were seriously injured. He was taken to Dr. Gilleran's sur- gery, where he was attended to, and then taken home. It is feared he will lose the sight of the eye, and also por- tions of two fingers. The detonator was damp from ex- posure; otherwise it would have gone off with greater force, and probably with fatal effects. The detonators are used in collieries to fire roburite.

RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTER

The monthly meeting of this Committee was held in the Boardroom of he Town Hall, Runcorn' on Tuesday evening, the chair being occupied by Mr. William Handley, There were also present Messrs. S. Pope, T. Riley, and J. D. Jones, librarian and secretary. Mr. Jones presented the monthly cash account show- ing that the receipts had been £l6 11s. 6d., and the amount spent in new books £ll lls. 6d. The books issued from the Library during the 20 days it had been opened in July were classified as follows :—Lending de- partment: theology, 18 ; philosophy, 6; fiction, 1154; miscellaneous, 121; reference department, 22 making a total of 1502. Compared with the same month of last year these figures showed a decrease of 43 in the lending department •, and 13 in the reference department. The following gifts have been received :—From the Co-opera- tive Union Limited : " Annual report relating to Co- operation 1893-4"; from Mr. Reginald Potts, clerk to the Cheshire County Council, two copies of the " County Medical Cfficer's Report on health for the year 1893."— The Librarian's report and cash statement were adopted and the committee gave its sanction for the sum of £5O to be drawn on the Library Fund for the conduct of the building. The Librarian read a circular letter from the Libraries Association, asking for the names of any delegates whom the committee intended sendinc, to Belfast to attend the annual conference which would "take place shortly and would last for three days.—Mr. Pope thought that the town would derive more advantage from the venture if Mr. Jones was sent as the delegate of the committee. He, being an experienced man as a librarian, would be the most likely to seize upon those points more beneficial in practice to the public of Runcorn. He moved, there- fore, that Mr. Jones be appointed their representative and report the result of his visit to the next meeting of the committee.—Mr. T. Riley endorsed the remarks of Mr. Pope, and seconded the motion..—The Chairman also agreed with the opinion of Mr. Pope regarding the cap- ability of Mr. Jones in representing them.—Finally, the proposition was passed and it wasP included in the resolution that the librarian's expenses should not exceed £5.

Mr. Pope, on behalf of the Book Selection Committee, reported that they had selected, and recommended for purchase, 135 volumes.—The report was adopted. The committee, after inspecting the incandecent lamps placed in the reading-room by Mr. Branch as an experi- ment, decided to retain and purchase them. They like- wise resolved to ask him to place another of a similar nature in the magazine-room on trial, with a view to its being purchased, if approved. This cencluded the proceedings. div.head: TUSSLE.
div.p: A TUSSLE.

The best tussle between counsel and witness noted in Cornish records was that which used to be related by William Robert Hicks, formerly Governer of the County Lunatic Asylum at Bodmin and Prince of Cornish story- tellers. The occasion was a horse-jobbing case; and the witness was an ostler, and alleged that he had been at work alone in the stable-yard, when the man who had stolen the horse came in. Counsel in cross-examination tries to get at the exact words of the conversation that followed. Counsel: "You were in the stable-yard at work, and defendant came in? Well, what then ?" Witness: "When I zeed 'un come in, I sea, sea I, How about that horse?' And he zaid he'd give me ten shillings to zay nothing about 'un." Irounseli: "He did not say he'd give you ten shillings.'" Witness: "Yes a did; that's azackly what a did zay." Counsel: "He could not have said 'he;' he must have spoken in the first person." Witness: "No ; I was the first person that spoke. He comes into the yard, and J ses, sea I, How about that horse ?' and he zaid he give me ten shillings to zay nothing about 'un." Countiel : "But he did not speak in the third person." Witness: There was no third person present. Only he

an' me." Counsel: "Cannot you give me the exact words that he used ?" Witness: " Zo I have; I've a-told 'ee." Judge (interposing) : "Listen to me. He could not have said he would give you ten shillings to say nothing about it;' I will give you ten shillings." Witness: "He zaid nothing about your worship. If a zaid anything about your worship I never heerd 'un. And if there was another person present I never zeed 'un." The crose-examination at this point was abandoned.— W. A. Couch, in the "English Illustrated Magazine."

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
SATURDAY.

Many questions were-Cli—sC-u—s-s—ea-and a great deal of work got through at Saturday's sitting of the House of Commons. In Committee on the Estimates for the Civil Service and Revenue Departments several questions were asked on colonial affairs. Mr. SYDNEY BurroN, in reply, reproved Sir ELLIS BARTLETT, saying that his continual intervention in colonial matters tended to create difficul- ties which would not otherwise exist. There was considerable debate on subjects relating to railways, particularly with regard to the treatment of traders, the hours of workmen, and Sunday labour. Mr. BRYCE said all that the Board of Trade could do to make the life of the railway servant safer and happier would be done. With respect to the appointment of practical men as assistant inspectors.it had been decided to appoint two of that character.

div.head: MONDAY.
div.p: MONDAY.

In the House of Commons on Monday Mr. COBB asked whether a statement would be made as to the course the Government proposed to take with regard to the veto of the House of Lords. Sir WiLLIAIs HARCOURT said the Government intended to deal with the question, but he did not see how he could during the present session make any definite statement on the subject. Mr. SEXTON, who said Parliament had been rendered impotent so far as Ireland was concerned by the rejection of the Home Rule Bill and the Evicted Tenants Bill by the Lords, asked if the Government intended in the Queen's Speech at the opening of next session to define their policy on the question. Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT said the Govern- ment were impressed with the gravity of the question and hoped to be able to deal with it, but they were not Prepared to make a definite statement on the subject now. Mr. HERBERT GLADSTONE, replying to MT. EVERETT, who asked if a statue of OLIVER CROMWELL would be placed in the palace at Westminstsr, said no series of historical statues would be complete without one of OLIVER CROMWELL. He had no funds at his disposal to defray the cost of such a statue, but hoped to be able to induce the CHAricELLort of the EXCHEQUER to make the necessary provision in the Estimates next year. The House then went into Committee of Supply. On the vote for the salary of the Registrar General Mr. LLOYD-GEORGE took indignant exception to the Census returns and comments with regard to the Welsh people and their language. Other Welsh members followed in a similar strain. Mr. SHAW-LEFEVRE said he would in- quire into the matter, and make a statement on report that would no doubt be satisfactory to hon. members. The Irish votes were agreed to, after Mr. JOHN MORLEY had stated that the police had instructions to spare no effort to secure the protection of threatened tenants.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

Monday's sitting of the House of Commons was con- tinued till four o'clock on Tuesday morning, and was notable for a remarkable scene. Mr. SEXTON and Mr. DILLoN indignantly protested against the postponement of the report of Supply,and asserted that the real object was to drum up the Tory party to vote for the House of Lords. Obstructive resolutions were proposed and re- proaches cast on the Government, though Sir WILLIAM HARCOHRT said they meant to act with due regard to the infinite danger and mischief caused by the recent action of the House of Lords. When the House met again on Tuesday afternoon Sir G. TREVELYAN in reply to a question said the Govern- ment approved of the proposals contained in Sir CHAS. CAMERON'S bill for putting am end to the Established Church in Scotland and dealing with its endowments. ' The House then considered report of Supply, and on the supplementary vote for three millions for public edu- cation Mr.AcrAND made his statement. He said he was practically asking for fit millions, which was a large in- crease on last year ; four millions for day and evening schools, two millions for day schools for the fee grant, and half a million for expenses of administration and training colleges. A large part of the increase in the es- timate was due to the increase in the average attend- ance. With regard to the working of the Free Education Act, there was 4± millions of children on the registers as free scholars,and 890,000 still paid fees, of whom half a million did not pay more than a penny per week. The curriculum in these schools gave excellent choice. In some cases a great deal of cramming took place, but he hoped the new generation of teachers would introduce a more reasonable and effective method of teaching and training children. He pointed out the importance of an extension of the years of school life, said all must feel glad at the steady movement for intermediate education referred to teachers' pensions and the necessity for the better training of pupil teachers, intimated that he pro- posed to introduce a bill dealing with teachers' work, denied that he had opposed Church schools, and main- tained that there was much cause for hopefulness in the general progress of education. After discussion the vote for the Education Department was agreed to,and many other votes were passed.

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.

In the House of Commons on Wednesday Sir E. GREY, I replying to questions as to the development of Africa, said he had reason to believe that the British East Africa Company's claim in respect of the charter was so large that it would be impossible for the Government to make any acceptable offer. The Lords' amendments to the Railway and Canal Traffic Bill were agreed to, and a similar course was adopted with regard to the amendments to the Building Societies (No. 2) Bill. On the Lords' amendments to the Local Government (Scotland) Bill, Mr. KEAY moved to reinsert the pro- vision, struck out by the Lords, empowering parish councils to provide or acquire land for the erection of workmen's dwellings. Some discussion took place on the obstructive policy of the Lords, but Mr. KEAY'S amend- ment was rejected by a majority of 31, and the remain. ing Lords' amendments were agreed to. The House then proceeded with report of Supply. On the report of the vote for the REGISTRAR GENERAL's salary Mr. LLOYD-GEORGE moved to reduce it, asking if the REGISTRAR GENERAL was prepared to defend his report on the Welsh census or withdraw his imputation against the Welsh people. After other speeches the vote was passed, the Welsh members, through some misunder- standing, failing to challenge a division.
Albert Dews, a Wakefield iron-moulder, war executed at Leeds on Tuesday morning for poisoning his infant son. The culprit laboured under the delusion that the child was not his son.

div.head: SERIOUS CRISIS IN TELE GLASS
div.p: SERIOUS CRISIS IN TELE GLASS
TRADE.

THE POSITION OF THE LONDON AND MANCHESTER GLASS COMPANY. A large attended meeting of shareholders in tbe London and Manchester Plate Glass ComPany,whieh has extensive works at Ravenhead and Sutton, St. Helens, and employ about 1,200 hands, was held in the Memorial Hall Albert-square, Manchester, on Tuesday. Mr. Hawkins, of Manchester, presided, and there was a full board of directors. The state- ment ot accounts showing a deficit of many thousands of pounds on the year's working was submitted,and dis- cussion invited. Some of the shareholders expressed themselves thoroughly disappointed, and the tone of the meeting alternated between a dispirited feeling and ani- mated discussion. The directors stated that everything' was straightforward. It had been found impossible to make plate glass at a profit. A number of gentlemen from St. Helens were present,and Councillor Foote asked what were the future prospects of trade. This, however, could not be answered in a way to inspire much hope,sa it was generally known that the plate glass trade of the country was passing through a serious crisis. it Wasi ultimately decided to call an extraordinary genera meeting of the shareholders to be held at Manchester next week, when the accounts will be gone into and the affairs of the company fully considered. A St. Helens correspondent says the position of en London and Manchester Plate Glass Company has cause" the gravest apprehension in St. Helens, and there is con- siderable gloom over the districts in which the works are situated, and where the 1,200 hands reside. A notice was last week posted in the works to the effect that after the 23rd inst., the whole of the hands would be working on a days notice, but hopes were expressed that the company would be able to tide over the diffi" culty. It will be remembered that in 1888 the fircti were engaged in a struggle with their castinghall meth who had given notice for a 10,per cent. advance. Tile Sutton works were nearly wholly stopped for about ten weeks. and then an increase was given. In 18901 further labour disputes took place with the men at Ravenhead, land there was a prolonged stoppage there.. The maflage. ment stated that the state of trade did not warrant anY advance in wages, and as concessions had to be Made the position became a serious one. it is stated that the firm date their retrogression from that period. It is also well-known that for several years foreign competition has been so keen that English manufacturers of OW Iglass could not make for at the price which they bad sell. Five years ago something like 2s. Bd. was obtain per foot, whereas the price has latterly been about 15.. Again it is stated than an understanding with Continen- Ital manufacturers as to the price of glass has for Soule time been disregarded, and that in consequence the Eng- lish manufacturers, who had to pay their skilled work' men about 7s. or Bs. per day of ten hours, and six der] a week, could not complete with the foreigner who nat."' 3s. or 4s. a day of twelve hours, and seven days a week' It is a remarkable fact that the Ravenhead Works of Ow company rank amongst the oldest in England. They were erected in 1793, French workmen being employe' to introduce the industry. The Sutton Works of the company are of more recent date, but they were estate lished in the early part of the centuary. A few Yea'r! since large additional capital was raised, and new plep" and machinery were put down, in hopes of better der; ;- but from the report of the directors, "the latter daY6 have been worse than the first." It was stated on Thursday that the whole of the employes at the Ravenhead and Sutton Glassworks' St' Helens, belonging to the London and Manchester Plate glass Company, have been informed that both works WI be closed on Tuesday evening next, and their servic,e! at present will not be further required. Aboto 1,200 hands will be thrown idle. An extraordinari meeting of the shareholders will be held in Blanchester on Thursday next, and it is believed voluntary liquids: tion will be decided upon. It is believed in this distil that the stoppage, as far as Sutton is concerned, only be of a temporary character, and a resumption 01' probably take place there in a few wetks,

div.head: RAILWAY TIME TABLE.
div.p: RAILWAY TIME TABLE.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN

A great number of Warringtonians have gone to America during the past few years, and it is always a source of interest and pleasure to their fellow townsmen in the old country to hear of successes they have achieved in the New World. I notice that Mr. John Edward Whitley, son of Mr. James Whitley, shopkeeper, Stockton Heath, has been gaining honours and distinctions in that country. His success has been entirely due to his own energy and perseverance, for when he went across the Atlantic five years ago he had to maintain himself by laborious work. However.he bought a number of books, and attended a school in Chicago. He afterwards went to Drury College, Springfield, Mis- souri, where he has been for three years. He has gained numerous prizes and honours at the college, and has a very bright prospect before him. I con- gratulate Mr. Whitley upon the success ot his son.

Whilst referring to Warringtonians abroad, I may mention that I hate had placed in my hands a copy of a letter written from New Zealand by Mr. James S. Edelsten who left Warrington no fewer than forty-three years ago. The letter mentions that there has been a destructive flood in the" England of the antipodes" as New Zealand is sometimes called, but. tortunately Mr. Edelsten's property has not been damaged. lam told, too, that Mr. W. A. Edelsten, of Ealing Dean, London, son of Mr. W. J. Edelsten, late of Warring ton, was a passenger by the mail steamer "lonic" which sailed for New Zealand on the 10th inst.

No doubt a great many people will be interested to learn that the passage from one side of the Ship Canal to the other, over the lock gates at Latchford, is now open to the public. This is no doubt due to the action taken in the ix atter by the Daresbury Highway Board at their last meeting. Formerly, any person wishing to cross the Canal had either to avail himself of the Latchford swing bridge nearly a mile away,or cross by the ferry at Thelwall which is still further. Another reason for satisfaction is the much increased cleanliness of the water, the smell from which caused so many complaints a short time ago. At present the condition of the water is excellent, there being no smell whatever. Whether this is due to the recent heavy rains or some action by the Ship Canal Company I am un- able to say, but the result is none the less satisfac- tory. The traffic on the Canal has also very largely increased, seeing that at least double the number of vessels of all classes, pass up and down the Canal, compared with the traffic of four months ago. People taking their Sunday afternoon's walk along the Canal can hardly now, miss seeing at least one boat during the time of their promenade.

A strong effort is being made at Stockton Heath just now to raise funds for the purchase of a more suitable building to hold the meetings of the Church Institute in,during the forthcoming winter. A room at Patricroft fully furnished, capable of containing 400 persons, and built of corrugated iron, is to be had for £lOO. This building belongs to the Ship Canal Co., and during the time the navvies were employed,it was used as a mission room. Towards the £lOO Lady Greenall and Mr. John Crosfield have both contributed £2O. It is expected that it will not be long before the other £6O is forthcoming. The building being of corrugated iron it is expected that another £5O will, in addition to the £lOO, completely cover the re-erection of the building in Stockton Heath. The Church Institute was inaugurated in Stockton_lleath last year, and it has been very suc- cessful. When the new room is acquired it is con- fidently expected that a still greater success will be the result.
MERLIN.
WEEKLY REPORT ON TEE HEALTH- OF WARRINGTON. Week ending 11th August, 1894. During the week, which was the 32nd of the current year, the following births and deaths were registered Births.
Deaths. 20
Warrington 24 Latchford 4
Total 2B

The excess of births over deaths was 6. The death- rate from all causes was equal to 204 per 1,000, against 157 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 273 the corresponding week of last year. The death- rate from the seven chief zymot ic diseases was equal to 4.6 per 1,000, against 2* the average rate of the four previous weeks,and against 12.2 the corresponding week of 1893. The ages of mortality were- -0-1 1-5 5-15 15-25 25-60 60 up. 7 3 1 8 1 20 2 2

The deaths included-4 from diarrhcea, 1 from scarlet fever, 1 from phthisis,2 from premature birth, 3 from brain disease, 1 from heart disease, 1 from lung disease, 1 from poisoning, 2 from scalds. The following cases of infectious disease have been reported during the week :—Erysipelas 1 case, scarlet fever 1 case. METEOROLOGY. —The mean temperature was 594 Fah, and therefore 6.1 deg. lower than the preceding week. The maximum temperature 68 F., was recorded on the sth inst., and the minimum temperature 50 F., on the 11th inst. _ _
The rainfall measured .63 inch. The general direction was S.W., the reading of the Anemometer denoting 1.055 miles.
JOHN H. GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health. IMPORTANT TO FURNITURE REMOVERS.

A WARRINGTON MAN FINED.. A ease was before the Warrington magistrates last Friday morning, in which Thomas Archer, of Catherine-street, who carries on a coal business and is also a furniture remover, was tharged with hav- ing on the 11th in st.,wilfully and unlawfully aided and abetted in fraudulently removing goods with intent to defraud the landlord of the payment of his rent. Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, who prosecuted on behalf of the complainant, Mr. Bostock, Wilderspool, stated that proceedings were takem in order to stop small contrac- tors from fraudulently assisting persons tz remove their goods during the night. A person named topford who tenanted a house from the complainant at Wellfield-st., owed Mr. Bostock 193. for arrears of rent, and laet Monday week, Mr. Bostock, jun., found that all the furniture had been removed and the house tenantless. The defendant removed the furniture to his own yard early on Saturday morning. He kept it there two hours, and sent for A London and North Western Railway Company's lurry to take it to the station. The furniture was labelled "G. Jones, Wolverhampton," but the tenant had given his name as Stopford. The defendant must have known that some fraud was going on, or why should he have taken the furniture to his own yard instead of the railway station? Mr. Bostock, junr., went to seethe defendant about the matter and in reply to some questions, he- ad- mitted that he knew that there was some/rent owing,but would not give a satisfactory answer as to whether he asked to see the rent book. The complainant had !seen unable to trace Stopford.—Mrs. E. Schule, 18, Percy- street, stated that she was getting up on Saturday morning at 5.30, when on looking through the window she saw the defendant driving a horse and lurry containing furniture past their house. The fur- niture was la'oelled.—Stephen Smith, 12, Wellfield-st., stated that he got up at 5.15 to go to his work when he saw a lurry being loaded with furniture from Stopford's house. The defendant was in charge of the horse.—P.C. Wood also spoke as to seeing the defendant in charge of the lurry in Wellfield-st.—John Stout, carter, in the em- ploy of the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany said he received instructions from the foreman to go to Mr. Archer's yard in Catherine-st. for some furni- ture. He arrived there a little after eight o'clock. The furniture was on the defendant's lurry and a woman,and a son of the defendant, helped him to transfer it to his lurry. The defendant's lurry was standing opposite a stable.—Mr. J. Bostoe.k stated that the furniture re- moved from Stopford's house, Wellfield-st., was worth about £B. On the Monday morning he was surprised tufincl; the house empty as he had not received any notice. Wit- ness went to the defendant who acknowledged that he removed tlierfurnitute at four o'clock. also stated that he was aware that rent was owing. The back door, of the house had been. left open, --Nineteen shillings. „were owing for rent. —The defendant's defence was that. -when he got borne- from work about 5.30. a.m. on Sat-, r,orday morning,he was told that the horse and lurry had , been taken to Wellfield-street. •His wife had taken the -order whilst 'he was at 'Work. On going to Wellfield- street he found the lorry- -loaded, and all he did was to bring itr.to Catherine-street.. IT is said that the agitation against Lynching the lynching of nearoes in the Horrors. Southern States of America which has been started in England, and in support of which a meeting was held in Warrington on Mon- day evening, is beginning to have a salutary effect. Public opinion even in the northern States has been singularly apathetic upon this subject, but it is being aroused. Miss IDA B. WELLS, the able and spirited coloured lady who has stepped for- ward as the champion of her race, has now re- turned to the United States and has been success- ful in establishing anti-lynching societies. The pl:rt ;CZ")

latest report must, we shouN think, even give the white Southerners sornethinq to think seriously about. They have for years tolerated andfindeed, encouraged and defended lynching,but the demon of lawlessness once invoked at length turns and rends those who have profited by its excesses. 11.°11 cannot indulge in the pastime of flaying and burn ing live negroes without in the eqd blotting ont all feelings of pity and all regard for the sacred- ness of human life. Where, for instance, but fro could m a country in which Judge Lynch holds swaY we expect to hear of such a story as the followinW ' "A horrible discovery has been made in the W°c'clil in Clay county,Kentuckv, by a number of lumber" men who were engaged in felling timber. 111 remote part of the bush they found a Pill woman of prepossessing appearance, stripped ° her clothing, and crucified on a wooden croam Large nails were driven through her hands and feet, and the marks on her body indicated that she had been otherwise maltreated. She had aid" ently been left in her terrible plight for several hours, and when found she was almost lifeless. It has been ascertained that the perpetrators of the fiendish outrage were several other women, the instigator being prompted by motives of jealoosY• When even the women have been so brutalised bY the evil example set them the time has snrelY come for a revolt of all the best elements society against the cruel and barbarous practice 01 lynching.

THERE is always some interesting Post Office • Statistics, information to be obtained fr°l3l tie annual report of the. Postgiks" TER GENERAL. Mr. ARNOLD MORLEY'S departinch deals with large figures. During the twelve months ending with the end of March this year there were transmitted through the Post Of6ce 1,800,000,000 letters, 28,00 0,000 post cardsr 574,000,000 circulars and samples, and 164,000°, newspapers. These figures are almost too Os' for comprehension. Looked at in another WhY: they show that if the p-mtmen had made an eciln' distribution amongst the whole pop ulation a the letters and other missives entrusted to them each person would have received 47 letters, 63; Pcsfr cards, 14-1 books and circulars, and 44 newspaPers' As a matter of fact, however, commercial centres. naturally absorb the bulc of the correspo. ndei4ce• Nearly thirty per cent. of all the F°sti Office missives are delivered in the Post'

area of London alone. Scotland received little over nine per cent., and Irelm.d only 5 9 Per cent. In the course of the year no fewer than 6,000,000 letters and 930,000 postcards were rO. turned through the Dead Letter Office. it i 5, noteworthy, too, that 34,000 letters were posteti without any address whatever, and of these contained cash, cash, bills, or cheques to the value 0` p 4,000. The Express Messenger Service is, it Dl' reported, increasing in usefulness, and in 000 instance at least it performed a service which WO not contemplated by its originators. A young woman lost her way in London, and fortunatelY for herself she inquired at the nearest post dace' The resourceful officials there at mice grasped the situation, and undertook upon the young woMellr paying threepence as " postage " to convey he by special messenger to her destination.

MITCHELL, M.A., vicar ° St. Michael's, Burtonwood. Referring to the (10° of the late SIR GILEgitT GREENALL and tile subsequent pulpit references at the local church° there are the following remarks in the Aug-- number : "Our local brewer millionaire, Sir Gilbert Gree°: all, has departed this life in a good old Mkt; Requiescat in pace! The Warrington Church pt% pits had mnch to say about the Brewer Magnate 0,4 the Sunday following his decease. But it vvas s'6l„ir poor weak stuff Nothing was said about the Po:, man's soul. But much wit, said about his The sermons really amounted to the grateful 'cis. knowledgement of benefactions. The charge tos not so long ago in "The ‘Varrinaton that the Warrington Churches were largely subshe dized by the brewers seemed t o be proven out of mouths of the preachers themselves ; proven UP '0 the hilt. But much was said ab°ll his money."

It is in relation to t' Parish Councils which are soon to be elect d. e following extract is, as will be seen, well sPle with a number of queries which every " villgero —whether he belong to Buttonwood, Stockt°lo Heath, Penketh, Padgate, or elsewhere—Would well to consider. tbe "is the Parish Council to be the Council Of people? Do our artisans,colliers,and labourers L'ocl eoop to remain inactive? Are they willing to be sclue out of the Village Parliament.? ,SUCCESS OF A RUNCORN STUDENT. At the recent examination keld inconnection with the London Victoria College of Music, at the Liverpool centre Miss Warburt )n, daughter of Mr. S. E. Warburton Runcorn passed in piauolorte playing with honours,and was specially commended by the examiner Mr. I. H. L.-wis Muc. Doc. D.C.L. Miss Warburton was prepared for the examination by Mr. S. Wadsworth F.C.C.G. Liverpool. TEE SUCCESSES OF A RUNCORN HORSE BREEDER. Mr. S. B. Chadwick, J.P., of Crofton Lodge, Higher Runcorn,' n gentleman generally known to be a success- fed breeder of horses, an occupaion to which he devotes the major portion of his time and attention, met with several worthy recognitions at the Lancaster Agrickl- tural Society's show on Wednesday, In the agricultural horses section, open to the United Kingdom he secured a second prize fora two year-old filv; whilst first priz. were awarded. him in the .sections for three year old geldings ;...brood mare which had produced a filly in 1894, anytage ; and pair of draught horses in gear, three years old "And upwards. -COLLIER'S -BREAD is the best money Can buy.—Advt.

../...PICNIC FROM RUNCORN TO OVERTON, On Wednesday afternoon nearly 200 scholars, teachers hnd friends, connected with tire Sunday School of the Eilesmere-4reet United Methodist Free Church,Runcorn, travelled 67y special train to Frodsham and proceeded from thence to Overton Hills for their annual outing. They wereloCiitripariled by Mr. Gandy, superintendent; Messrs. John Holford and Walter Gandy, secretaries ; White, trehAtirer ; , and the Rev. J. Stafford, newly- appointedfpastot. The usual programme of amusements was gone titrosigh, after which tea was served and enjnyed. The rettrn journey was completed by about eight o'clotiks- a very pleasant afternoon having been spent. 4-6 • - - R/PIaORN SCHOOL CHILDREN'S OUTING. Betweestithree and .four hundred children connected with the Holy Trinity Church Sunday School, with their teachers and friends, had a pleasant sail down the canal to Preston'Zrear, on Wednesday, on the occasion of the annual 011 y rig: A large boat was lent by Mr. S. Taylor, J.P.,, anct, a, smaller one and horses by Mr. Jonathan Horsifield7, The school drum and fife band attended, and played- a:: programme of excellent music en route. There were also of the party the Rev. Dr. and Mrs. Pre- ston, the Mfsies Preston and Tyrie, the Rev. A. and Mrs. Bartram, Mrs: Meadowcroft, Mes srs. Westbrooke' Han- kinsOn, Divers games were indulged in, arid sub- sequently Asn..ersjoyable tea' was eartaken of. More sports tookeplace until finally, the party had to return, Runcorn being.. reach ed quite safely at about eight o'cloOk. . A CHILD :NARROWLY. ESCAPES DR OWNING AT RUNCORN. , Whilst a narrow, bAt was proceeding on Wednesday afternsion'aleng the Bridgewater Canal at Runcorn to- wards the crane in,Halton-road a child was seen to fall from it into the twat'er. A Man named George Dutton, of Pennqigton's-row,seeing the child in the water ran to- wards the bank and immediately jumped in to render assistanee: -By the time he reached tire boat, however, the fatherbf the little one bad succeeded in rescuing it from the water and lifting it upon deck. Tne occur- rence created considerable excitement in the locality and though Dutton was not instrumental in rendering assist- ance yet he deserves much praise for his generous action in so readily entering the water. The child soon re- covered from the dip and is now none the worse for the accident. A RUNCORN BOATMAN'S SUDDEN DEATH. An inquest was held at Manchester on Wednesday, relating to the sudden demise of Richard Harrison, boat- man, employed by Messrs. Bate and Co., of Runcorn. From the evidence adduced it is apparent that the deceased, 'who was about 40 years of age and resided at 29, Albert-Street, Runcorn, Lad been for sometime past in declining health. He left his lodgings on Monday night to undertake a journey to Manchester on his fiat. Having completed the journey at about two o'clock the next morning he went to bed, but was suddenly taken ill. A doctor was summoned and on his arrival Harrison was found to be much worse. The medical gentleman treated him, but all his skill proved of no avail, as Harri- son, in a c oniparatively short time, sank and expired.— The jury returned a verdict of " Death from natural causes."—Mr. William Shaw, missionary, of Runcorn, attended the inquiry and made all arr angements for the conveyance of the body to Runcorn on behalf of the relatives of the deceased. The remains will be interred this (Friday) afternoon, in Runcorn Cemetery. ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH, RUNCORN. The choir and teachers' annual picnic took place on Tuesday lad to Caergwrle. The party travelled by the L. and N. W. and C.L.C. Company's route, reserved compartments being provided by the latter Company for their convenience. Immediately on arrival at Bridge End Station the party proceeded some distance along the .Rossett-road, from whence, could be seen, Eaton Hall, Beeston Castle, Rossett, Wrexham, Brymbo, Summerhill, Gwersyllt, &c. Then, returning to the village they partook of luncheon. The old ruins of Caergwrle Castle were next visited, from the top of which there is a good view of the surrounding country. gter engaging In various games and amusements for some time. The party divided, one portion going for a drive, and the other, accompanied by a native guide in the person of Mr. M. Thomas, decided to attempt the ascent of Hope Mountain, and were well repaid for the effort, as; from the summit a still more extensive view was obtained, the wide range and variety of scenery being much appreciated. It is said that nine counties may be seen from this position on a clear day. At 5.0 p.m. tea was served, for which the exercise and the fresh mountain air had well prepared them, and therefore full justice was done to the good things provided. The catering by Mrs. Edwards, and the attention given by Miss Sabina Edwards and her staff of waitresses gave .general satisfaction. The return journey was com- menced at seven p.m., and after spending some time looking round Chester the party arrived home at 10.15 p.m., having tad a very pleasant and enjoyable day. Mr. James Kirkham, superintendent; Mr. J. E. Warbur- ton, choir master; Mr. James Richardson, organist; and Mr. R. W. Harrop accompanied the picnic.

TOUR OF THE RUNCORN Mn RSI.Y MISSION BAND. The members ot the drum and fife bind connected with the Runcorn Branch of the Mersey Mission to Sea- men, completed their week's tour on Saturday evening, when they all reached Runcorn in sate ty and apparently much improved by their excursion. The boat in which the youths travelled had been fitted throughout in a most comfortable manner, and was under the charge of Captain Thomas Phillips. Leaving the Bottom Locks on the Bridgewater Canal early on Monday morning, they had sailed first to Lymna, wherein the evening an open air cencert was given in the Market-square. The night ha ving been spent here, the tourists resumed their voyage along the canal in the morning through Patri- croft to Eccles, where another open air concert was given and another night passed. The following day a concert was given at Bedford Leigh,and the next morn- ing a move was made for Wigan. Here a concert tok place in the evening in the Market-square, and the next morning the journey was again continued. Sale was the stopping place on Thursday night, and an open air concert was held here also. Mr. Edison, the missionary for this district, delivered an address, dealing in the course of his rernarks,with the object, of the Mission,and appealing to those assembled for assistance. The next day (Saturday) the route lay towards home via Lymm. Having again visited that locality a pleasant sail was experienced to Runcorn, where, at about six o'clock, the boat re-entered the Botuom Locks. Mr. Wm. Shaw, missionary, and Mr. Wm. Byfield, drum major, both ac- companied the band, and in each of the places named the former gentleman gave addressos explanatory of the Mission and the work which it was zarryi ng on. The tour proved highly successful, and the instrumentalists were often complimented upon their musical talent, whilst performing in the towns mentioned. The pro- ceeds were in aid of the band funds. WIRRAL AND BIRKENHEAD AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY. We would again remind our readers that the entries for the 52nd annual show of this Society positively close to-day, so that no time should be lost by intending exhibitors in sending in their entries. So far they have been" disgustingly poor," in many classes there is not a single entry. Any exhibitor not having received a schedule, can have one on application to the Secretary. CAgiS AT THE OCCASIONAL COURT. - - -

At the Warrington Occasional Court on Monday, before Mr. Tinsley, Martin Higgins was fined 2s. 6d. and costs, or seven days' imprisonment in default for being drunk at Rixton on Sunday, 19::h inst. Pk. Ryder proved the case.—David Carrie was charged with being a deserter from the Royal Navy The prisoner had walked from London to Golborne, and gave himself up to the police at the latter place He was remanded tor inquiries, and P.C. Simpson, who proved the case, was granted the usual re- ward.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 25, 1894. ____

APPOINTAIRNT FOR MR. W. ALLEN. Mr. Walter Allen, who occupies the position of second master of the Hamilton-street Practising Schools, Warrington, has been selected headmaster of the St. Paul's Schools, Hampstead, near Birming- ham. He will commence his duties next month. ST. MARY'S R.C. CHTJRCH, LATCHFORD. On Sunday the annual sermons in aid of the schools were preached at St. Mary's Catholic Chapel, Latchford, by the Very Rev. Father Bernard, 0.5.F.C., superior of the monastery at Pantasaph. Both morning ana evening services were well attended.

A FUTILE EXPERIMENT. The experiment recently tried by the Board of Guardians of dressing the children of the Industrial Schools in clothing of various patterns has been abandoned, and on Sunday morning th, y attended the Padgate Church attired, the boys in cord suits and the girls in blue serge frocks.

WESLEYAN SERMONS AT MARTINSCROFT. The annual chapta sermons were preached on Sunday by Mr. Walter Brougb, of Sankey Bridges. Special and appropriate mu.ic was creditably ren- dered by the choir. Both the afternoon and even- ing services were well attended, although the weather was most unfavourable.

APPOINTMENT OF A. WOOLSTON CLERGYMAN. The Rev. Father T. Alyerscough, of Woolston- with-Sfartinscroft, has been appointed to the new mission at Longton, between Southport and Preston. The rev, gentleman, who has been at Woolston some years, has endeared himself not only to his congregation but to all sects and creeds, and his removal will be greatly regretted.
ALL HOUSEHOLD LINEN', hem-ned and marked free of charge.—J. and W. Durros, Smkey-st., Warrinton.—Advt.

EXCURSION TO BUXTON. On Saturday the men employed in the engineering department of the Cheshire Lines Railway had their annual excursion, the place selected this year being Buxton. There were four special trains placed at the disposal of the excursionists, one conveying the Warrington contingent, which numbered absut 500, and the others starting from Southport, Chester,and other places. Unfortunately, the weather was not fine, and the outing accordingly did not prove as enjoyable as one might wish.

PRESENTATION TO A COLOURED PREACHER. • On Saturday evening a presentation was made to the Rev. P. T. Stanford, a coloured preacher, in the Temperance Hall. Buttermarket-street. Tile present Was a glass jug, the workmanship of Mr. J. Rigby, secretary of the Workingmen's Temperance Mission. On it were elegantly engraved portraits of Mr. Stanford and the Rev. J. Wesley, and the following inscription :—" Presented to the Rev. Peter Stan- ford as a token of their esteem by the trustees of the Workingmen's Gospel Temperance Mission, Warrington, August, 1894." Mr. J. Drury and Mr. R. Storey having spoken in high terms of the ser- vices rendered by Mr. Stanford, the rev, gentleman suitably replied, and the proceedings terminated.
NEWTON-LE- W ILLOWS AND DISTRICT HORTICUL-

TURAL SOCIETY. The ninth annual exnihition of this society will be held to-day (Saturday). The judges report upon the seven cottage gardens entered is : " Very clean considering the weather, full of good stuff, alto- gether very satisfactory. Very few points dividing the winners. Ist, Mr. W. Boardman, Vulcan; 2nd, Mr. T. Howard, Ashton-road; 3rd, Mr. T. Rutter, Winwick.

ODDFELLOWS DEMONSTRATION AT COLLINS GREEN. The anniverz•ary of the St. Helens district Far- mers Refuge Lodge of Oddfellows, Collins Green, took place on Saturday afternoon, A procession was formed at the lodge, Pear Tree Inn, and pro- ceeded by the Earlestown brass band, visited the residences of Messrs. Forshaw and Jackson, Mrs. Wilson, and the Vicarage, returning to the lodge, which was reached about 5 o'clock. About 60 afterwards sat down to a well served dinner, which was much enjoyed. and reflected credit upon the host and hostess. After dinner the table was cleared and the after proceedings were presided over by Dr. Nalentine, the lodge surgeon; P.P.G.M. Bro. Gilmour, of the Loyal Viaduct Lodge, occupying the vice-chair. The Chairman in a brief speech, dwelt on the necessity of all young men joining some such society as that, and making provision for old age. The usual loyal toasts were given, and duly responded to. The toast "Prosperity to the Farmer's Refuge Lodge," was responded to by Mr. Wm. Seph ton, secretary, who said that the Farmer's Refuge Lodge was one of the oldest lodges in the district, and was opened in 1832. The lodge of which he was proud to be the secretary, at one time was on the point of dissolution, and would have been dissolved, but the district came to their relief, and made' them a grant of ~EBO, which encour- aged the members to make another effort, and they succeeded in placing the lodge on a proper footing and it is now improving yearly. The finances showed a balance of £l5O in hand, with a roll of 84 members, and 12 for initiation. A vote of thanks was,at the close, accorded the Chairman.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

On Tuesday afternoon the fortnightly meeting of the, above Board was held at the Dutton workhouse, under the chairmanship of Mr. John Mclntyre. There were also present Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, Dr. Gastaldi, and J. Hanby, Messrs. J. M. Williams, W. Whitlow, H. E.Heywood, James Whitlow, J. Know- les, J. Weir, E. Aaron, J. Brandreth, S. Taylor, E., A. R. Norman, A:Broome, D. H. Jones, S.Yarwood, T. Lewis, C. T. Whitley, John Ashton, clerk, and George Ashton, deputy-clerk. A MEDICAL OFFICER'S DEPUTY.

A letter was read from Dr. H. E. Bower, medical officer for. the Ruclworth district, intimating that Dr. 'F. Starkey Smith, of Warrington, had consented to act as his deputy.—The Hoard approved of the selection. REPORT OF THE AUDITORS.

The Clerk produced the certificate of the auditors who had just completed the audit of the Union books, and which stated that everything was correct and satisfac- tory. THE ENLARGEMENT OF THE UNION BOUNDARY.

An order was read by the Clerk from the Cheshire County Council, stating that the townships of Grappen- hall, Latchford-Without, and Thelwall had been trans- ferred to the Runcorn Union. PROPOSED IMPROVED DINING ARRANGEMENTS

Mr. S. Woodward, in the absence of the Chairman of the Committee, who had considered the above question, moved that a general servant be appointed to assist the matron in her duties. The committee had decided upon this ceurse after having made exhaustive enquiries in tne progress of which they found that Mrs. Cunnah was overtaxed both with responsibility and work. The movement had not arisen through any complaint on the part of the matron or anyone else, but the committee, in endeavouring to improve the present dining arrange- ments,had found these facts. The work devolving upon the matron had increased and there was not a woman in the house who could relieve her with advantage.—Mr. Yarwood moved an amendment to the effect that no servant be employed.—Mr. Whitlow seconded and expressed the opinion that there were females in the house who could be trained to be domestin servants and render whatever assistance was required.—After some discussion-Mr. C. T. Whitley proposed a second amend- ment that the quests be deferred for the new council who would take nffi 'e probably in about four months. It would only be handicapping the coming council to pass resolutions of this nature now.—Mr. Yarwood fell in with this motion and withdrew his amendment in favour of answer to the Rev. J. Hanby, Mr. W. Whitlow said the employing of such a domestic would incur an annual expense ot quite £4o.—Eventually Mr. Whitley's amendment was put and carried by a large majority.

div.head: LADIES VISITING COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE LADIES VISITING COMMITTEE.

The report of this committee was read, stating that after a two hour's inspection of the house recently, they had found everything in a satisfactory condition.—Mr. Heywood stated that as there was a vacancy on this committee he had pleasure in submitting the name of Mrs. C. T. Whitley, of Stretton, to fill it. That lady would prove, he was sure, a very useful member.—The name was accepted, and the proceedings terminated.

div.p: lIELSBY.

THE PROPOSED WATER STJPPLY.-At the fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, held on Tuesday attern,on at the Workhouse, Dutton, Mr. John Mclntyre in the chair, a letter was read by the Clerk from Mr. G. C. Taylor, of Helsby, who therein asked the Authority if they would return to him the plans prepared by Mr. Radford respecting the proposed water snpply. They were probably of no use to the Authority but he should find them useful himself.— After some discussion the Authority decided to retain possession of the plans.

PAINFULLY SUDDEN DEATH OF A HEMET GENTLEMAN.— Mr. Mark Barbritige Smith, of Flelsby, a well-known railway contractor, expired suddenly on a platform of the Chester General Railway Station on Friday night. The deceased gentleman, who was 57 years of age was returning home from London, with his wife, and was crossing from one platform to another when he suddenly fell to the ground dead. Upon examination by a medi- cal practitioner it was announced that death had been brought about by heart disease from which Mr. Smith had been a sufferer. l-J
