div.head: CHIEF CONSTABLE'S REPORT.
div.p: THE CHIEF CONSTABLE'S REPORT.

The following is the report of the Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) presented to the magistrates on Thurs- day :—" To the Worshipful the justices assembled at. the annual licensing meetings of the borough of Warrington, August '23rd and 24th, 1894. Gentle- men,-1 have the honour to lay before you my twenty-ninth annual return relative to the Brewster Sessions. The information and tablee, herein submitted show the number of licensed victuallers and beerhouse keepers proceeded against since the last Brewster Sessions, the number of persons proceeded against for drunkenness, numbers convicted and discharged ; the number of licensed victuallers, beerhouse keepers, and off-license holders in the borough, and the number of such licenses which have been transferred dining the year. The appLcations are :—On Thursday, August 23rd, 1894, one for a full alehouse,' The Borough Arms,' situate at the junction of Irlam and Mersey-streets, now occupied as a beer- house by Mrs. Elizabeth Riley ; and one to sell wine to be consumed oal or off the premises, the occupier of which, Benjamin Kenyon, is the holder of a beerhouse license, The Green Man,' situate in Green-street. The other applications are for the renewal of existing licenses. On Friday, the 24th, there will be three new applications (two for public music and one for public music and dancing), and applications for the renewal of existing music and dancing licenses. The transfers have been to 18 licensed victuallers, four beer- house keepers, and ten off-license holders. The diminution in the numbers proceeded against for h t the drunkenness this year may he accounted e extreme badness of trade and the exodus of the Slip Canal hands from Warrington and the district since the canal was completed and opened, the lodging-houses which took these men and their families in being now almost depopulated. The number of license houses in the borough is :—Licensed victuallers, 87 ; beerhouse keepers, 45; and off-license holders, 71 ; total, 206. I may here say that there was the same number of deensed victuallers in the borough in 1824, with a population of probably 14,000, as there is now with a population of 56,000 or thereabouts, which is four times greater than in 1824. Efforts are being made to carry out the licensing laws strictly and impar- tially, and the holders of licences are very careful as to how they c. nduct their business.—See table of drunken- ness during last ten vears.—Thirty seven full alehouses and beerhouses and twelve other public rooms were licensed for music (total forty-nine) for the last twelve months, during which time there was no report against any of them. 'Professionals are not employed at public or beerhouses licensed for music." Then follows a table giving the number of licensed victuailers, beerhouse keepers, and shorkeepers, with the number summoned and convicted, at well as the number of persons charged with drunkenness and convicted or discharged. The figures for 1893 and 1894 are as follows :-1893, licensed victuallers 87, convicted three, discharged one ; beer- house keepers, 45, one discharged, shopkeepers, 72, one convicted; persons charged with drunkenness,cmtivictetl, males 349, females 142; discharged, males 54, females 61, total 606 ; 1894, licensed victuallers 87, convicted three; beerhouse keepers, 45, discharged two ' • shop- keepers 74, two convicted ; persons charged withdrunk- enness, convicted, males 308, females 85 ; discharged, males 30, females 35, total 458. The figures for 1894 show the drunkenness between July 31st, 1893, and August Ist, 1894.
REPORT OF THE SUB-COMMITTEE.

The report of the sub-committee appointed by the justices to consiler alterations to licensed prembes is as follows:—" The sub-committee appointed to confer with the owners of the licensed houses re- ferred to in the Chief Constable's report of last year have to report: That they have held ten sittings, and dealt with 53 houses; 42 of these have been altered in accordance with the requirements of the law, five others will be altered IP r dealt with by the Bench at the next annual licensing sessions, and others are more or less altered, but in such an unsatisfactory way that they do not comply with the conditions re- quired; and your sub-committee recommends that these cases be adjourned to give the owners time to complete the alterations agreed upon in a satisfact_ry manner, and, failing this, we recommend that the license be not renewed, on the ground that proper poiice supervision is impossible. We cannit commend t highly the spirit in which your committee have been met by the owners and occupiers. fa almost every case the greatest wil- lingness has been shown to make the neces=ary altera- tions, and to carry out any suggestions that had been made to them. Arising out of the examination of these houses, we must express the opinion that many of them are structurally unfit for the he,althy accommodation of large numbers of people, and that either they should be re-built altogether or such further alterations made as will give greater air-space and light and more comfort- able accommodation to these frequenting them.—JonN FAIRCLOUGH (chairman) F. Mornms, R. W. FIII.NCOMB, T. H. SUTTON, W. PIERPOINT, H. ROBERTS."

div.head: OBJECTIONS TO LICENSES, THE WOOLPACE.
div.p: OBJECTIONS TO LICENSES, THE WOOLPACE.

Upon Mr. WHITE (the magistrates' clerk) asking Mr. Hunt (chief constable) if he had any objections to any licesses, Mr. HUNT in reply said that he had not a single objection to make against any license that morning. It was his misfortune, however, to ask their worships to be good enough to adjourn the licence in the case of the " Woolpack." Most unfortunately, a man went there the other night at about eleven o'clock and it was found necessary to eject him. He was seen to fall on the ground heavily, and was found by a policeman to be unconscious. The man was at once conveyed to the Infirmary, and on Sunday morning he died, having been unconscious all the time. An inquest had been held and very little evidence had been taken, and the proceedings had been adjourned until Friday. He would theretore ask that the case be taken at the adjourned licensing day. Mr. ARTHUR BROWNE objected to the adjournment,as he said that even admitting the worst, the charge of manslaughter would not come before November, and therefore, the magistrates would not be any nearer at the adjourned licensing day than they were at present. The magistrates decided to reserve their decision. THE SWAN INN.

Mr. WHITE then asked if there were any objections to other licences, whereupon Mr. Alfred T. Davies,solicitor. Liverpool, said that he appeared on behalf of several in- habitants viz., Mr. Arthur Henry Lee, 22, Brick-street, the Rev. John Yonge, Mr. Samuel B Sringer, Wilder- spool Causeway, Rev. D W. Roberts, Rev.J.Kirtlan,Rev. J. W. Varies', Rev. W. H. Drummond, and the Rev. E.T. Reed, to object to the licences of the Swan, Shak .speare, Hop Pole, Pelican, and Gladstone Arms. Mr.Mulliolland, barrister, Liverpool, instructed by Mr.A. Browne, Mr.R. Dobson, and Mr. R. Davies, appeared for the first four public-houses. Mr. DAVIES, in opening the case against the Swan, said that the inhabitants of the. town for whom he appeared exercised their statutory right in objecting to certain licenses. The objections to the Swan Inn were several. The character and interests of the neighbour- hood and locality in which the licensed premises were situated did not require the license. The licenses held in the neighbourhood allowed undue facilities for drink- ing. There was also not sufficient police supervision. The sanitary convenience attached to the premises were also objectionable. Another reason for objection was that the house had not been well conducted as was shown that James Cheadle who had formerly kept the house had been fined £5 and costs for supplying two policemen with liquor while on duty. As to the objec- tion that it was not needed he did not think that any- one could be prcud of the state of the town near the Swan. He did not think that the magistrates would recreate it to-day if they had the power and if they were going to grant the licenses to a town free from them. The proportion of licensed houses in Warrington was some- thing like one in 25. When they considered that that included the whole of the town, it must be remem- bered that in the congested area ef the town there were far more than was reasonably required. Locking at the plan produced they would see that the area adjoin- ing the Swan was one in which he thought that their worships were entitled te do something to rectify the existing state of affairs, and take a judicial note of the facts. There was an important fact in regard to the place in question as the house was not uuder police supervision owing to the fact that it had not a front to the public street. It was entirely set in the middle and between some blocks of building. It was approached by two tunnelled passages which pre- vented the police from having a proper control over the house. At the end of the tunnelled passage was a most objectionable urinal which had to be passed to get to the house. In addition to this there had been a most serious charge against the former licensee of the house which had resulted in a fine of £5 and costs and the license being endorsed. There could have been no possibility of mistake in regard to this case. There were undoubtedly hardships when the publican could not always dctect drunkenness in his house. In this case, however, the two constables were in uniform with their armlets on when they were served. It was also proved that the landlord saw the constables. It might be said that a new tenant had taken the license. But that tenant knew that there was a blot on the license when he took it, and therefore he had no right to complain about it. It might also be said that the license had been out for a long time, but if tile license had outgrown its use- fulness and failed to keep up with modern requirements then that was a reason why it should be refused.

THOMAS COOK, architect, and surveyor, Liverpool, and councillor in the Birkenhead Town Council,said that he had had forty years' experience. He proceeded to discribe the various approaches to the Swan Inn. Be did not consider that the house fulfilled the requirements of the Sanitary laws. Mr. MULHOLLAND said he would like to know why the gentlemen whose names had been mentioned as objec- tors had not been called to state their groundF, of objec- tion to the licences. He had no evidence whatever to answer as the only evidence brought forward was that of an architect, unsupported by further evidence. Councillor ROBERTS: There are the plans. Mr. MuLaoLLAND : The plans of Warrington had been male years ago, and therefore there is nothing fresh in that

' Alderman SUTTON: I suggest that the other magis- trates should endeavour to bottle their private personal feelings until we have heard everything. Councillor ROBERTS protested against Alderman Sutton's remarks, and said that he had come there with- out prejudice to hear the evidence. Mr. MULHOLLAND said that it was unusual for magis- trates to express any opinion before the case had been gone fully into. Councill,r ROBERTS said that he had not expressed any opinion whatever, and he could not let Mr. MullWland's statement go uncorrected.

Mr. MULHOLLAND continuing said that it was extra- ordinary ti,at an architect should be brought from Liver- pool to prove that there was not proper police super- vision. He thought that the Warrington police_ knew their own business. Why did not Mr. Davies call the Chief Constable to prove that there was no proper police supervision? With regard to the conviction which had been inflicted upon Cheadle the former tenant of the house, a new tenant had been engaged since then. This case had been the only one against the house, and therefore he thought that it was not fair that it should be brought against them. If there had been habitual convictions then there would he reasonable cause for the magistrates inquiring into the cause of those convictions.

J. M. BEACON, the landlord, Was then called and said that he considered the house was properly constructed and had sufficient police supervision. His business was increasing.—Cross-examined: He knew about the recent charge against the house, aad did not think it very seri- 6US. The passages were never shut, and were thorough- fares. A policeman in Bridge-st. could see two of the entr tnces out of the three.

_ Mr. HUNT (chief constable) said that Mr. Beacon had an excellent character. With the exception of the charge mentioned, the house had always been well con- ducted. He als,) considered that there was ample police supervision. --Cross-examined : If the 'Swan" were shut up drink could be got somewhere else. The pass- ages were thoroughfares. JAMES ATKiNsoic also gave evidence. WM. OWEN, architect, said that the hous2 was kept in proper or&r, and that the police could excerise proper Control over it—Cross-examined: The house did not comply with the present bye•laws, and the plans would not be passed at the present time. Evidence was also given by Mr. Jennings, and Mr. J. Walker, architect, the latter stating that lie agreed with Mr. Owen.

div.head: SHAKESPEARE INN.
div.p: THE SHAKESPEARE INN.

Mr. DAVIES said that his oi•j,•ction to the Shakespeare Inn was that it had been badly conducted. The last tnant of the house had been fined on June 5,1893,305. and costs for selling adulterated whiskey, and on December 4, 1893, she had been fined 405. owing to the servant having supplied beer to p liceinen while on duty. The hcuse was also in a neighbourhood which was not a very high class one. He therefore thought that there were serious objections to this license, as there had been two convictions in a short space of time. Mr. COOK then gave evidence to the construction of the house, and also gave in,plans of the district. He did not consider that the house was necessary to the neigh- bourhood. _ _ _ _

Mr. MULHOLLAND having addressed the court, Mr. Green, the Lindlord, gave evidence and said tat his house was properly conducted, and no loose characters were allowed in the house. Mrs. Green also gave evidence.

div.head: TEE HOP POLE LICENSE.
div.p: TEE HOP POLE LICENSE.

Mr. DAVIES stated that in regard to the objections to the renewal of the Hop Pole license they were rather of ' a different character. There was also in this case an objection by a neighbouring tenant, Mr. Dean, of Peter- street. He complained of the very defective sanitary accommodation of the house. The sanitary arrange- ments and conveniences of the house were not only inadequate but they led to very serious nuisances, and more than that, they led to a state of things which was grossly indecent, which he was quite sure the magis- trates would stop. Another serious objecti 3n was that the classof business done in the house and the conduct of those on the premises during the past year rendered it undesirable th.it the license should be renewed. It was a house with a music-room, and as a result the house was frequented by young persons of both .sexes. It WAS not desirable thit licensed houses should be frequented by young people. The management was detective, maybe it paid them to allow conduct of that kind. According to the evidence which was to be given, grossly indecent, and lewd songs were sung there without restaint. The licencee was there and knew what was going on. He was not going to repeat the words of the fiong but he would hand a copy of it up to the Bench. Very young girls were employed as waitresses, and also in the singing-room. It was a very undesirable type of house and he asked the magistrates to take a vigorous course and there could be no excuse for such conduct. Mr. Jour; DEAN said he resided at 7, and 8, Peter-street ' said his premises were at the bark of the Hop Pole pre- mises. The scullery window looked out on the yard of the publichouse. On Bank Holiday at 7,30 About eight or ten men came out of the Bop Pole publichouse, under his window which was in the yard of the public house, and used the place as a convenience instead of the urinal. It was objectionable to the servants in the house and he had to get " stuff " from the Town Hall to abate the small. On being questioned as to whether it had occurred previously he replied " many a time." , Mr. Coox, architect, Birkenhead, produced plans of the publichouse and stated that the acc,mimodation in the yard was insufficient.

Mr. Was. G. HUCKLE said he resided at Fairmount, Exeter, and he was by profession a private enquiry agent. He was asked to visit some licenced houses in Warrington in the early part of Januiry. In conse- quence of that invitation he visited the licenced house in question—The Hop Pole on several occasions. His first visit was on February Ist. He entered the house at 9.45 p.m.,accomnanied by his man Marshall. Whilst there he saw a man who was drunk served with drink in bis presence. That was in the snug ronm,but he didn't ray long on that ocrwion. He made another visit on Feb- ruary 4'.ll,again areomnanied by Marshall. He went into the side parlaur at 855 p.m. There was there a soldier, and shortly afteiw irds another man catne in followed by two others. The salier entered into a most indecent 1 conversation with another person. During the time thel cnriversation was proceeding a young waitress fre- quently came into the room to serve liquor, but she did not stop the indecent conversation which was continued for some time.—Mr. DAVIES : Could she have heard the conversation ? She must have hear 4 it. Was any attempt made to stop it ? Not the slightest. In further cross-examination witness said it was the most obscene language he had heard. By Mr. Mulholland: What do you say you are? A private enquiry agent. Have you an office? I have an office at my house at Exeter. How long have you been in this lino of business as a professional detective ? I have been in the business sixteen years. Mr.Mulholland: Dirty work. Witness : Yes, and you have come here to defend it. Who engaged vou ? The Rev. D. W. Roberts of this town invited me to come. Was it arranged that you should get. your fee after your report? I got a portion before, and the rest, after I had given my report. When you saw the person drunk, did you call the attention of any person in the house to it ? No. Why not? Beenuse I understood my profession. Did you not consider that the police were the proper authorities to complain to? I did not want myself to he known. When you visited the house on February 4, who was in the room ? A soldier. What uniform had he ? Red, with white facings. You didn't com- plain to anyone in the house about his conduct ? It was not my business to do so. Are you an Englishman? Yes, but I question whether you are. What have you done with your notes taken at the time? I destroyed them, after writing out my report. Why? Because it is easier to take care of one than two. After some further cross-examination in which the witness gave some sharp retorts. Mr. Mul- holland complained hf the way in which he was being addressed. The witness contended that he was only treating him as he was being treated. Alderman Sutton told the witness to answer the questions properly. The witness stated that he was not going to be insulted by Mr. Mulholland. Councillor H. Roberts : I think the way the cross-examination has been conducted has invited the whole of the remarks from the witness. Alderman Sutton should speak for himself and not for the whole Bench. The man is a member of an honour- able profession (some commotion amongst the audience). The cross-examination was then continued. The wit- ness said he was not aware that the Rev. D. W. Roberts acted on behalf of the " Social Questions Society." He handed his report to Mr. Roberts the day following his visit. Mr. CHAPMAN MARSHALL said he resided at Winder- mere and he visited certain licensed houses in Warring- ton in eninnany with Mr. Huckle. On January 27, wit- ness visited the Hop Pole alone. He went into a large music room, and found the room packed with young men and young women. Singing and dancing was going on. Those who were dancing con- ducted themselves indecently. Obscene songs were sung, and the audience seemed to appreciate them very much. Witness remained there about twenty minutes. Several persons were served when under the influence of liq nor. Men served the drink. On the Ist of February and also on the 4th he again visited the house in company with Mr. Huckle. He corroborated the statements made by the previous witness as to what occurred on those two visits.—By Mr. Mulholland : Who did you receive your instruc- tions from ?—I was in the employment of Mr. Huckle. How long had you been with him? Eight months, we were then both in Liverpool. When did you come to
Warrington? About a week before the Ist of January. Mr. fluckle was away. The witness described the in- decent behavii)ur which he saw on his first visit.

- Rev. D. W. ROBERTS deposed that he paid several visits to some licensed houses in the town, and from what he saw he formulated his objections to thelicences. On Saturday night, August 11r h, he visited the Hop Pote at 10.10 p.m., and lett shortly after 10.30. On entering at the side door he heard music going on up- stairs in the music room. The room was filled with about 70 or 80 persons.the maj-rity of whom were young men and young women. IVnile he was there a very sugges- tive and improper song was sung, and the audience join( din the chorus. A sheet of paper containing a portion of the song was handed to the Bench. 'He gathered from the way the young people took it up that the song had a suggestive mean- ing. A number of male and female waiters were going about the room at the time. He again visited the house on the 13-h of August. He went in at 930 and came out at 10.5. He proceeded to the first room to the right on the ground fib r. There were about 20 or 30 persons in. Singing was going on. There was a woman in drink trying to get into conversation with the men. The young woman who was serving liquor looked at her several times, but did not order her out. She after- wards went out with one of the men. On August 1811 he went again to the house. He proceeded to the music room. There was one little girl in short clothes, supply- ing liquor,who would not be more than 12 or 14 years of age. Mr. Mulholland cross-examined the witness at great length. Witnesg stated that he was secretary of the anti-gambling committ-e, and said he engaged Mr. Buckle to visit some licenced houses on their behalf. He refused to give name of the person who paid the ex- penses of Mr. Fluckle and his assistant. He considered that the licensing laws were not enforced in Warrington as they should be. _

Mr. MULHOLLAND in his reply said that they were at last having ,oinetliing tangible to meet. There was a complaint against the house of a serious character. They had the evidence of Mr. Roberts and the two inquiry agents to meet. With regard to the latter, he would point out that they were unknown, and they were paid by the job. He understood that the Anti-Gambling Committee paid these men, and if any gentleman on the bench was a member of that committee, he hoped that he would decline to take any part in the decision upon those licenses. The men Huckle and Marshall had been sprung upon them, and had been carefully kept back without any communication being made to the licensee so that no investigation caul(' now he made. With regard to the things they were alleged to have seen, he would like to know whether anything worse was done there than was done at theatres or operas. He,however, made his prote,st against th un-Eaglish :ne:hod of priv- ate espionag.? and spying which had been carried on in this case.

Evidence was then given by Mrs. Coop. Annette Ccop, Rowena Coop, James M'Clecv. Richkrd Bolton, Mr. Buck. and Colour-sergemit Stacey, to state that the house had been carried on in a proper manner, and to deny that any of the indecent conduct complaine d of had been committed.

div.head: PELICAN INN.
div.p: THE PELICAN INN.

MT. DAVIES said that the objections to the Pelican were of a similar class to the last one, and comprlzer+ others as well. The grounds of objection were, first, it was not needed as it was in the congested area. It was also structurally inadequate for its purpose in its internal arrangements. There would also be evidence produced to show that the house was badly conducted, and that solicitation was carried on in the house, Mr. Roberts would tell them that he had seen girls sitting upon men's knees, and also other improper proceedings. He did not know what was the standard of morality in Warrington, but in other towns that was not considered proper con- duct to be carried on in licensed premises. Mr. Cook then handed in the plans of the building and said that the premises were very old, and had to be bolted up. The Rev. D. W. ROBERTS said that he visited the house on February 3rd accompanied by Messrs. Huckle, Hall, and Mardian. They entered at eight o'clock and left at 8.25. On going 9pstairs to the music room he found it full of young pe,,p!e, some drank, and drink was sup- plied to persons in a sta'e of intoxica'ion, and while he was there, he distinctly heard a girl ask Mr. Fluckle where she should meet him later on. The persons in the room were of a very low class indeed. He visited the house again on August 11 from 950 p.m. to 10.5. He went into the music room. There would be about 60 or 70 in the room a good number of whom were drunk. He saw two or three girls sitting upon men's knees. On August 18, he again visited the house and went into the same room which was again filled with men who were drunk. While in the room, he saw a soldier enter into conversation with two girls, and then another soldier came in, arid event ually they all left the room. Cross- examined: He did not tell the police because he believed that they were not empowered to do as they ought to do. He had heard that their hands were tied in such matters by the Watch Committee of the town. He had it upon the reliable authority of Mr. Hunt, the chief constable, who told him that his hands were tied, _

Alderman SUTTON said that he should like to ask Mr. Hunt concerning the alleged conduct of the house, whether the pollee were ever prevented in taking any proceedings by any action of the Watch Committee. As a member of the Watch Committee he required to. know that.

The Rev. D. W. ROBERTS said that in his capacity of secretary of the Anti-gambling Committee he had entered into conversation wi:h Mr. Hunt, and it was with regard to a certain house that he said his hands were tied. It was in reference to a place where gambling was car- ried on.

Mr. Hunt said that he must ifi justice to himself and Mr. Roberts give some explanation. On one occ.a.sion. three or four dissenting ministers called to see him with re4ard to a gambling place in Warring,ton. He told them that such things could be stopped directly if the Watch Committee would consent to it. 'the Rev. D. W. ROBERTS said that his intention in asking as he did was to find the gambling cases. Councillor ROBERTS said he would like to ask the Chief Constable whether he had report the cases of alleged offences against the licensing acts to the Watch Com- mittee.

Mr. DAVIES also ask,A the same question. Mr. HIItiT said he did not like to answer the question because it was a matter between himself and Um Watch Committee. He did not report to the Watch Com- mittee.

Mr•PAvms : Do ”u know in your 30 years' experience any other town in which that regulation prevails? Alderman SUTTON : The Watch Committee help the police to perform their duty in every pDssible way. They do not tie them in any way. Councillor ROBERTS : That is a simple piece cf rot. (" On, oh ;" and upriar.) ISAAC WILKINS )1.4 Longford.street, was next called, and corr-)b Tated the R.,v. D. W. Roberts with reference to seeing the girls upon men's knees. WILLIAM G. BUCKLE said that he visited the Pelican on January 26 alone. Be saw a sergeant inside and three civilians, one of whom was so drunk that he could scarcely sit. He was served with drink. He visited the house again on Fenruary 3rd and he there saw a number of prostitutes, and the language used was most disgusting. Two girls were waiting and one of them asked witness to stand drinks. She had had two drinks when she askel witness. Witness gave her &I.—Mr. Mulholland said he did not wish to cross-examine witness.

Mr. MAR,HALL said he visited the house on January 27:h. He was attracted by the rowdy talk upstairs,and when he g t there he found the room full of men and women. There were half-a-dozen men beastly intoxi- cated but who were served again. JOHN MCCRACKEN said that he was an insurance agent in Liverpool. He visited the Pelican on June 16. He went into the snuggery and there saw some men and women. Some of them were drunk. They were paying for drinks. He saw that the women were prostitutes. He then went into the snug room, and found ;t filled with young men and women dancing, and an old man playing a flute. On June 22 he went there again. The barmaid asked him to go into the snnggery, and he then asked for drills. She ten called her colleague saying, "He wants you." They both then asked him to treat them to drinks, and they both had some whisky. On June 25 he went again. There were then one man and two women. The man was drunk. Another man and woman then came in and they sat down to drink toge- ther. He heard unmisttkeable soliciting on the part of the woman. Ha visited the house also on June 29 and 30, and found rowdy scenes there again.—Cross-ex- amined : He was employed by Mr. Davies. Mr. Mul - holland demanded what society he was an insuranee agent for, but on Mr.McCraclcen refusing to answer, Mr. Mulholland declined to cross-examine him further. Mr. MOLUCLLAND then proceeded to address the bench. He said that as they did not know the antecedents 01 the private inquiry officers, their evidence was worthless. With regard to Mr. Robert's evidence, he was practically unsupported. After a lengthy address in which he attacked the system of private detective work, he called the following witnesses to prove that the house was well conducted : Councillor Flood, and Messrs. Whatmough. A. Mather, Webb, and Oxley. Mr. Hunt said that of late he had no complaints to make of the house, and he did not think there were many prostitutes resident in the borough at the present time.

div.head: GLADSTONE ARMS.
div.p: THE GLADSTONE ARMS.

Mr. DeviEs said that the offence alleged against the Gladstone Arms was that of encouraging gaming. Hav- ing regard to the hour, he took the responsibility of withdrawing the objection to that publichouse. The license was accordingly renewed.

div.head: DECISION.
div.p: THE DECISION.

At ten minutes to six, the magistrates retired to con- sider their decision, and at a quarter to seven, they re- turned, and the Chairman announced that the applica- tion for the renewal of the licence of the Woolpack and the Pelican would be adjourned until September 27th,the date fixed for the adjourned licensing day. The appli- cation for the Swan would be refused, and the lieence of the Hop Pole would be renewed with recommendation to the Licencing Committee to refuse the music licence. The licence of the Shakespeare would be renewed. Having regard to the lateness of the hoar. the fresh applications were adjourned until September 27.

div.head: STOCKPORT.
div.p: STOCKPORT.

There was an unusually large attendance of magis- trates on Wednesday at the annual brewster sessions for the borough (it St )ckport. On the minutes of the Licens- ing Committee being submitted, Alderman W. L's pro- posed the ra jection of that portion granting a six-day license to the proposed Hollywood Hotel. at the main entrance to Hollywood Park. An animated discussion took place, and the amendtnent was carried by 13 votes to 12. The applicant demanded that the case Should be gone into by the whole of the magistrates present. Wit- nesses were then called, and on a vote being again taken the license wes refused.

THE CREWE MAGIS CRATES AND "MANAGERS." The Crewe Brewst-r Session were held on Tuesday. It may be remembered that last year the mauistrates refused to renew the licenses of applicants who were merely managers on weekly wages; and Messrs. Walker who own seven of the largest licensed houses in Crewe, had their licenses refused on that occasioc. They, how- ever, appealed to the Cneshire Quarter Sessions against the decision, and it was upset. On an application being made on Tuesday for the renewal of the licenses, it was stated that the applicants occupied practically the same position as last year. The magistrates adjourned the whole of the licenses, and said they should require the applicants to attend,' with the conditions of their tenancies.

div.head: PRESCOT DIVISION.
div.p: PRESCOT DIVISION.

On Wednesday the annual licensmg sessions for the Prescot Petty Sessional Division of tne county were held at the Present Police C tint, Derby-street, Present. The magistrates were Messrs. H. H. d'A. Willis (in the ('hair), A. R. Gladstone, F. S:apleton-Bretht rton, and W. Lee Pilkington. Police-superintendent Baxendale submitted his annual report, which stated thae tile total number of licenses issued was 70, and the pepulation being 16,343, there was one license for every 233 persons. None of the holders of licenses had been convicted, bat there had been an increase in the number of persons proceeded against for drunkenness. The report of Superintendent Keighley concerning that portion of the Widnes police division situated in Present Petty Sessional Division stated that the number of licenses was 122, and that there were three clubs within the borough of Widnes, which were open the whole of Sunday for the sale of drink to members. Toe numb-r of parsons proceeded against for drunkenness was 639, as against 576 last year, an increase of 63. The popillation in 1891 was 35,072, there being an average of 287 persons to each licensed house. An application was made by Mr. John Ashton for a full license to premises situatt d at the corner of Tarbock and Sc. John's roads, Huy ton. The application was opposed, and after deliberating for half an hour the magistrates refused it. ST. HELENS (COUNTY).

The annual licensing sessions for the St. Helens County I'4-try Sessional Division, including portions of both the Preset and liridnes sections, were held at St. Helens Town Hall on Tuesday, when the mazistrates present were the Mayor (Alderman A. Sinclair) and Alderman T. Cook.—Superintendent Baxenda'e, of the Present division, reported that durnig the seir ending the 31st ult. ;he licensed persons had conducted their houses very well, and none had been proceAed against. There were at present doing business 24 :icensed victual- lers, 13 beersellers fer consoinn,ion on the premises,and two off license holders, total 39 During the year two public-houses, two heerhouses, au. i p )pulation of 1285 persons had been taken into S. Helen,' by the extension of the bou9daries of the borotirh. The present popula- tion was 7096, an average of 182 nersons to eveil license. The number of persons or ,c .enel q,,Riust for chinken- ness was as follows :-1894, 46; 1893, 51; 1832, 48 ;1891, 55; 1890, 58. All ela-s “ife,:e-s-1894, 157; 1893, 158; 1892,130 ; 1891, 129; 1890, 193. The licenses and populat ton in acti towns in were as follows :—Ec.cleston (rural) 15, popula' ion 2754; Rainford 21. population 3472; Windle (rural) 3, population 870.—Superintendent Keighley, (91 the Widnes division, reparted that in his district there were three public-houies and one beer- house. No proceedings hid hem taken against any license holder during the year, their h,.aises having been. well conducted. div.head: MAKERFIELD CYCLING CLUB,
div.p: MAKERFIELD CYCLING CLUB,
100 MILES TIME COMPETITION.

On Wednesday, F. Cooper of the above club competed for the gold medal which is given by the club to those of its members who ride 100 mdes in seven hours. The weather and roads were perfection. A start was made at 1.30. In the early part of the race fast times were made. T. Garton rendered valuable assistance by pac- ing from the start to 67 miles, the first 50 of which was covered in 2 hours 47 minutes. M. Can ,y of the North- road C.C. (London), made the pace from I:i7 miles but unfortunately after going about eignt milas he retired owing to a ourictured tyre. From here Cooper rode, alone. for 15 miles when Nl,ssrs. J. Whitham and J. Newill, of the WArrinz-noi C.C., and C. Nrtington, Mak,!rfield C.C., paced alternitelv to the finish, the last. 11 miles being c,ivorerl in 35 inintres. The finishing point was passed at 817 p in. Therefore the dim for the 100 miles was 6 hours 47 minute. The machine ridden was a " Wright " Racer, fitted with Qrappler tyres.

div.p: GOOD TEMPLARY.

The weekly session of toe llope of Earlestown lodge of Good Teinplars was held in the C i-opera- tire Hall on Monday evening. Bro. J•is. Atiderton presided and there was a large attendance of mem- bers. Four candidates were initiated to member- ship and four were proposed. Bro. W. H. Dale pre- sented the statement of accounts for the musical instrument fund, which was adopted. The pro.. gramme of the evening was " Aaction Night" for which Br.). G. E. Warburton was responsible, an enjoyable time being spent. T. JOHN'S CHURCH CHOIR, TRIP.

The annual picnic of the above choir, and Sunday school teachers took place on Saturday to Black- pool. The party numbering 63 left Earlestown at *345 and r,.ached Blackpool shortly after 9 o'clock. The headquarters were made at Brougliton's res- taurant, where breakfast, dinner and tea were par- taken of. The day was pleasantly spent in visits to the various places of interest, and the return journey was made at 8.15 and 1030. Tne arrange- ments which were in the hands of Mr. Foden and Mr. Latimer, were fully satisfactory. MARRIAGE OF Mn. WALTER BLAIR.

An interesting ceremony took place on Tuesday at the Parish church, Padgate, Miss G. B. Pollitt, daughter of Mr. William Pollitt, The Willows Orford, being united in we:ttilock to Walter, secend son of Mr. W. Blair, of Earlestown. The bride was dressed in a lovely shade of French grey, trimmed with white moite and steel, with hat to match, and looked very pretty indeed. Her bridesmaids were two of her younger sisters, and a sister of the bridegroom, the " best " man being Mr. W. F. Pollitt. The bride was given away by her father, and the wedding ceremony, which was a bright and happy one, was enlivened by music supplied by :qr. F. Booth. Theofficiating minister was the Rev. J. Phillips, M.A.. late chaplain at Orford. After breaktas-,, at which covers were laid for 24, the newly-married couple departed for E linboro', amidst a showtr of rice and good wishes. The presents were numerous and varied, and were selected with a view to usefulness. EARLESTOWN WESLEYAN DAY SCHOOLS.

The report of the examination held in connection with the above schools has eome to hand, and is as follows :—Mixed school: "Good order prevails in the school which is, as to instruction, in a satisfactory state of efficiency. In English, geography, hand- writing, spelling. composition and needlework Vie results are as a rule successful. Mental arithmetic might be stronger generally and written arithmetic equally efficient in all the standards. Reading should be improved in the upper standards and else in the first standard which however does better work in other subjects than might have been ex- pected considering its poor attendance." Infants school: "This school is conducted with commend- able earnestness and zeal. A bright and intelligent tone pervades it, and the children display very. , creditable proficiency in their work. There is how- ever too large a proportion of children over seven years of age who ought to have been prepared for examination in the elernentary subjects in the first standard; hence the classification cannot be re- garded as entirely satisfactory." The average at- tendance is 3GI boys and 142 girls. Miss F. Higgins. and -Miss J. 11. Blair have each obtained a second. class in the Queen's scholarship examination,

div.head: 'CAPITAL" CHAT.
div.p: 'CAPITAL" CHAT.

A speech by Mr. John Burns on the stationery and printing vote on Saturday, must have rather startled the Government and opened its eyes as to the gross waste of public money which prevails in connection with it. The certainty is that the Government had no idea whatever of the manner in which the country is bled by the existing arrangements, and the officials in the department have no practical experience. Mr. Burns' speech, therefore, will fall like a bombshell upon the Treasury and on the sleepy individuals who govern the department by the rules of use and wont. He strongly urged, on the ground of economy and efficiency, that the Government should do its own printing. His speech led Sir J. Hibbert to promise on the spot that the whole subject should be inquired into next session, though no change could be made until the present ten years' contracts expired in 1896. Another promise which the dis- cussions elicited was that the present system of supplying boots to the metropolitan police force by contract would be abolished as soon as possible, and an allowance given to the men to enable them to provide their own boots. Here, again, Mr. Burns warned the Home Office that great care would be required in applying that rule, as the experience of the London County Council had been that a considerable number of men in their employment had misapplied similar allowances.

The impression is gaining ground among such members as are still left at Westminster that next session will be another Irish session. Any Bill to amend the Land Act of 1891, and the Acts with which it has been followed up, will absorb the whole time of the House of Commons ; and if there are engrafted upon it evicted tenants' clauses, or if that subject is dealt with in a separate Bill, it will be more than the Government can overtake with- out the closure. Among Ministerialists the belief is now shaping itself very strongly that, although the Welsh Disestablishment Bill will be introduced it will take a place quite secondary to the Irish Bill or Bills,and be shelved at furthest at the thres- hold of the committee stage. Two reasons are as- signed for this belief. First, the strong Irish bias of Mr. Morley ; and, secondly, the united front and determination of the Irish members to dictate the policy of the Government if necessary, under the belief that they hold the key to the Ministerial situation. They unquestionably do hold it--first,so long as the Government are willing to let them thitsk so; second, as long as the Welsh members cannot act in common and with a resolute policy; and thirdly, so long as the London members and their Radical friends leave the Irish members under their present delusion. The key is really held by each of several groups ; but the Irish group is the only one that has the determination to exercise such power as it has; and while that is so, Welsh- men, Scotchmen, and London Radicals must be con- tent with the crumbs that fall from the Irish table.

The answer of Sir W. Harcourt on Monday night to Mr. Cobbs' question as to the policy of the Government in reference to the House of Lords was listened to with anxious interest. The House was unfortunately almost empty, there not being more than a couple of dozen members in it. Mr. Cobb, though a Liberal,had taken a seat on the Opposition side; but Sir William crossed the floor before the question was reached and had a short conversation with him, probably with the view of getting him to postpone it. Nevertheless Mr. Cobb put it, and when Sir William rose there was a cry of " hush " from all.quarters. It was answered amidst the pro- foundest silence. In a few words the Chancellor of the Exchequer referred to the great gravity of the subject, and added That be did not think he could 'take during the present session any definite state- ment upon it. Mr. Sexton tried to wring from Lim a promise that the policy of the Govern- ment would be announced in the Queen's Speech at the beginning of next session, but Sir William would not make any such promise. All the leading Radicals were absent, and seem to have left for the session. No other answer could really have been expected, but it will probably be greatly mis- understood by many Radicals, and it will form the theme for unbridled denunciation at Sunda's Hyde Park meeting. It will be more ominous if Lord RosEbery allows his autumn visit to Bristol to pass without a plain hint of what the Government mean to do. If that occasion passes also the Radical forces below the gangway will compel the Govern- ment to speak out next session.

A writer is greatly exercised in his mind as to the preservation of the Protestant succession to the Throne when the Church is disestablished. With disestablishment, it is pointed out, the Sovereign will not be called upon to take any oath to main- tain the Church, and he or she will be free to pro- fess Roman Catholicism. But the Protestant Suc- cession does not depend upon the oath of the Sovereign ; and even it all existing restrictions were removed, and the Soverign were free to pro- fess any religion he or she pleased, there would be no danger to the orderly course of our national de- velopment. As the democracy, which will have disestablished the Church, advances, the nation and the governing body of the nation will be launched upon a totally different sea of political problems, which will engross the minds of all men and women, from the top to the bottom of society. Compared with such problems, the personal religion of the Sovereign will be a trifling matter. 'What nation will then be engaged upon is a social recon- struction which will be very fundamental and organic indeed.

Down to the end of 1892 the London School Board has spent on the building of schools a sum of close upon three millions gterling, and the expenditure of 1893 brings the total cost of all the schools ,erected out of the rates in London to upwards of • that sum.. Last year alone 14 new schools were onened and 25 old schools were enlarged, and the accommodation thus provided afforded place room for 22,000 boys and girls. The development of the technical Schools is a marked feature of the board's arrangements for the year. Thirteen new cookery centres have been opened, also 18 new laundry cen- tres and 15 Centres for manual training. Two centres for the blind and three for the deat have • also been established, so that, while the board itself has been wastink its time in religious and sacerdo- tal discussions, its committees have been usefully engaged in pushing its legitimate work forward. People are asking if an assertion in the " Daily News" is both inspired and true, and Liberals are hoping so. This is that the Prime Minister is thoroughly in earnest in the necessity for taking action against the House of Lords, and that in this be is supported by a unanimous Cabinet, for there has been and still is a very strong impression that there are influential members of the Cabinet who come very far short of earnestness in this matter, and men are found who believe that the way of dealing with the House of Lords has never been seriously made a subject of Cabinet discussion. Meantime, as Lord•Rosebery has• asked for a lead from the county, steps are being taken to give Car- diff, Bristol, Shields, Newcastle and Glasgow an opportunity of expressing their opinion of the Lords and of calling on the Government to declare theirs.

The Empress-Dowager of China is in many respects an extraordinary woman. She is a Ritualist, and keeps eighteen lamps, representing the eighteen provinces of China, burning in her palace. One of these happening to burn badly, she was greatly disturbed, and anxiously inquired of the Chief Astronomer the cause. The reply is said to have been that the peccant lamp represented Canton, and indicated an epidemic of the plague. A party of Americans tramping over the hills in the grounds of Balmoral came suddenly upon an elderly lady sitting alone before a table and writing rapidly, says " Cassell's Saturday Journal." "Tell me, madam," said one,politely lifting his hat," are we far from Balmoral ?" "You are on the grounds now," said the lady; "and I greatly fear you are trespassing." They respectfully announced their intention of getting into the public road at the first opportunity. Thereupon the lady wrote a line and handing it to them said, smiling, "Here is a safe conduct if you meet a bailiff." "Victoria R." was all the slip contained.

A Hint about Soap. Instead of throwing away the pieces of soap which become too small for convenient handling, make a small flannel bag of suitable size, leave one end partly open, and put in the pieces as they collect. When it is full. baste up the opening, and it makes a nice bath-tub accessory. Another way is to add a little water, set the pieces in a saucepan on the stove, and let them simmer slowly. When cold you have tolerably good soft soap. By letting most of the water boil away, you may make the soap hard enough to be moulded in small cakes, which can be dried for use.

Cupboards and Closets. A house, whether large or small, can never be con- venient if it has not plenty of closet and cupboard-room for the greater part of the convenience of any house con- sists in having an abundance of closets. Closets are never in the way unless they are dark ones, and the fewer of these kinds in a house the better for the general health of the family and the cleanliness of the house. They are difficult places to keep sweet and clean, for, no matter how hard you may try, you cannot prevent them from being musty and close. They have no ven- tilation at all but the door, and, as they are chiefly used for storage, they get little air from that opening. They are always placed in some out-of-the-way corner, where it is next to impossible to get into them to give them a thorough cleaning, and they are very tempting recep- tacles, when a person is in a hurry, into which to threw articles of very little use. A woman who has a closet of this sort in her house ought to be very particular about seeing that it is properly and frequently cleaned, and ventilated as much and as well as possible. She should be careful about leaving anything damp in such a place, as it will be sure to mildew. There should be a clothes closet in every chamber. Ventilate the clothes closets,if they have not windows,by leaving the doors open when airing the rooms,and there will be little danger of moths taking up their abode in them.

Six English excursionists who had been in custody at Boulogne for ridiculing a religious procession were on Wednesday released on the intercession of friends. The house of Mr. Edward Dreyer, the millionaire banker of Chicago, is now being protected by a special guard of police, owing to threats of assassination by a man with whom he has had business differences.

IN a continental sea-side watering-place there was a reading-room kept by an English lady, who, on the strength of her position, supposed herself to be connected with literature. Lord Macaulay passed through the town, went to the reading-room, and wrote down his name in the subscription hook. His money was returned to him with the remark, "No, my lord, we literary people must not • take money from each other." - -

AT an evening party, Dumley was introduced to a young lady, and after a remark about the weather he said, gallantly.: "And have I really the pleasure of meeting the beautiful Miss Smith, whose praises are being sounded by everybody ! " "Oh no, Mr. Dumley," the lady replied, "the beautiful Miss Smith to whom you refer is a cousin of mine." " Oh, that's it? Well, I thought there must be a mistake somewhere," said the gallant Dumley.—New York Sun.

SOME years ago a man whose marriage had been published in a paper with his name wrongly spelled called to have it corrected. He said he was one of that class whose name never appeared in a news- paper but twice during the course of their lives— once when they are married, and again after death. As he could not see to having the name given cor- rectly on the last occasion, he was very anxious it should be right on the first.

ONCE, when John Kemble played Hamlet in the country, the gentleman who enacted Guilderstern was or imagined himself to be a capital musician. Hamlet asks him, "Will you play upon this pipe ?" "My lord, I cannot." "I pray you." "Believe me, I cannot." "I do beseech you." "Well, if your Lordship insists on it, I shall do as well as I can;" and to the confusion of Hamlet and the great amusement of the audience, he played "God save the King." AT a meeting of the Fife Magistrates some years after 1745, a Whig gentleman gave as a toast "The Duke of Cumberland." David Beatoun, of Kilcon quhar, a zealous Jacobite, immediately after pro- posed "James Sibald, the butcher of Colnesburgh," to the great indignation of his Whig neighbour, who said he must decline to do so much honour to a conunon tradesman. "Sir," said Kilconquhar sternly, "I've drunk your butcher, and you'll either drink mine or be put over the window."— Chamber's Journal, THE proverb, "The drunken man aye gets the drunken penny," was probably never so truly verified as in the case of two tipplers in Lock- winnock. They had exhausted funds and credit, yet still they might be seen describing right argles in their course towards home. One day, having failed in all their schemes for raising the necessary funds, "Gang awa' in, Peter," said John, "and see gin they'll gie us credit for a gill." "Na, John, wad it no' be likelier that ye wad get it; ye're far better acquaint ? " "It would be useless ," replied John; "I'm ower weel kent."

THE little town of I— was many years ago deluged by the overflowing of its beautiful river, and the occupants of the houses cr, its banks were only able to escape with their lives. So rapid was the rising of the water that those who lived in the upper fiats of the houses had to be rescued by boats from their perilous position. One of those was found, when succour came, in an attitude of prayer, importuning hish heaven in the following terms :-- "Lord, -thou saidst thou would never again drown us with a flood, but I am getting very doubtful." "WHY, how wonderfully lifelike," said Mr. Der- rix, gently caressing a bumblebee which reposed among the artificial flowers and insects of his wife's new bonnet. • "If it was a garden flower I'd swear it was al—G-r-eat Cesar-r !' he suddenly shrieked, inserting a wounded fin,,rcr in his month and danc- ing around like a whirling dervish. "Why, the blamed thing is alive." A WELL-KNOWN beauty has one drawback; her hands are the colour of boiled lobster. Some one
happened to mention her name to a celebrated wit, who said, "She is very pretty.: I see only one fault in her; her hands are a trifle too—ltf...l
THE DOUBLE LIFE Oa, THE HAMPTON MYSTERY.
By the Author of " DABIEWOOD."
CHAPTER XXIX. WHAT LORD ADLOWE SAW.

Would he were wasted, marrow, bones, and all, That from his loins no hopeful branch may spring, To cross me from the golden time I look for SHAKESPEARE'S Henry VI. The observations of. Detective Rush, in regard to the Lady Beatrice Hampton, had been correct. The earl's daughter had, openly quitted Hainptor House, on an ostensible visit to friends in the country, and had made her way, by a circuitout route, to Limely, where she had found the pony carriage and faithful old coachman from The Evergreens in waiting for her. Assuring herself that she was not watched or followed from the station, she had set out directly for the hidden home.

As the carriage neared its destination, and the old (x.achman prepared to get down from his box, the wide gate of The Evergreens swung open on its well-oiled hinges, and, as they passed through, it closed noiselessly behind them. The hour was between sunset and dusk. It had been light out in the pleasant street, but a soft, obscure twilight reigned here under the thick. spreading fire, larches, and pines. The Lady Beatrice bent a quick, searching glance into the brooding shadows, and at the same moment a gay, childish laugh rang out, and her youngest darling bounded forward, climbing into the carriage, which had halted.

"My boy! My little Fay I" said the Lady Beatrice, fondly clasping him to her bosom in an excess of motherly tenderness, her proud face glowing. "You received my letter, then, that I should be home to-night to spend a week with you? Are they all well—papa, Rupert, and Meggy ?" At the mention of his name, before Fay had time to reply, Rupert emerged from the shadows, and approached the carriage. In a moment more he too was seated in the vehicle, clasped in a warm embrace, and then the whole party moved on up the shadowed winding drive toward the house. The Lady Beatrice had been at home but once since the departure from it of Giralda, and that was on the night on the Hampton ball, when she had passed out as one of the guests. She had deemed it best since, knowing the vigilence of her enemy, Lord Adlowe, to remain away from The Evergreens entirely, lest she should bring discovery and trouble upon her husband. Her anxieties and her affections had at last conquered her discretion, as we have seen.

The house was lighted, and the self-styled count, beaming with happiness, was on the steps to give his wife welcome. He lifted her out of the car- riage as she drove up, and half carried her into the drawing-room, the two boys following. "A whole week of bliss before us !" said the hus- band, drawing the Lady Beatrice upon a so:a be- side him, and gently removing her wrappings. "A whole week of pure, unalloyed happiness! I ean scarcely realise it." "Not unalloyed happiness,' papa," said Rupert, gravely. "We can never be entirely happy again until Giralda comes back."

The mother looked at her eldest boy, her heart echoing his words. And then she noticed, for the first time, how he had changed of late. He seemed taller, older, and more serious. A strange gravity shaded his brow and made sombre his splendid black eyes. His face was pale, and the shadow of a great trouble brooded over all his features. The high-spirited lad was drinking deep of the cup of sorrow which his parents would have forever with- held from his lips. The mother held out her hand and drew him to her side.

"What is it, Rupert ?" she asked, anxiously. "What trouble has changed you so?" The boy's lip quivered. "We miss Giralde so," he said. "It seems as if the light of the house had gone." "But she will be back soon, Rupert. I do not mean to spare her always. Papa and I miss her, too."

"Wet that isn't all," said Rupert, speaking by a brave effort, his pale face flushing. " Giralda is a delicate girl. She isn't fit to go out in the world to earn her own living. It is I who ought to work in her stead. I cannot stay here idle and let her work for me." "Be patient, Rupert," said the mother, with soothing tenderness, laying her hand on his. " Giralda is in good hands—with one who loves her. I cannot explain to you yet where she is, nor what she is doing, hut she has a luxurious home and tender care. She is under the guardianship of a relative—"

"A relative ? " interrupted Rupert; in surprise. "I never heard either you or papa speak of a relative before, mamma." "Let me explain," said the count, with sad gravity. "You are old enough, boys, to under- stand and keep a secret which I will now confide to you. Years ago before you were born, before even I was married, I had the misfortrne to greatly offend my guardian, whom I dearly loved. The offence was unintentional. I was made, by some strange chain of circumstances, to appear guilty of a crime of which I was in heart innocent. My uncle cast me off. Your mamma, who was then betrothed to me, was the only person in all the world who had a living faith in my innocence. In the face of all the feeling and evidence against me she married me, and made the life happy which would otherwise have been a cruel desert." Instantly two pairs of boyish arms were entwined about her ladyship, and two pairs of boyish lips were nressed to her cheeks. The Lady Beatrice, or the countess, as we may call her here in the second phase of her double life; Laughed, even while her eyes grew wet with sudden tears.

"This uncle of mine, cruel as he was to me, bitterly as he grew to hate me," resumed the count, "was a man eminently just and honourable. He is alive now, alone and aged. Giralda went from us to earn her own living—the generous darling She saw an advertisement in the Times, which she answered in person. The advertiser was my uncle. He was pleased with her, and en- gaged her as his secretary, both knowing nothing of their relationship to each other. He has grown to love her, and desires to adopt her as his granddaughter." "Giralda loves him, too, said the countess, as her husband paused in his narration. "I have seen her since she left home, and have told her papa's story. She has devoted herself to the task of softening the old man's heart towards papa and I have strong hopes that she will succeed. if she does, we will emerge from this obscurity and take our rightful places in the world. Have faith and patience, Rupert !" "I will—l will !" said the boy, humbly, his im- patience completely subdued. "I am willing to stay at The Evergreens till I am gray, only I would give much, everything, to have you and Giralda here all the time, mother." .

At this juncture Meggy announced that supper was waiting. The parents, despite their own se- cret anxieties, assumed a cheerful gaiety, and the meal became, as usual in that house a delightful little social reunion. After supper a pleasant even- ing followed; the mother then attended Fay to his chamber, and afterwards sought the delightful little study in which the so-called Spanish count was first introduced to the reader.

She found him there now half reclining on the tiger-skin couch before the hearth, the curtains drawn and an aspect of cosy comfort reigning throughout the little room. He held out his arms to her, and she sat down beside him, enwreathed in his embrace. "You have seen Giralda, dearest " he said. "You have seen my uncle? How did it happen ?" "They have been up to London. The marquis brought her to town with the intention of seeking out the Countess of Arevalo,' and making an arrangement to adopt Giralda,. I wrote you a mere outline of the facts. I could. not givn full explanations in a letter. Lord Trevelyan formed the idea of taking Giralda to the theatres, believing ' that they would see me on the boards. div.head: IT IS EASY TO ASK QUESTIONS.
div.p: IT IS EASY TO ASK QUESTIONS.

A child can ask questions that a wise man can't an- swer. Yes ; and there are some questions that the ablest doctors don't like to have people ask them. Say a question of this sort—w bile we are about it, however, we might as well tell the s tory straight away and have done with it.

Mrs. Sarah Mace was very ill with influenza. That was in February, 1892, the time of the epidemic. The attack was very severe. She was suddenly seized with a violent pain in the head (both front and back) and temples. She had pain in all her joints too, and was , hot and feverish. She went to bed and sent for the doctor. He came, examined her, to o k her temperature —over 100 degrees—and said very little, like a wise man. The lady could not turn herself in bed. She lived on slops, such as milk and broth ; she could not swallow a morsel of solid food. Her husband pressed her to take strong food, saying, "If you don't eat, you will starve." Right enough ; but he forgot that when one can't eat he can't ea, and there's an end. Well she got weaker and weaker, an fell away until there wasn't much left of her but skin and bone. Then, in her anxiety, she put her question: "Doctor, do you think I shall get well ?" The doctor's answer was true and honest ; we like and respect him for it. H e said. " Mrs. Mace Ido not know." He couldn't tell. Neither could any other doc- tor, No, not even if he had a string of titles to his name as long as a kite's tail. But did she get well? Wait a bit. We must hark back a minute now. Along about the 10th of March, 1880, Mrs. Mace began to feel tired, languid, and weary, as if her work were too much for her, she said. She had a bad taste in the mouth, poor appetite, and whatever she ate gave her pain at the chest and heart. " I had." she continuess "a dull heavy in in at the right side and between the , shoulders, and a sinking feeling at the pit of the stomach and a rising of foul gas in my throat. Later on I had rheumatic pains in my heart, chest, and back. I sent for a doctor who attended me for six weeks, but I got worse. One .day the cook said, Why don't you try Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup ?'—this being a medicine my mistress (I was living with a lady in Camden Town) kept in the house for family use. I did so, and was soon as strong as ever. Years fled away,and in 1891 she had the first attack of influenza, and in 1892 the second, already described in part. We now complete the account of the 1892 lattack.

Mrs. Mace says : " The doctor continued to attend me for five weeks, and I took his medicines for that time, but gained no strength. After having suffered for seven weeks I said to my husband, I will now see what Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup will do for me. Perhaps it may cure influenza as well as other ailments.' I carried out this resolution ; began taking the Syrup,and was soon on my feet again, and have since kept in ex- cellent health, taking an occasional dose when needed. (Signed) SARAH MACE, Monk's Farm, Great Warley, Brentwood, Essex. August 27th, 189 2." Now we have never advertised Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup as a remedy for influenza. Yet the facts stated by Mrs. Mace cannot be disputed. What is the conclusion? A very simple one indeed. She did not have influenza until her system had been debilitated by indigestion and dyspepsia. It is such people generally (almost wholly) that all epidemic diseases attack. The dreaded cholera scarcely ever touches any- body except a dyspeptic—cholera is a malady of the bowels only. The more we hear of disease the more the proof piles up showing that persons with a sound diges- tion are safe against dying of anything except violence or old age. The Syrup cured Mrs. Mace's influenza by taking away the ground it stood on—the torpidity of her digestion.
She once asked, "Doctor, do you think I shall get well 2" Time and Mother Seigel have said "Yes."

div.head: LITTLE DOROTHY DREW.
div.p: LITTLE DOROTHY DREW.

A PEN AND INK SKETCII AT HAWARDEN. A member of the Abercromby Women's Liberal Association, who visited Hawarden last week, has written the following : At four o'clock when we paid our sixpence admission to the terrace, the sun was shining brightly in the castle and grounds. A space immediately opposite•the centre walk from the house was roped off for Mr. Gladstone and his party. A few ladies had already taken their seats on the wall and on chairs within this enclosure, when, like a little bird, Dorothy Drew came dancing along from the castle. When the immense crowd in the field below caught sight of her they cheered loudly. Eventually she is well-accustomed to " being received" for she danced up to the wall and stood smiling with the most perfect self-possession. She is only a tiny mite, and was very simply dressed in a pink print frock and a white washing bat. She began pulling at her frock, and in a moment, with her mother's help, off came her little brown shoes and stockings, and she was barefooted. For the rest of the afternoon she remained so, and ran about with equal ease on both gravel walks and grass. While we waited for Mr. Gladstone she sat on the terrace wall, plucking ivy leaves and throwing them to the crowd. Then she stuck the leaves between her toes and waved her little foot to the people. She has exquisitely formed legs and feet, and I was told that she is often seen in the village barefooted. She was greatly taken with an umbrella one of the ladies handed up to her. She soon tired, however, of merely holding one end, and, much to the general amusement, she suddenly drew it up. Laying it on the terrace wall, she asked for another and yet another. Then she called out, "Now, lam going to throw them down." She was told to hand them back, not throw them, and when she had done so she said, "Now, I want them all hack again." She caught sight of, a little girl in the crowd d, not beds, at with so g her Pansies, made them u ivy leaf, she ran off aitrionttbie ow a button-hole with some ivy, and passed them over the wall. When her grandfather alluded so prettily to her in his speech, Mrs. Gladstone lifted her up on to the wall beside him, where they stood hand in hand, while the crowd cheered themselves hoarse. It was a pretty sight. The old man's face glowed with pride while he bent down and told her to kiss her hand to the people. She was lifted down again out of sight, but for the rest of the afternoon she-was dancing—always dancing— here, there, and everywhere, on her little bare feet.

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

MY DEAREST Thrum Muslin is having a wonderful vogue this season. I have seen some wonderful dresses made of an infinitesimally striped muslin with an embroidered spot upon it. Grenadines and silken crêpes also number their partisans by the thousand, and on all dresses made of these thin fabrics the sleeves are fashioned with puffs from the shoulder to the elbow, and fit tightly in rucks right the way down the wrist. A rucked sleeve is very easily managed. You need only to make it to fit, and then out it some eight inches longer than the arm, and it will ruck by itself. The original idea of these was, believe, that they should imitate the suede gloves. But to-day we have become reasonable in the length of our gloves, and wisely limit it for ordi- nary occasions, though, of course, long gloves still obtain for special festivities. Turning to winter costumes, an afternoon dress which shall amiably submit to be covered by our winter jacket, and yet play its part decoratively in the house, is assuredly amongst those garments deserving our greatest respect. One I have seen shows a mulberry faced cloth trimmed with a striped ribbon of black and Maeda green, and boasting a re 41a green chiffon vest.

For travelling dresses alpaca is much worn, the brilliant surface not retaining the duet; these costumes are made simply. A plain skirt with deep hem and several rows of stitching, little open jacket just coming to the waist of the same, under it a white piqué waistcoat with a double row of buttons, collar and revers of piqué, are made moveable so that they can be worn or not, accord- ing to fancy. These alpaca costumes are made in various shades—black, white, beige, loutre, oar- melite, and all the useful tints—and are also used for bicycle costumes for the hot weather, often without a skirt, only the wide, full trousers, pleated at the waist and drawn in at the ankle, and a light blouse. This reminds me of a charming blouse which came under my notice the other day. It is in pink silk gauze striped in thin lines, the neck band and cuffs being of the same material, with pink rosette bows at the wrist.

All the habe and bonnets, which are being packed up with our seaside outfits, have east from them the blossoms which decorated them in the early spring, and are gay with wings and tulle and chiffon trimmings; but it really is a noticeable fact that the osprey is not half so popular as it was, although it is questionable whether we show our kindness more convincingly in the new craze for wings than in our old fancy tor the heron's plumage. Most of the hats are made in the open shape, over which it is difficult to properly adjust a veil, the one way being to gather it very full in the centre of the front. A particularly elegant bonnet has the crown one mass of lilac in a salmon shade, veiled with cream-coloured guipure, while the black moire ribbon bow and jetted osprey make an effective contrast. Of buttercup coloured straw, with a jet diamond shaped crown, is another bonnet, and the trimming is black feathers, osprey, and rosettes, with lace lining to brim. A stylish hat in fancy open straw, is bound with velvet, and outlined with jet beads, with bows of chine ribbon, and pleated gauze caught down with antique buckles.

Pique is always trash or cool looking, and is equally pretty either plain or with a tiny spot. A plain white piqué eat and skirt looks remarkably well with muslin blouses in some artistic shade of blue, pink, green, or mauve, fancifully tucked and trimmed with insertion, the large frilled collar, falling over the coat. Corded linens, too, make up remarkably well. The distinguishing feature of all tennis, boating,. and such like gowns, common alike to all, is the latitude allowed in the materials and arrangementlof he blouses and vests. These get hotter cut and more artistic as time go on, and, however plain or ordinary the material used for the gown, V/e fancy can be given free play when these are in consideration.
Your JENNIE.
