having quitted the theatre immediately alter I did, called upon me, and sent up her nap" The chil& was stunned at her discover/ of TnY .entity with the Lady Beatrice Hampton She had heard the whole story of Geoffrey Trevelyen the marquis's point of view. My husband. I told her all—your wrongs, our hopes, our fears —all!" " All !" echoed the count. "What did she say? "What could she say? Her tender Mess heArt was wrung with grief. I shall never forget the piteous, woe-stricken little face she lifted to me. She said the marquis loved her, and she loved him. She proposed to go home with him, and to ass her Influence over him for your benefit. I have faith, Geoffrey, that your reconciliation to the marquis, if it ever occurs, will come through her. I con- sented to her wish, and let her go.' "But how did you manage in regard to the marquis?" asked the count, thoughtfully. "He , must have wondered at seeing none of Giralda's relatives." "lie did see one—her mother !" The Lady Beatrice narrated the particulars of her interview with Lord Trevelyan, in her disguise as the Countess of Arevalo, concluding with her meeting with Lord Adlowe at the door. "By the way," she added, "Adlowe called upon me to-day, for an explanation, I suppose. I sent word I was engaged. He then left a message that be would call to-morrow at three, and should expect to see me without fail." "There is a covert threat in that message!" "True. But Ido not fear him so much as I did. Our secret is too safely guarded for even Adlowe to easily penetrate 1" "And how did my uncle look ? " asked the count In a low tone. " Happy ? " "Better than he has looked for years. Happier, and healthier in mind and body. He is a grand- looking old man. His awakening love for Giralda is humanising him. He looks as if he might live twenty years yet?" The count sighed deeply. "Twenty years more of estrangement, bitter- ness, and hiding! Where shall we be then, sweet wife? Where will our children be? But, Beatrice, highly as I would prize my freedom, much as I long to claim you and our children before the world, I would not, if I could by a single wish, shorten that old man's life by a day I If I could only he friends with him! If I could only see him smiling on my children as he smiled on me in my boyhood I Vain wishes !" Not vain " said the true and tender wife, nestling closer to him, her glorious beauty made warm and tender by her love. "It was fate or Providence that sent Giralda to Trevelyan Park. That Providence will guide and guard her through all, and will make her the instrument of your restoration to all you hold dear—the right to acknowledge your family, the right to bear your own name—shown to be spotless—the right to your uncle's remorseful love! It will all come out right, Geoffrey. We have been a long time wading through the deep waters, The strong, dry land is near!" Thus tenderly she comforted him, like an angel of promise and peace. The two sat up late, and conversed at length. Their daughter, far from them for the first time in her young life, their spirited, ambitious Rupert, and their own prospects, were all discussed again . and again. And at last, weary yet cheerful, they retired to dream of their loved ones.

The next day was a gala day. Yet the tender mother stole away from her family to pack Giral- da's little trunk and to write a letter to her dar- ling. The father and the boys also wrote at length, as did good Meggy Fleck, who had been duly enlightened as the whereabouts of her young mistress. The trunk, when packed, was dispatched at once on its journey. It was on this day that Lord Adlowe called at Hampton House, by his own appointment, and failed, of course, to see the Lady Beatrice. The earl informed him, however, that his daughter had gone to visit the Charltons of Surrey—a statement which the •hearer interpreted to suit himself, be- lieving that Lord Hampton was endeavouring to cover from his—Adlowe's—too close observation another of her ladyship's periodical absences or se - elusions. Enraged, and determining to proceed on a new plan, Adlowe set out that very afternoon for Wales, stopping over night at a way station to call upon a friend, and continuing his journey to the Park in the morning. By this abrupt departure Adlowe missed seeing Detective Rush, who called upon him at his hotel directly after the profligate lord had left it. 1 It was on the morning subsequent to Adlowe's ' departure that the detective telegraphed to his , lordship at the Park. The events of that day, as - connected with Adlowe and Giralda have been . traced.

At The Evergreens it passed like the preceding one gaily and delightfully. The third day passed, and evening came on with moonlight and starlight. a rarely pleasant evening for the season. The breezes moaned through the pints. making home IPotritorts aounly sweet. The fires glowea brightlY behind the steel bars of the grate, the lamps were lighted, and music and pleasant conversation gave .4 fleetnes to the hours. The curtains had not been drawn. They seldoM were, save on stormy nights, the perfect shade and seclusion of the place rendering intrusion into the - grounds nearly an impossibility. "How pleasant it is I" said the countess, break- ing a long silence, with a shiver and a look of pain. , "And yet I feel strangely anxious to-night. Some- thing is wrong with us, my husband! Can any- thing have happened to Giralda ? I wonder what # she is doing !' "You are nervous, Beatrice," responded her husband, tenderly. "I believe I have a touch Of the same disease," he added. "I do not feel 9uite myself to-night. Our anxieties are too much

_ for us." _ He drew her head upon his breast, and looked ; adoringly into her glorious eyes. . It was at this mement that his bitter enemy..." 7. Lord Adlowe—crept up to the window, parted the vines, and peered in! At the sight that met his gaze, Adlowe reeled sg .' if struck with a mortal illness. He beheld the woman he loved—the woman 118, • had deemed haughty, icy cold in her nature, mu: '. heartless—he beheld her like a very goddess el : love, brightly glowing, her eyes shining like twill , stars, her countenance radiant with a rare hap& ; ness, her head pillowed on a man's breast. . And that man! How Adlowe's burning eye* searched his features I . Evidently tall, he was magnificently formed, broad of shoulder, deep of chest, and majestic of ; mien. His bronzed, even swarthy complexion, hi° heavy black eyebrows, his black hair and beard, , made up a perfect Spaniard in seeming. Adowe had believed him to be Geoffrey • Trevelyan, in disguise. This belief received •, sudden shock at sight of him. "That man Geoffrey Trevelyan ?" he asked himself. "Can time have changed the bright, laughing boy, of alight figure and delicate constitir , tion into this grave, dark, bearded man? lee :. hardly believe it. This must he some new comPii; cation. Heaven! Row Beatrice leans on hirn How she loves him 1 I wish I could hear 1111 - voice I " His glance roved around the room and rest . upon the two boys, who were seated on a Ouch :- close together, the elder brother engaged in putting : a few finishing touches to a drawing. . His gaze might have scorch them both—it via° : so keen and burning. "The elder boy is the Lady Beatrice -all over, he thought. "If that dark count be really Geoffrey', , that black-eyed boy is the future Marquis Trey*" _ lyan. The younger boy—that lily-faced, Ode*" haired, blue-eyed girl-boy—is much like Geoffrei was in his boyhood, only that my Cousin had were life and spirit and vim." He pressed his face closer against the glass- The Lady Beatrice turned towards the windoir —started—stared—then leaped to her feet with . ' wild and ringing shriek. . "She saw me 1" cried the villain, leaping be_....eks "I'm in for it now. I must face that man Wu.' he has time to escape." div.head: WITH DI. ON THE DEE.
div.p: WITH DI. ON THE DEE.
A TALE OF A TUB.
BY MR. JOHN PEERS.

I was rather surprised, one day, in the spring of the present year, to be accosted by an old acquaint- ance as I was passing down Bridge-street and straightway enlisted as a pressed-man for a voyage from Warrington to Chester, by way of Hoylake and Hilbre. My friend Diogenes—Di.---for short, had determined to buy the yacht "Torn Bowling" and rig her up as his " tub " to reside in on the upper waters of the Dee; as a "fishing box." Other members of the aristocracy having their "shooting boxes," he—the unconventional aristocrat—would set up a floating "fishing box." Now my friend, all the world knows, at least all the world w3rth knowing, the world of Warrington, all this world knows my friend "Di.," alias Captain Joseph Clare, is not an integer—not in fact an individual, but a fraction of one—the better part of a man let me hasten to add, with the addendum that it will not do to say that he is not all there! I hope no one will think this, as it is quite the reverse of the Cap- tain's own estimate. lam glad of this. It is such a comfort to have a good opinion of one's self; so sustaining in our passage through this vale of unsagacity. Now Di. and I, we are of one opinion, —we are at one in this ; he has a firm belief in the entire wisdom of his own opinions, and so have I. But this is a digression. Now Di., although all there in this respect, is only the fraction of an individual and is not the man he once was. Though a man of more than average understanding, he has unfortunately only one leg; and, though in good health, has one foot in the grave. Now, two legs are very useful in knocking about the narrow decks of a small boat. Hence it was determined between us that the boat should have the Manx complement of legs in her crew—if his one and my pair of odd ones could be so called. Be this as it may the boat was bought and had to be fetched from the Weaver above Frodsham Bridge. So one fine day—let this phrase,be regarded purely in a conventional sense —the day had lucid intervals when it did not rain but spent its energies in blowing—we went over and found her with plenty of water inside and a strong sediment of mud. The water we got rid of— the mud we took as ballast. Threading the wind- ing shallows of this little river.raightily encouraged by the native expression of opinion that we never should escape the toils of the many mudbanks, we emerged, in a squall of wind, upon the waters of the Ship Canal. Here we were met by the demand of a pound as toll! This unjust and illegal demand, Di. most emphatically refused, but Was at last pre- vailed upon to sign an agreement to pay all legal demands. Now as the boat had gone up the Weaver I in its natural state of a tributary of the Mersey,and I tbe Ship Canal Co. had obstructed this natural right of waterway, they were bound in equity, and I be- lieve in law, to permit free and untolled passage, in this case, back into the Mersey. Howbeit, after all these trials of temper and judgment the good ship "Tom Bowling" was beached successfully near the Iron Bridge. Thereupon ensued an era of of scraping and tarring—of rubbing and polishing —of caulking and paying—of painting and puttying —till that beach had the semblance of a carpenter's yard. All through the flowery month of May and the genial days of June the sights and sounds of these varied industries enlivened the beach, and the young days of July had given place to those of the middle—ere the word was passed that the ship was ready—but was hopelessly neaped. So, from the 16th, the start had to be deferred to the 23rd Julflast, when we started from the dred- ger-haunted vicinity of the New Diversion and sped before a favouring breeze past the old familiar "locaties" and landmarks of our river, until brought up by that ugly bit of shoal at Thorn ,Hedge. The incoming tide at last enabled us to continue our course down to New Ferry where we landed our passenger Mr. G. Roughley and then went up to our anchorage for the night. Then, "Lodgings for single men "were required by two singular men—a pair of oddities—Captain Clam and his oddman. Now the" Tom Bowling" among her other good qualities cannot enumerate that of having" spacious and commodious sleeping accommodation" No! "Bowl- ing" is a shallow, light draughted craft, with a re- markably low freeboard. Hence it may be easily conceived that there is no great waste of headroom under her decks. Indeed when squatting upon the "ceilings," i.e., the flooring boards in the cock pit, the head and shoulders are above the decks. But. to properly appreciate the excessively limited accommodation afforded to her crew by this floating dish, the reader should submit to the experience of being a foremast man, as I was, and " pig in " be- tween the cable and the mast, under the foredeck decklight. Having once got in—and it is about as difficult to get out as it is to get in—the modus operandi consisting of a peristaltic action of the body when dorsally recumbent ; in other words you lie on your back and worm yourself under the dells, due care being taken not to abrade the personal pro- minencies. This mode of vermicular progression must be aided by grasping the canines of the deck or other auxiliary projections. Then having reached the confines of your berth—which will be suffi- ciently indicated by the bump your head may get from contact with the bulkhead of the cable tier— you may rest—but you must not be rash, when thus "cribbed, cabined and confined." The man who would too hastily be stirring, must be a spoon, for if, like myself, he was not behind the door when noses were given out,he will find that projection in most uncomfortable contact with his wooden canopy, for there is I should say a liberal allowance of some six inches between the head and the deck when sleeping. Considerable circumspection is required on awakening to prevent undue lessening of this most desirable distance, the consequences of which are uncomfortable and are often accompanied by sounds which could not be mistaken for orisons. Then, what time the cook rings the breakfast bell— otherwise, clinks the somewhat limited culinaries of his cuisine—we have to worm ourselves retro- gressively out of this dog-hole until behind the mast, and then to save the prolonged agonies of a backward scramble down the long tunnel-like hatch-covered cockpit, we kick off one of the four hatches and emerge—a la Jack-in-the-box—into the free air of heaven, and pass, by way of the deck, to the after part of the cockpit where Di. has rigged up a removable arrangement of boards as a cabin under which it is possible to sit upright when it rains or blows or is cold. Here we luxuriate in the delicacies of the season—or rather of the seasoning— the best of all, that given by constant exercise in the open air. We usually prefer to breakfast with the " lid " off, a/ fresco, when free from the too obtrusive observation of an inquisitive public. Coffee and eggs, sometimes rising to the ulterior extravagance of fried bacon, these with an occasional change to tinned meats, were our materials for breakfast. The " ser- vice " for this meal consisted of three pint cups,two pocket knives,l6 fingers, and four thumbs. An inverted bucket saved for a seat, and the sea breezes furnished us with a sufficient appetite to render welcome even this homely fare. Now on Tuesday morning, July,24th, 1894,the tide was at full at Liverpool at the early hour of three in the morning. All round,the clank of pauls and the rattle of cables indicated preparations for a start by many of the vessels near us. We, like-minded, weighed and set sail before a whole-sail breeze from about S.E. The full tide and strong breeze made old "Tom" jump about in a very lively fashion, but she soon skipped the distance between New Ferry and New Brighton. In the Rock Channel we found some boats, line fishing. We must follow so laud- able an example; but the results were not of an encouraging nature, were not, indeed, an adequate reward for even the small amount of patience ex- pended upon it. Besides, was not the tide running out, and the lake into which we wanted to get, rapidly emptying? So why stay here wasting our persuasive powers upon unappreciative fish? So we again weighed, and fled rapidly before the in- creasing gale, over the still covered portion of the Dove spit, until we met the out-coming waters of Hoylake. Here the opposing forces of tide and wind kicked up a considerable bit of hollow sea, making careful steering a matter of necessity. This being given, we rounded No. I L. red buoy in safety and ran up to No. 2 L. red buoy,and there grounded her on the clean sand, and—fed—small word with large significance under the circumstances,i.e., early start and little or no breakfast. While waiting for the incoming tide which was to carry us through the lake,and after collecting a few of the arrears of sleep due to us from the morning, two of our complement of three feet went barely over the sands in corn-. pany with a bucket in search of certain bivalvular delicacies these sands afford. These Di. and I thoroughly enjoyed and he.indeed,afterwards, when far away from these cockle strewn sands, expressed his desire for more, his appreciation being probably none the less because of their small cost. For Di. hates to give a penny for what he can get for id., and he would have read his prototype of Athens a lesson in economy for throwing away his cup wihen drinking from his hand. Our modern tub- dweller would have sold it, or stored it up for future use. For Di. has the bump of acquisitive-

div.head: IiTE EKAIVIINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 25 1894.
div.p: IiTE EKAIVIINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 25 1894.

ness largely developed. The maxim upon which he acts is—" Throw nothing away which may be of future use." The exercise of this faculty once nearly caused the coat to be torn from his back. in set- ting the mainsail he managed to get the "yang" under the bulging odds and ends filled pocket of his coat and, had he not cried, hold! I might have gone near to hoisting him out of the boat. This same pocket contains a wonderful collection of miscel- lania. The articles are perhaps too numerous to mention separately but if you will get one of Lewis's catalogues and knock off about 10 per cent. that might give a fair idea of its inventory. In this emnium gatherum there may be everything you want, but the difficulty is to separate the goats from the sheep. Indeed Di. suffers from a plethora of oddments—an embarras de riehesses of uncon- sidered trifles—anything from a monkey-wrench to a sail-needle finds a place in that capacious pocket. However, Di. has the merit of pocketing only that which is his own, a quality which is not too fully developed in the 'boating fraternity. But, bless me, I have got so entangled amongst the tranklement of Di.'s pocket that I forgot to mention that the tide has now reached the boat and the sails must once more be cast loose, or rather must not be cast loose, as the wind is now very strong and blowing up the lake in the direction we wish to go, and, as we wish to ,go easily, and the lake is full of craft, we start under bare poles and get opposite the coast-guard houses, where again the anchor is cast, to stay until more water has made. This soon occurs,when we pole our way up to the head of the lake and through the intricacies of the too level sands which stand in the place of a "deep "at the Red Rocks. Passing these we soon got into the haven of Hilbre Pool and settled there for the night. Now for these who love the sea I cannot imagine a nicer place to lie in than Hilbre Pool in fine weather. You have the ' advantage of diversity, not always afloat and impri- soned in the boat, but part of the time aground on the sands and able to take exercise on the Island and mark its sea-worn rocks, or, when afloat, admire the pellucid waters on which we live. Now, when the sea does you good it is a good thing, but when it makes you bad I Bah! Now these remarks may serve as a prelude to the mention of the fact that my friend Di. did begin to feel pale when that bothering ground swell set in. I thought some- thing was in the wind when he quietly extracted from his mouth what now stands, for him, as the sole representative of one of Nature's early gifts to man—his manducatorials. But let us draw a veil over the subsequent events, remarking only that the preparations were not thrown away along with that which caused them. Oh! how Di. did long for as solid a foundation for his " tub " as had his no less philosophic Grecian fore-runner, He would have given heaps of sunshine for an accession of stability. But, however, all things must have an end—even sea-sick patients malison of the sea—and so, as the sea subsided, so did our stomachic per- turbation, and when, in the evening, the tide was out we replenished the inner man,and then strolled round the shores of the Island admiring its scenery and surroundings. (To be continued.)

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held on Tuesday afternoon at Dutton Workhouse, Mr. John Mclntyre presiding. The remaining gentlemen present were the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner. and J. Hanby, Messrs. James Brandreth, H. E. Heywood, J. M. Williams, James Knowles, S. Wood- ward, John Weir, T. Lewis, W. Whitlow, James Whitlow, John Ashton, clerk, George Ashton, deputy clerk, and J. Farrington, nuisance inspector. PROPOSED 1111-APPOINTMENT SF THE NUISANCE INSPECTOR. _ _ .

Mr. Heywood gave notice of his intention to move at their next meeting the re-appointment of Mr. J. Farring- ton as nuisance inspector to the Authority at a salary to be then affixed.—Mr. Aaron enquired if a committee could be appointed and meet early for the purpose of considering the subject. —The Rev. J. Hanby thought it would be necessary to review the work and also to dis- cuss the question of salary.—Mr- Aaron remarked that there would be additional work when the new townships were added to the Union.—Mr. Heywood considered that it would be as well to think about the new townships when they were added to the Union.—Ultimately it was decided to meet at such a time as would allow of the question receiving the required discussion. SANITARY INSPECTOR'S REPORT.

Mr. Farrington submitted a plan for the approval of the Authority for the extension of Whitley Board Schools.—The plan was approved.—The Inspector applied for a certificate of occupation for eight houses which had been erected by Mr. Thomas Goulden, in Halton-lane, Halton. The certificate was granted.

TYPHOID FEVER AT *WESTON POINT. Mr. Farrington reported a case of typhoid fever at Weston Point, in a house where two other cases had previously existed. He had reason to believe that some- thing was wrong with the water at this house which was supplied frem the Runcorn Improvement Commis- sioners mains. He had been told that the water changed in colour about three times some days and was not fit to drink. The Inspector suggested that a sample of the water be taken from the tap for the purposes of analysis.—Mr. Aaron thought that the water main passed under the Weston Point Canal and that there was a leakage somewhere near this point which would prob- ably account for the condition of the water. He there- fore proposed that the Inspector be instructed to obtain a sample and submit it to the County Analyst for the purpose of its being analysed.—Mr. Heywood seconded, and the proposition was carried.

div.head: DIPHTHERIA AT WESTON POINT.
div.p: DIPHTHERIA AT WESTON POINT.

Mr. Farrington further reported a ease of diphtheria existing in a house at Weston Point. He had visited the house on the previous Monday and after an inspection had found that the drainage was defective and of primi- tive construction. The back yard to the premises was very small. He had spoken to the agent who superin- tended the houses and he had promised to make certain improvements which would remedy the nuisance. AUDITORS' REPORT.

The Clerk read a letter from the auditors who had just completed the audit of the authority's books. They reported that they had examined all vouchers &c. and had found everything correct, and satisfactory.

div.head: FINANCIAL.
div.p: FINANCIAL.

Mr. Brandreth,in submitting the report of the Finance Committe, intimated that the accounts passed on to thern authority for payment was £133 13s. sd. These were pressing and he desired them to be paid at once.—Mr Heywood seconded the adoption of the report which was carried.

AN INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL REQUIRED. The attention of the Board was drawn, by Mr. Hey- wood, to the fact that a notice had been received by the Board of Guardians from the Runcorn Commissioners relative to the termination of the agreement between the two bodies referring to the reception of patients in the infectious diseases hospital. He was under the impres- sion that the agreement only embraced Runcorn, Halton, and Weston townships.—The Clerk said that was so. Mr. Heywood, continuing, observed that the only reason why he referred to it was that the three months, in which they were to terminate the agreement, only urged upon the authority the greater necessity of possessing a hospital themselves. If they had one they could then enter into arrangements with the Guardians for the re- ception of patients. He suggested that the corn mittee who were dealing with the question of providing an in- fectious diseases hospital should make more strenuous efforts to secure one.—Mr. Williams replied that neither of the sites they had had in view would be approved by the Local Government Board who required that the hospital should be a quarter of a mile from any inhabited house. The committee were meeting again in a fort- night for the purpose of discussing the matter, fully.— The Rev. J. Hanby asked that if the authority would have to acquire a piece of ground of the size mentioned to build a hospital upon, would it be possible afterwards to build a house about 100 or 200 yards distant from the hospital?—Mr.Heywood replied that it would be possible, but it would remain with the Sanitary Authority to decline to give their certificates of occupation.

div.head: "LYNCH LAW IN AMERICA."
div.p: "LYNCH LAW IN AMERICA."
MEETING AT WARRINGTON.

A meeting was held in Golborne-street Baptist Chapel on Monday evening, when an address was given on the above subject by the Rev. Peter Stanford, a coloured preacher, and for some time pastor of the Wilberforce Memorial Church, Bir- mingham. The chair was 'occupied by Councillor Henry Roberts, J.P. Letters of apology were read by the Rev. D. W. Roberts, from the Mayor (Alder- man E. Greenell), Rev. J. W. Varley, Mr. E. J. Guest, J.P., and Mr. John Caldicot. The Camastaie said there were not many subjects without a humorous side, but in regard to the subject they were met to consider that night there was no humorous side to it. Not more than a century ago or thereabouts, the people then living in the United States, men and women of their own kith and kin,rebelled against the government of this country because those who repre- sented us at the head of affairs at that time, were foolish enough to attempt ti make them pay that which was not fair and not honest. They succeeded in throw- ing off the yoke of this country, and were recognized in a few years, as a people of themselves, with their own right to self-government. In the manifesto which they issued as a justification for their rebellion they used the words _that all men were created equal. Those words had been in the forefront in the civil, religious, and political progress in the United States ftom that day to the present. Years ago there was another terrible fight in that country for the maintenance of the very same principle. He remembered going with other school boys to the shop of Mr. Powlson, at Market Gate, who was editor and proprietor of a newspaper, since. defunct, to see the notices of the results of conflicts during that war, and how sad they were to see the con- tinual defeats which the Northern army suffered at the hands of the Southerners, because they knew that if the North did not succeed, slavery would be established and maintained upon a more solid basis than before. They knew the result of that war. It secured the freedom of the slave. But it was not sufficient to purchase his freedom by blood and money. Freedom from slavery was only one step towards brotherhood and political progress. But instead of the progress that should have been made since that time, there had been during the last few years a distinct retrogression. In the southern states if a coloured man was only suspected or accused by a malignant enemy in wrong doing he was in 'many cases taken in hand by a mob without trial or anything else. (Shame.) Well in a country like America it was a slur upon her honour. It was a matter of respon- sibility to all people who had regard for freedom and right. They were met that night to hear from Mr. ' Stanford some further details in order that they might help to form public opinion on the matter. They could not have a better exponent, as Mr. Stanford was born a slave. They welcomed him amongst them, and he could assure him that they would assist him as far as it lay in their power. The Rev. NUM STANFORD at the outset of his address quoted a number of statistics showing the remarkable progress which the negro race had made since their emancipation from slavery about 30 years ago in educa- tional and other matters, and denied the imputation that they were an idle and lazy people. It was hardly to be expected that people who had spent the greatest portion of their lives in slavery should all at once arise to that position of civilization which many of their friends wished to see them. But those who had watched them closely since their emancipation were prepared to admit that under the most difficult circumstances they had cer- tainly taken a position which they need not be ashamed of. (Applause.) The speaker then dealt at length with some criticisms of the Rev. J. Hall in a letter to the "Christian Commonwealth "in which he stated that the white people of America bore with the negro as no other people would. The speaker stated that he had received an invitation to take the pastorate of a church with over 800 members in one of the Southern states but because he was married to an English lady he was unable to go back to his people. If he did go he would most likely receive five years penal servitude, or perhaps be lynched by white people, because a black man there could not live with a white woman. The negro race had borne with the doings of the Americans as no other race under the sun would have done. Referring to lynching at present being carried on, he stated that he had a letter from a friend two weeks ago stating that an English minister paid out of his own pocket one hundred dollars to aid a lynching party. (Shame.) He was not pre- pared to say that the church was looking on and doing nothing to stay lynching. Latterly, he had noticed in the newspapers that the number of persona lynched had averaged one person each day. What was America doing in order to solve the problem? Some of the people of the States had suggested the emigration of the negroes to Liberia. He (the speaker) was of the opinion that after living for years in the Southern States it would be impossible for them to live long in Liberia. Further, the negro had a right to stay in the United States, and there they intended to stay, and would not be crushed out. The speaker afterwards spoke of the steps the negroes were taking against lynching by means of the Equal Rights Society. When lynching occurred, the matter was investigated by the society, and compensa- tion was sued for. He spoke of the work the Society had done, and gave an instance of how a negro was lynched for an offence which was afterwards proved he had not committed. In conclusion he asked his hearers to assist them in obtaining just treatment at the hands of white people. The Rev. D. W. ROBERTS moved the following resolu tion : "This meeting having heard the Rev. Peter Stan- ford, England's coloured preacher, on the lynch law question in the United States of America resolves that we call upon and plead with all white Christians to exert their influence in preventing further reprisals and in in- sisting upon the enforcement of law and order, and also that a branch of the Birmingham committee for the con- sideration of lynching be formed in this town." Mr. E. PICKAVANCE seconded the resolution, which on being put to the meeting was carried unanimously. The Rev. PETER STANFORD asked for volunteers to form a committee in Warriagton. Several persons held up their hands in response, and a committee was formed. A vote of thanks to the Chairman was passed on the pro- position of the Rev. Peter Stanford, seconded by Mr. R. btorey. A collection was taken, and realised a satis- , tory amount.

BRUNNER, MOND, AND CO. -- A BIG DIVIDEND. The shareholders of Brunner, Mond, and Co., Limited, held their twenty-seventh half-yearly general meeting on Tuesday, at the Law Associa- tion rooms, Cook-street, Mr. John T. Brunner, M.P. presiding over a large attendance. The report for the half-year was submitted, and the directors therein reported that on the profit and less account there was a credit balance for the half-year of £150,714 Bs., which, with the amount of £81,929 9s. 7d. brought forward from the previous half-year made a total of £232,643 17s. 7d. The directors proposed to deal with the above balance as follows :—Dividend on the preference capital at 7 per cent, per annum, £15,257 16s. 3d.; dividend on the ordinary 'capital, at 30 per cent. per annum, £124,793 12s. 6d. ; amount to be written off patents account, £2,500 ' • balance to be carried forward, £90,092 Bs. 10d.-232,643 17s. 7d. The directors have made a call (final) of £3 per share on the ordinary shares, now £8 103. paid (L 1 103. to rank for dividend and £1 103. as balance of premium), payable on the let October, 1894. The directors resolved on the 4th April, 1894, to adopt the Forged Transfers Acts, 1891 and 1892. The Chairman moved that the report and balance- sheet be adopted,and that the dividend as therein recom- mended be declared, and stated that the directors had made some additions to the freehold land of the corn- pany, besides considerable additions to the alkali works. They were building works at Silvertown, on the Thames, and he was happy to say that, although they were not completed, they were successfully started a few 'weeks ago. They would have to spend more money on those works. Their intention was to double the present capacity, so they would have to look forward to a fur- ther capital expenditure on that account. An amount of £2,000 had been written off the freehold land, but a similar thing had occurred before. A few years ago they bought a small quantity of land in the neighbour- hood of their works at Winnington, at a price which they considered to be above its intrinsic value, and on that account they wrote off a certain sum. Cn the present occasion also they had bought land for the protection of the company at what they regarded as a fancy price, and they had again written off £2,000. The fact that they had on two occasions taken this course ought to be to the shareholders an indication of the spirit in which the capital account had been worked. If ever a body of shareholders ought to be content with the efforts of those to whom their money had been entrusted, those whom he was addressing occupied that position. (Hear, hear.) The market price of their products had fallen in the last twelve or eighteen months to an enormous extent, and it must be perfectly clear that something had been done to meet that great fall. The staff also had worked most admirably. The income-tax was continually growing, and he warned them that it would be larger next time. (Laughter, and a shareholder: "Then change the Government.") Mr. C. J. Galloway seconded the motion, which was carried. Alderman James Webster moved—" That the director!' other than the managing directors be paid the sum of £5OO for their services during the half-year ending the 30th June, 1894." Be said the shareholders were de- lighted to have an opportunity of acknowledging the great services rendered to them by the directors. Mr. Geo. Jones seconded, and the motion was adopted. Messrs. T. W. Read and Co.. chartered accountants, were reappointed auditors; and on the motion of Mr. Ludwig Mond, seconded by the chairman, a cordial vote of thanks was tendered to the staff. A vote of thanks to the chairman closed the proceedings. Ask

div.head: ODDFELLOWSHIP IN WARRINGTON.
div.p: ODDFELLOWSHIP IN WARRINGTON.
PAPER ON SECESSION.

At a meeting of the above lodge, on Monday evening, Bro. F. G. Emson in the chair, there was a large number of members, in addition to district officers, to listen to a paper announced to be read by Bro. Barnwell on "Secession." In introducing his paper, he said he had tried to find out what was the cause of so many secessions from the Order year after year, and what should be the remedy. No fewer than 23,617 seceded from the Order last year. It was, there- fore, time that the members of the Manchester Unity consulted together to prescribe a medicine for this ter- rible disease of secession, for it must be known that for every three members initiated into the Order last year they lost two. Admitted by initiation in e Deaths „ „ ...................8,596
- Secessions IP /.

10.647 Number transferred from Juveniles to Lodges The following proposition was made In event of any member being in distress by reason of sickness, or loss of employment, or other cause, proved to the satisfaction of the lodge, provided the members give notice to the secretary in. writing of his distress through loss of em- ployment, illness or otherwise, the lodge shall have power to allow such member to fall into arrear for any length of time in their discretion, such member to be in full benefit for sickness and half benefit for death during such time he is allowed to be in arrear. When a mem- ber is allowed to be in arrear, a resolutionshall be passed by the lodge to that effect, and a copy of the resolution shall be sent to the member." If this proposition, or one similar, was passed by the A.M.C. to be inserted in the general rules, they would be directing a severe blow at secessions. It might be said that such a proposition would not affect that lodge, because they could relieve poor and distressed members from their distress fund—he did not suppose it would—but it would greatly affect those lodges that had not a distress or benevolent fund. Another point was that the distress funds, as laid down in the general rules, were not made compulsory and, therefore, it was that so many lodges had not such a fund, simply because they were not forced by rule to have one. He believed that if lodges deter- mined to have a certain number of social evenings each year, it would be the means of bringing together a large number of members to whom the ordinary routine of business was too dry. The old saying that "Music hath charms" would be a first class remedy for such mem- bers. He had another suggestion to make, and that was the filling up of the minor offices of the lodge, viz., the right and left supportors to the N.G. and V.G. the warden, conductor, and guardian. Such offices, small and insignificant as they may appear to some of their brethren, were a source of great encouragement to young members. Another way to meet the difficult subject of secessions would be to establish a fund in lodges to which the members could voluntarily subscribe to enable the lodge officers to pay the contributions of members who were in distress or out of work, and who were not able to pay their contributions, thus keeping the mem- ber in benefit, the officers to have power to pay such contributions without a resolution of the lodge, avoiiing the exposure of the brother's name. Of course they would rely on the officers satisfying themselves as to the brother's need. He hoped that after they had discussed the matter they would find a solntion that would give satisfaction to the members of the lodge, the members of this district, and the members of the Manchester Unity in general. (Applause.) The paper was criticized, and a lengthy discussion ensued, in which the following took part :—P.G.F.J. Whittle, P.P.G.M. Massey, N.G.F.G. Emson, P.D.G.M. A. Boyle. Bro. Lincoln Scott, and P.P.G.M.John Emson, secretery. The resolution suggested by the essayist was adopted by the lodge. Votes of thanks to Bro. Barnwell for his paper, and to the officers, brought a happy evening to a close.

div.head: OXFORD LOCAL EXAMINATIONS.
div.p: OXFORD LOCAL EXAMINATIONS.
LOCAL SUCCESSES.

The Oxford Local Examination division lists for the year 1894 have been issued at Oxford. The examinations were held in July at 94 centres (an increase of 13 on the previous year), of which 12 were new centres, and 36 were special local centres, at which the local examinations were combined with school examinations. The total number of candidates examined this year was 4,242, viz. 2,878 juniors and 1,354 seniors; of these 1,975 juniors and 852 seniors passed, making a total of 2,827. The total number of candidates and other persons entered for the examination was 4,308, 76 of whom were absent from the examination.

OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WARUINPTON.
WYCLIFFE P.S.A. SOCIETY.

A largely attended meeting of this society' was bold on Sunday afternoon. The chair was occupied by Mr. William Hickman. He urged them to makethe society a greater power for good in the town, and said he hoped that before long they would have a P.S.A;-brotbersitt- ing on the Town Council. Mr. A. Corney delivered the address. He took for his subject the "speedwell" plant or veronica, and in a most interesting manner, drew some useful lessons from the life of Saint Veronica. The. Rev. J. Yonge announced that the membership was still increasing, several members having been enrolled that day. Mr. W. H. Payton the organist, played an organ solo, and the Rev. J. White condtnted the devotional part of the service,

ACCIDENT AT LYII2II BRIDOE.—James Stubbs, a carter 1 in the employ of Mr. John Forster, farmer, Rush Green, Lymm, met with a rather serious accident on Saturday. He was leading a horse attached to a cart down the canal bridge when the animal stumbled and fell,and one of the shafts struck Stubbs in the middle of the back. Medical assistance was procured, and it was found that Stubbs' injury was of a serious character. BAPTIST SUNDAY Scnoot.—The annual Sunday school sermons in connection with the Baptist Chapel, Higher- lane, were preached on Sunday, morning and evening, by the Rev. A. Tyldesley, of Sunnyside. The subject of the morning's discourse was "Spread Litter," and of the evening "Unknown Power." A children's service was , conducted during the afternoon. There were good con- gregations, and the collections taken were in aid of the Sunday school.

MESSRS. CROSFIELD AND THEIR WORKMEN. —AN ABSURD Rl.l‘lOl3R. Sir,—WO shall be glad if you will allow us to con- tradict in your columns an extraordinary rumour that has been spread to the eff.ct that we are about to 4' sack " 200 men at our works, and replace them with Germans. We heard of this absurd report, which has not a sha- dow of foundation for it,about a fortnight since,and ig- nored it as idle gossip, set going at the instigation of some prejudiced or interested individuals in order to in- jure us in our t -ade. The same report has, however, since come to our ears from various quarters, and as it had now reached districts outside the town, where it has less chance of being refuted, we think it is about time to put a stop to it. But in doing so, we should he very sorry to join in any cry of mere pr ju lice or intolerance. With your permission we have a word to say on this point. The intensity of modern competition has been felt in Germany even more severely than in England. One result of this is that, as Professor Huxley puts it, the sciences are one after another dragged in to assist manufactures. And so in Germany, chemistry as ap- plied to practical manufacture has been developed to a high degree, and to a very large extent the success of German manufacturers (so far as it goes) is due to it. Those who have been actually engaged on re.earch work involved in this development, or who have on the spot followed up the investigations and results so obtainen, are, in our I judgment, the best men to apply them practically. we believe that such men of eminent scientific attainments, vebere they have been induced to settle in Eruland and become naturalized among us, may contribute to our commercial success. not less than those who came over telaclt.the time of the Flemings and Flugennts. The simple fact is. that English manufacturers can in this way,beotlight the Germans with their own weapons. Between availing ourselves of the assistance of such scientific specialists and importing cheap and cotnpara- tively unskilled foreign labour to replace British labrair.l there is,we are sure your readers will agree,all the differ- ence in the world. Among tle 600 workmen we employ, one only is German, if he can he called so, a t-r having lived 20 years in this country. Nor, as it happens.do we at the moment, contemplate adding one single foreigner to our staff. It has not even crossed our minds to do so. Whether we may at any time con-id.r it neces- sary to do ao, is neither here nor there. We ar.ly men- tion the fact in order that your readers may know that this report is purely a work of imagination, in fact an impudent fabrication and fiction, which we beg to con- tradict in a manner as flat and Strang as the Queen's English,wittun parliamentary limits, will allow.—Yours etc.. JOS. CROSFIELD AND SONS. --- NEWTON COMMISSIONERS' POSTAL ARRANGE- MENTS, &C. Sir,—ln reading your raper last week I noticed with pain the chastisement the Chairman gave to Mr. Brierley for giving, as I understand, some information to the Secretary of the Newton Ratentyers Comtnitteee, Mr. Byrne. I take it Mr. Brier'ey is the acting cffiy.er for the ratepayers, and if the representative of such an influen- tial body as the Newton Ratepayers Committee call on him specially, as was done in the present instance, and ask him a few questions of a public nature, I say dis- tinctly, be is bound to answer them. lam informed Mr. Brierley did not tell anything that was not well known. and the public censure the Chairman took upon himself to admini-ter was in the worst possible taste, being entirely undeserved and uncalled for. But why all this secresy ? If the Chairman and Mr. Ormand, who !understand are really the Board, are doing right, why should they be afraid of the ratepayers knowing what they are doing. At present certain things only are allowed to appear in print, and we have not yet forgot- ten the important Commissioners meeting held last year tie consider the wards question, when the press was excluded. The town's business should he conducted openly; tiff ra should be no cause for sucpicion by con- cealment. I hope this vestion will be taken up by the condidates at the election in November next. Can an autocratic Chairman keep the ratepayers in the dark as to their own affairs? Could another eight men be found (professing to his public men) who would sit in silence and allow a Chairman to censure a tried and faithtul officer of 30 years standing for doing his duty! It is monstrous to think of.—l am yours respectfully, RATEPAYER NO. 3. Newton, August 21st, 1894.

On Monday evening, when the time allowed for the nomination of candidates for the vacancy in the Howley ward expired, two candidates had been nominated, viz., Mes‘rs. James Battersby and John Evans. The following is the list of the nomination

papers. JAMES BATTERSBY, 22 Cartwright-street, filesmith. proposed by Samuel Wright, seconded by Henry Leigh, and assented to by William Gregson, John Hill, Samuel Johnson, William Spencer, George Beckley,John Ellison, William Hewitt Dutton, and Charles Wainwright.—Also proposed by James Parr, seconded by Henry Malkin,and assented to by Frederick Leigh. Benjamin Hell, William Hill, James Weave, John Berry, Joseph Whinow, Thomas Dakin, and George Hunter. JOHN EVANS, 33, Church street, Warrington, licensed victualler and brewer. proposed by Arthur Browne, seconded by James Crawford Ross, and assented to by Joseph Dolan. Jacob Sankey, Thomas Locker, Richard Jones, James Atherton Gibson, Alfred Downes, Joseph Albinson and Thomas Dinwiddie.—Also proposed by John Dewhurst, secor.ded by Joseph Harrison, and assented to by Thomas Grime, Wm. Johnson, David Hooley, Arthur Percy Grange, Henry Johnson Longton, Moses Eckersley, Frederick Robert Pierpoint and John Stainforth Hill.— Also proposed by James Cannel!, seconded by Thomas Mason, and assented to by John Cross, Joseph Birchall, John White, Samuel Johnson, Charles Daniels, Napoleon Bailey, Jabez Smith and S imuel Keen.—Further pro- posed by Wm. Bolton, seconded by Samuel Davies, and assented to by Andrew Richardson Robertson, T. James Emmess, John Ewings, Wm. Lee, Wm. Clare, Herbert Thomas Bolton, James Spencer and James Appleton. On Tuesday afternoon the Mayor (Alderman Greenall) attended at the Council Cbimber at the l'iwn Hall to bear objections to any of the nomination papers. As neither Mr. Battersby nor Mr. Evans lodged any, the candidates will now go to poll. Tile election will take place on Monday, the polling berth being at the National schools. It will be remembered that Mr. Battershy is the Trades Council candidate, and relies for his success upon the labour vote. Mr. Evans comes out as an "independent "candidate.

NOTES ON GAMES AD
ATHLETICS.
CRICKET.

Still another draw for the Warrington team ! They have surely this season earned the title 01 champion dra,wists. They have made some very lucky draws too, and that on Saturday was one of them. The scene of their latest exploit was at Sefton Park, where they met one of the clubs they had obtained the upper hand of earlier in the season. They took a wry strong team with them in order to emphasize if possible the first match. They however found the SAtonians equally determined to show that the first match was a mi,take, and they almost succeeded in doing so, but not quite.

The Warrington team went in first, and were unfortu- nate in finding Oakley, who sometimes plays for Lan- cashire, in a very dangerous humour with the ball. He bowled with such effect that he obtained seven wickets at the expense of only 47 runs. They began very disas- trously for R. Smith was dismissed by Oakley when only four had been scored. Bates and Wordsworth carried the score to 23, when the latter had also to go back, and S. M. Crosfi. Id simply walked to the wickets and then had to walk back again. Callon contributed 14, but Clarke only made three when Bates, who bad gone in ; first was dismissed with the score at 43, his share being 13. G. Clarke then came in, and as on many previous occasions, when his side was doing badly, he began hit- ting the bowling all over the field, and s-) well did he bat, that before he went the score had riseu to 110. He was very unfortunate in missing his 50, for he was only three off it when he was stumped. The " tail" also did very well for before the side was out 135 had been

scored. - The Sefton team soon made it appear that they would come very near if not past the Warrington total, for 45 had been scored before the first wicke. fell. It however almost appeared that a rot had set in then, for the next two batsmen were dismissed without a sing'. extra run being scored, Clarke the wicket keeper catching one,and stumping the other. Edwards now came in, and as- sisted Jones to raise the score to 101 when time was up. C. Jones was at that time only on run off his half cen- tury. There were no less than six bowlers who tried to obtain those three wickets, and the spoiling ot the bowl- ing analyses of several Warrington players was the result. S. M. Crisfield obtained one wicket for 13, and It. Smith two for 31. The remaining four bowlers had not a solitary wicket to reward their efforta. Maidens were very plentiful which without doubt prevented Sef- ton from gaining the victory. Out of 59 overs bowled, 26 resulted without a run being scored. It is therefore pretty evident that although the Warrington howlers could not obtain wickets, they could keep down the runs.

To-day (Saturday) there will most probably be a large crowd on the cricket enclosure at Arple7 to witness the benefit match of the two Warrington professionals,Bates and Clarke. The engagement is with the Werneth team, and as will be seen from the following names from which the teams are to be selected, there is every promise of at interesting match. Werneth : Messrs. W. L. Carritte, J. Armstrong, H. Heyworth, R. Scholes, A. Lowe, J. Parkes, J. H. Stott, F. Dixon, J. V. Andrew, S-aton, Bedford, Hall. Warrington : Messrs. S. M Crosfield, (Lan. Ctv), J. J. Crosfield, A. C. McLaren. (Lan. Ctv.) G. Clarke, J. Callon, W. Wordsworth, E. C4nnor, E. M. Grirfin, J. W. Bibby, L. A. Voisey, Mold, (Lan. Cty.), Bates, (Yorkshire Cty.) Clark.

The second team was much more successful than their seniors. '[hey played the match out and were ,uccessful by 31 rues. the Warrington team just reached the cen- tury when they were all dismissed. Bibby RA usual was very successful with both bat and ball he being the top scorer with 30, and having obtained the highest number of wickets, five for 17 tuns. Parry and Woo,ls were also very successful as they each obtained 19 runs. : '

The Sankey Wire Mills were too good by 18 runs for Earlestown St. John's, although the latter were assisted by Bates, the professional for the Newton Crirkat team. Their success was in a great measure due to the excellent batting of Marshall who scored 27. TIJe highest of the remaining scores was seven by Woodcock. Hobson and Simpson shared the wickets between them, the former taking six and the latter three.

The Christian Endeavour gained an easy victory over Buckley-street on Saturday. They made a very good start by Woods scoring 18, and this great advantage they were able to maintain and won by 51 to 28. Not one of the Buckley-street team got into double figures.

The Cairo-street Unity had to submit to defeat on Saturday, at the hands of St. Elphins. There was some good scoring on both sides, Phoenix with 24 and Scans- brick with 23 showed that they could play cricket as well as association football. On the Unity side Knowles obtained 23, and Monks 21. The big scorers on either side therefore almost balanced each other. It was ac- cordingly left to the smaller fry to decide the victory, and this the St. Elphins team did,gaining the victory by 70 to 60. The match presented many points of similarity between the two sides. The first =an in each case was run out, and it required three bowlers to get each side I out.

-- Among other matches, I notice that a v,!ry exciting game resulted in a win for St. Ann's over Bank-street by 46 to 42. Duckworth tried hard .to give his team the victory for he scored 20, not out. He could not find anyone to keep in with him, or he would without doubt have pulled off the match. Ellesmere-stOet could only score 17 against HolylTrinity 33. Towix—ds this 'Miller , scored 15.
FOOTBALL.

From the list of _fixtures of the Warrington Football Club published in another column it will be seen that the forthcoming season promises to be as successful as any of its predecessors. There are, of course, eighteen en- gagements in the Lancashire Rugby League competition, in which Warrington reached third position last year. It will be noticed that the two clubs which have been raised from the 2nd division to the first, are St. Helens and Leigh, and the Barrow and Broughton clubs have had to retire in their favour. The fixture with the latter club has been dropped, but Barrow maintain a place on the card. The Warrington club have been successful this year in arranging fixtures with Ulverston, and West Hartlepool.
CTCLING.

The weather, of late, has been far from encouraging to cyclists; nevertheless a fair number of the W.C.C. turned out for a run to S de Botanical Gardens on Saturday Unfortunately the pleasure was somewhat marred owing to the rain repeating its disagreeable performances of the past few weeks. "J. Pluvius " was also responsible for the limited number of wheelmen who took part in the " spin" to Knutsford on Tuesday evening. •

The party of seven who have been touring through North Wales have returned after an exceptionally plea- sant week's outing. Their route lay through Llangol- len, thence via Bettws, to Llandudno and from there, along the coast to Carnarvon. Then over Snowdon to Beddgelert and again down the coast to Barmouth. From the latter place the party wended their way along the Mawddach, through Dolgelly and Bala—home. The weather was very fair throughout the tour which ex- tended over 300 miles and is one of the best in North Wales, for anyone desirous of seeing some of the grand- est scenery in the British Isles.

At the National Cyclists Union meeting at Liverpool, on Monday night, Mr. E. Pickavance, sub-captain of the W.C.O , was elected a representative of the N.C.U. for the Warrington district. It may be mentioned that Mr. Pickavance is also the hon. secretary of the Roads Committee of the Liverpool Centre.

To-day is what is known as "Presidents day," when the president of the club (Mr. T. Morris, F.G.S.), the vice-president and friends are to go by 'bus to Cranage, acco;npanied by the members of the club on their machines. On reaching their destination the Party are to be provided with a free tea at the Cyclist's Farm. A start will be made at two o'clock by the con- vevance, followed by the cyclists at their usual time- -2.30.

Warrington cyclists gained further honours on Saturday. At the Whiston F. C. Snorts, B. Newcombe, of Warrington, took the first prize in the two-mile bicycle race, and Dutton, Warrington C.C., was third in the three miles. At the Leigh Athletic Club meeting on Saturday, A T. Daintith, Warrington, seciired second place in the mile bicycle handicap. " A Padgate cyclist. named Percy D. Gardiner, was also successful at the Wavertree Sports on Saturday. He succeeded in carrying off the first prize, obnsisting of a I silver tea and coffee -.Service, in the two milesrbicycle race.

BOWLS. A successful main -of bowls promoted by the pro- prietor of the" Bull's Bead," bowls, was brought to a condlusion on Monday evening. The first pGrtion was played off on Saturday aPernonn, and many exciting games were witnessed. But by far the most interesting game was the final tussle betwers E. Shaw, who received one point start, and John Jorieti, who was allotted four. The scratch man graduAlly; overhauled his opponent, and the record stood at one period—Shaw 14. Jones 12. The latter played pp splendidly, and effected a surprise at the finish by running out wini:ier, the final score reading as Jones-15, Shaky 14,

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY AUGUST 25, 1894.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY AUGUST 25, 1894.

ASSOCIATION. The members of the Orford Association Football Club held a general meeting on Friday night week. Mr. Chas. Grounds occupied the chair. It was announced that the club had entered the second division of the Warrington Football League, and Mr. W. J. Woods was elected to ' represent them at the meetings of - the League. The question of club colours was discussed, and it was decided to wear Oxford and Cambridge blue coloured jerseys. The Secretary (Mr. R. W. Corbett) stated that a good list of fixtures for the coming season had been arranged, including Farnworth C.E.T.S., Orford Cres- cent, Runcorn, and Warringtou Baseball. A most suc- cessful season is anticipated.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: SHIP CANAL.

UNFORTUNATE "TRIPPERS" ON THE CANAL. On Sunday, the Ship Canal Passenger Steam-hip Co., Limited, conveyed a: party of from 4,000 to 5,000 pas- sengers from Manchester to Liverpool. Sevf n steamers including the welt-known ferry boat." Snowdrop "of Liverpool were required to convey the excursionists to their destination. They left Trafford Wharf at 7 a.m., and passed through Latchford about half-past, 11, and on the return journey at half-past eight. Ile weather, •unfortunately, was very unfavourable. On the arrival of the steamers at Liverpool it was announced that ow- ing to the state of the tide it would be necessary for them to return at fouro'cloek,instead of half-past five as originally arranged. A considerable number of the excursionists appear to have either not heard or not heeded this inti- mation, and about a thousand of them found on return- ing to the Landing Stage at half-past five that the s,eamers had gone. As rain had been falling all day many of them were by this time drenched to the skin, and large numbers of them had not money enough to pay for railway tickets even if trains could be provided to take them back to Manchester. In their extremity they waited on the officials of the Cheshire Lines Committee, who at once made arrangements with the view of reliev- ing the excursionists from their dilemma. Some of them were able to return by ordinary train, and f)r the re- mainder a special train was provided. Those of them who could pay their fares did so, and the other gave their names and addresses to the railway officials.

div.head: A. STRANGE SIGHT.
div.p: A. STRANGE SIGHT.

. On Saturday afternoon about two o'clock, the inhabit- ants of Latchford were somewhat startled to see advanc- ing majestically up the canal, what appeared to be aroer ' of houses—minus the roof. On approaching nearer, it was discovered that the apparition in question was a floating dry dock deitined for .t.;iilford and for use on the canal, and which had been expected for some few days. The dock, which was towed by two large tugs, is 350 ft. lone and 631 t. in width. It has been a fortnight in com- ing from the port of construclon—Newcastle-on-Tyne— and owing to its large siz- is capable of accommodating the largest vessels which can possibly get up the canal. The dock is supplied with steam machinery for pumping out the water after a vessel has been berthed. It is made of steel plates and is painted a brick-red. A large crowd of people were assembled at the Latchford Lick to watch the huge -tr icture enter, and some anxiety was felt with regard to this movement, as there was only 12 inches to spare at each side of the dock when entering the lock. All went well.however,and after about an hour's nianteuvering the graving dock was berthed without a scratch. Owing to the great width of the appliance,five passenger stearnrrs had been compAlled to follow (at the rate of four miles an hour) behind, all the way from Eastham t Latchford. On reaching the latter place, however, they were given first place and put through the lock in advance of the dock. RUNCORN AND THE ASSESSMENT OF THE CANAL. The question of assessing the Ship Canal again sup- plied fond for discussion at the monthly meeting of the lAssessment Committee of the Runcorn Union held at Dutton Wo-khouse on Tuesday morning, Mr. John 1 Mclntyre presiding. Messrs. Riley and Wallace were -present on behalf ef the Ship Canal Company, Prob- ably it will be remembered that the joint committees of the two unions 4;;L,c;clad to levy a uniform assessment of £5OO per mile. Against this charge, however, the company appealed, contending that it was far two high for urging a reduction of £2OO per mile. For the pu r- nese of giving the matter fuller consideration it was ad- journed, and on Tuesday morning after a lenethv dis- cussion the Committee finally decided to accept £350 per mile without prejudice as representing the assessment of the land within the Rencorn Union's boundary. It will remain to be if the Company will agree to this conces- sion.

RAPID DISCHARGING AT RUNCORN. The following is an example ot the expedition with which vessels may he discharged of their cargoes at Runcorn. The screw steamer" Gut ian Thomas," with 1,450 tons of pyrites from fluelog on board, consigned to Messrs. Bowman, Tnompson and Co., and the Davies Patent Process C«mpany, Limited, Lostock Gralam, arrived at Runcorn Lay-by at half-past three on Friday afternoon. Half an hour later discharging operations began and ware so admirably conducted that at six o'clock the fellowing evening the vessel was clear of her cargo which had been transferred tm flats and forwarded to the c.nsignees. Considering the nature of the cargo and its amount, the work was accomplished in what might be termed ree.rd time. The agent and brokers have recognised this fa.,-t, and very properly too by forwarding to Mr.llla,shal! Stay..ns the following letters. From the agent, Mr. E. W. Turner, of Garston :—" Dear sir,—l must congratulate you on the very splendid despatch given to this steamer at your Runcorn Lay-by. I have had, as you know many years experience with ore carrying steamers, but have never known better despatch than that given to this boat and for which I am much obliged."—The brokers of the vessel, Messrs. Naylor, Benson and Company, Abchurch-lane, London, write as follows :—" We are in receipt of your wire advising us that this steamer finished discharging at six p.m. on Siturday. We are quite satisfied with the despatch given, and beg to thank you for your kind attention to the rapid discharge of this boat, which reflects credit on the management. In this instance it is a matter of importance as the steamer arrived on demurrage and each hour saved, reprensents 15s. to us."

div.head: F RODS RAM.
div.p: F RODS RAM.

CAUGHT NAPPING.—On Thursday mornine., before Mr. A. Thomas at the Frodstrim Occasional Police Court, Samuel Cawley. of London-road, Northwich, was sent to gaol for seven days for sleeping out at Alvanley on the night of the 22ad inst. ANNIVRRSARY OF THE UNION CHURCH SUNHAY SCHOoL. —The Rev. Thomas Robinson, 8.A., of Colchester, preached two powerful sermions in the Union Church on Sunday last on the occasion of the Sunday school anni- versary. Special hymns were ~,ting in excellent style by the choir, teachers, and scholars. Mrs. R-nton con- ducted a service in the afternoon. In spite of the un- favourable state of the weather, fairly large congrega- tions'attended the services, and the collectiens, which were in aid of the Sunday school funds were satis- factory. 'THE WATIR F.,'CrIEHE : ANOTHER PAYMENT TO THE CONTRACTORS.—At the fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon, Mr. John Mclntyre presiding, the Clerk read the minutes of the last monthly meeting of the Frodsham Parochial C umnittee for confirmation. These showed that under the presi- dency of Mr. A. Thomas. J.P., the committee had transacted the following busine,s :—Deferred for further consideration, plane of seven houseg proposed to be erected by Mr. H. G. Linaker in Sindfields off Church- street, Frodsham, in consequence of tleir not being in accordance with the local bye-laws. The Nuisance Inspector having reported that the property recently built by Mr. Walker was being occupied although the Authority had not granted a certificate of occupation, the committee resolved, after a lengthy discussion, that the Inspector should draw Mr. Walker's attention to the matter. It was reported by the superintending. engineer that Messrs. Timmins had practically completed their first contract. He produced his certificate for £lOO, which makes the total payments £2,750. Messrs. Williams. Riley, and Lewis were appointed a committee to examine the various water eonnections.—The Authority approved of the minutes and they were passed. A CHAPTER OF ACCIDENTS.—On Tuesday afternoon an old man named Massey, a resident of Frodsham Bridge, Sutton, and engaged as farm labourer by Mr. S. B. Chadwick, fell through a trap door of a loft at Sutton Farm and is supposed to have broken his back. Dr. Burton attended him, and it was reported on Thursday afternoon that the unfortunate man was recovering as fast as could be expected.—On Wednesday afternoon James Gould, a painter, living in Main-street, who is about 35 years of age fell from a ladder whilst painting the premises of Mr. Peter Booth, Church-street, and sus- tained a fracture of the leg just below the knee. Dr. Burton of Frodsham, was communicated with and treated the injured man who isnow progressing towards recovery satisfactorily.—The third accident was one in which Henry Percival. 46 years of age, of Five Crosses, and employed on the Frodsham Sewerage Works, disloc- ated his shoulder blade. It appears that Percival was engaged in some operations in a man-hole on Tuesday afternoon wed having concluded his work was trying to get out of the hole. He was unable to do so, however, and two other workmen went towards the hole and each caught hold of one of his hands. When climbing out in this 'way he missed his footing and fell forward with some force against the bank. Dr. Selby was sent for and attended to the injuries which the man sustained. He is now stated to be Unmoving. FRousu.Am CONSERVATIVES OUTING TO BLACEPOOL.—A most enjoyable day was spent by a number of members of the local habitation of the Primrose League on Wed- nesday. They left Frodsham station rather early in the morning and had a pleasant journey to Blackpool. Here they whiled the day away iii a series of amusements and eventually returned home all quite safe, feeling much improved by the short excursion to this renowned watering place. ASSAULTING A WIFE.—At the Frodsham Occasional Police Court on Wednesday morning before Mr. A. Thomas and Dr. Steele, a man named Thomas Ains- worth, of Bradley, Frodsham Lordship, was summoned by his wife Eesma for assaulting her on the 20th inst. at Frodaham Lordship.—Evidence was ca led, and eventu- ally, the defendant was ordered to pay Bs. 6d. .costs and was bound over to keep the peace for six months in his own recognizance of £lO and one surety of £5.

div.head: WARRINGTON FLORAL AND HORTICUL-
div.p: WARRINGTON FLORAL AND HORTICUL-
TURAL SOCIETY.
FIRST ANNUAL SHOW.

The first annual show in connection with the Warrington Floral and Horticultural Society was held at the Gymnasium, Palmyra Square, on Wed- nesday and Thursday. The proceedings on Wednes- day were opened by Mr. R. Pierpoiut, M.P., and there was a very large attendance, among others I present being, the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman I and Mrs. E. Greenall), Revs. Morley Stevenson, J. Warnock, G. B. Thurston, Mr. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), Mr. J. Fairhurst (borough treasurer), Alderman Bolton, Councillors Cannel], Greening, Shaw Green, and Smethurst, Captain Chorley, Messrs. J. White, J.P.,Ziba Armitage,J.P.,J.W. Hay- ward, Hayward, W. Gill, E. Green, T. Birtles, J. Mclver, W. Walker, J. Fulton Smith (treasurer), J. Ryan (hon. secretary), Miss B. Dutton and Miss Pierpoint. Mr. R. FIEF/POINT, M.P., in formally declaring the show open, said that he felt honoured by being chosen the president of the Association and he felt particularly honoured at being asked to open their first show that day. He could have wished that someone had been chosen by the committee who could have spoken to them with a more intimate knowledge of flowers and gardens than he had. It was, as most of them knew, more in his way to have ilawers of speech, not always beautiful, brought Under his notice, rather than flowers of the gar- den. Still he had some knowledge of the cultivation of fl ewers, for he had a garden in London of his own, and he had in cases in his window what he hoped would be oak trees and fruit trees, at least if they could survive the winter. He commended the cultivation of flowers to both rich and poor, and especially the latter who had an opportunity of occupying their spare time in useful work. There was a proverb in Latin which said that it softened the manners and prevented men from being savage. They all knew how the flowers had been chosen in former times to be dedicated to the Saints, such as the crocus to St. Valentine, and the daisy to St. Marguerite. They had later the dedication in history, of roses in the , wars between Lamcashire and Yorkshire. It might pos- sibly be for that reason that the red rose was almost always worn by that distinguished man, Mr. Gladstone, who was a Lancashire man. They had many distin- guished men who appeared to be devoted to various flowers. Mr. Chamberlain was seldom to be seen with- out .a beautiful orchid in his coat. He also knew as an absolute matter of fact that Mr. Disraeli, afterwards Lord Beaconsfield, had a special fondness for the prim- rose. He could not finish without saying how glad he was to see not only that they had an exhibition of flowers, but they also includel one of vegetables. They had thus the beautiful flowers and also the useful. vegetable, lie was also very glad that in Warrington the Society had been formed as it would be a great' encouragement to the cultivation of gardens by the people. He hoped sincerely that the Society would prosper and enlarge itself until it had become one of the recognised institutions of the town. (Applause.) In thus wishing prosperity to the institution, he had great pleasure in eeclaring the show open. (Applause.) Alderman BOLTON proposed a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Pierpoint, and in doing so hoped that the show w6uld be a success. Mr. J. FULTON SMITH seconded the vote of thanks, He said that he thought the show was a very creditable one indeed. It was a matter of congratulation that the society had begun its work free of debt. He had no doubt that they would be able to accomplish much more by and by. Me. Smith went on to give an account of the visit of the judges of the best and neatest back- yard in Warrington, when they went among other places to Tirnmis-street, off Cockhedge-lane, a place where they were surprised to find a neat garden with flowers growing in a most uncongenial neighbourhood. The vote of thanks having been accorded, the show was then open for inspection. Tie various exhibits were placed in a very pleasing fashion. At the entrance and leading across the middle of the room was a number of flowers growing in flower pots. At the extreme end were miniature models of gardens which were much admired. A stall kept by Mrs. Massey at the far end looked extremely well, and during the afternoon it was photographed ny Mr. T. Birtles. Along each side of the room were various exhibits of fruit and vegetables, and in the ante-room was a large number of exhibits of vegetables. There were not very many competitors for the priz-s for the best basket of wild flowers, but those who entered had evidently been very industrious in their search for the wild flowers, for some of the baskets contained a large variety of these too-much neglected beauties of nature. During the afternoon a large number of people visited the show, and the result has been decidedly encouraging.
