div.head: ALLEGED ROBBERY FROM AN EX-CONSERVATIVE AGENT AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: ALLEGED ROBBERY FROM AN EX-CONSERVATIVE AGENT AT WARRINGTON.

At the Borough Police Court, on Tuesday morn- ing, Peter Higgins was charged with stealing from the person of John Hampson, Academy-street (late Conservative agent) on the 13th of August, a purse containing six £5 notes, a sovereign, and a set of gold studs.—Mr. Hunt stated that the defendant is a brick-setter's labourer, and has no fixed abode. On Monday afternoon, the 13th of August. Mr. Hampson, the complainant was in the bar-room of the" Wagon" public-house, Buttermarket-street. The prisoner, in company with another man and two women, was also there drinking. Mr. Hampson entered into conversation with the prisoner and his friends, and treated them to two quarts of ale. One of the women gave a pitiful tale of her poverty and hunger, and Mr. Nampson taking pity on her gave her a two shilling piece. About six o'clock Mr. Hampson, the defendant, the other man and the two women went up Academy-street together, Mr. Hampson returning home. Soon after he entered the house the complainant missed his purse, containing six £5 notes, a sovereign,and a set of gold studs. He went to the " Wagon" and made inquiries,but could not hear anything of the missing articles. The complainant then went down to the police station where he was advised to go home and search there, as he might have mislaid them but they were not found there. D.S. Monaghan and Inspector Spinks went to the public-house and inquired about the notes, but without success. Mr. Hampson did not know the number of the notes. On the Wedesday the defendant, together with the man and two women was seen in Manchester-road, going in the direction of Manchester. The same day Detective Harris, of the Manchester police force, arrested the defendant in Deansgate. On taking him to the police station there, 353. and 10-id. were found upon him. Defendant gave the name of Peter Walsh, from Wigan, and on being asked to account for the money, he said he had worked for it. Detective Harris managed to find two of the missing notes. The notes were clearlytra.ced to the defendant. He was tried at Manchester for being in the unlawful possession of the bank-notes, and remanded. D.S. Monaghan went to Manchester and the prisoner and notes were handed over to him. The pris- oner took Monaghan to Irlam and there another note was found. He was ultimately brought to Warrington. —The prisoner stated that he found four notes in the yard of the " Wagon "on Monday. They were lying loose in the yard,and were not in a purse. The same day he saw Mr. Hampson who was drunk at the" Wagon" and was treated to some beer by him. It was after this that he found the notes. He did not know that they were Mr. Hampson's.—Mr. Hunt asked for a remand until to- day, as it was possible that the other notes might be recovered. The remand was granted.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.
A CORRECTION.

In a recent issue, in an adjourned case of clandestinely removing goods, heard at the War- rington Borough Court, we erroneously stated that the defendant was John Corradice,whereas it should have been Miranda Wilson. BAND OF HOPE MEETING. On Tuesday evening the first of a series of meet- ings and entertainments for the coming winter season in connection with St. Ann's Branch of the Church of England Temperance Society was held in the schoolrooms, Dannett-st., when about 100 mem- bers were present. A selection of temperance hymns and songs were gone through,and a variety of amus- ing games indulged in. At intervals during the evening there was handed round to the members fruit, &c., which had been provided through the generosity of Mr. Gorton (superintendent )awl Mrs. Gorton. A vote of thanks having been given to Mr. and Mrs. Gorton for their kindness, a very enjoy- able evening was brought to a close. P.S.A. AT THE Y.M.C.A.

The above meeting on Sunday afternoon was pre- sided over by Mr. Allen. A very practical address on "Self-denial" was delivered by the Riv. J Kirt- lan. The rev, gentleman divided his address into two parts, viz. :—Christian self-denial and the self- denial necessary to material progress. Two solos, "Crossing the Line" and "0 rest in the Lord" were rendered in a very feeling manner by Mr. Scatter- good. The Rev. Peter Stanford (England's coloured preacher and late pastor 'of the Wilberforce Memorial Church, Birmingham) ant Mr. Grogso n also took part in the meeting. Mr. F. Hickman was the accsumanist,

div.head: FISHING MATCH.
div.p: A FISHING MATCH.

The twelfth annual fishing match in connection with the General Woolfe Angling Society took place on Saturday. The competitors, numbering over forty, journeyed from the club's headquarters, the General Woolfe, Church-street, in a brake, the venue selected being Vale Royal, Northwich. Capital sport was the order throughout the after- noon, and the return showed that a record had been established amongst the few angling clubs in the district. Much credit is due to Mr. Joseph Langley, the secretary of the society, who has been unremit- ting in his tffarts to further this class of sport: The prizes, which were distributed at the General Woolfe Inn, on Monday evening, were a useful assortment, and included a dinner service, macin- tosh' clocks, copper kettles, pictures, carvers, Stc.,l and had been kindly given by the leading trades- people of the town. The following made catches, the weight of the fish caueit ranging from 11b. lloz. to loz. ldrm. :—J. Holmes, B. Shaw, W. Bolton, J. Hough, T. Dobson, E. Nach, J. Ellison, J. Bradshaw, E. Berry, J. Taylor, J. Bancroft, W. Bate, PI. Green (Warrington), J. Langley, J. Singleton, W. Woods, W. Crooks, P. Green, W. Hall, J. 'Alcock, S. Walker, W. Lester, H. Green (Padgate), W. Hankey, E. Kendall, T. Gray, and A. Lockwood. BOY DROWNED AT BANK QUAY.—THE INQUEST On Sunday afternoon, James Duckworth, aged 9 years, and residing at 3, Glasshouse-yard, Bank Quay, was accidently drowned by falling into the river behind Messrs. Crosfield's works. The inquest on the body of the deceased was conducted by Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, in the parade room, lrlain-street. Mrs. Duckworth, the mother of the deceased, was the first witness called and she statedl that she last saw the deceased alive at a quarter- past four on Sunday afternoon. He was then in the I house and witness gave him something to eat, after which he went out. Shortly afterwards witness heard that deceased was in the water, and at five o'clock he was brought home dead.—William Welsby, aged 13, said that he was with deceased on Sunday afternoon and they both went down to the river-side, near Messrs. Joseph Crosfield's works at Bank Quay. On reaching the water deceased saw some pieces of wood coming down with the tide. To get these deceased climbed on board a vessel which was moored to the side and from thence slid down a rope into a small boat which was fastened to the stern of the vessel. In swarming up the wet rope to return, deceased's hands slipped,and he was precipitated into the water. Witness ran to fetch assistance, and told a man named John Norman of the accident.—John Norman, said he lived close to he scene of the accident, and on the date named he was having his tea, when Welsby rushed in and informed him Gf the occurrence. He immediately tan to the water's edge and sprang into the boat. With a boat hook he managed to reach the drown- ing boy but unfortunately could not hold him and deceased sank. About 10 minutes afterwards the body was recovered, but life was quite extinct.— The jury returned a verdict of "Accadental death."
ST. HELENS
THE MURDEROUS ASSAULT.

John Thughan, of Crank, was, at St. Helens, on Saturday, further remanded on a charge of murderously attacking a fellow workman named John Graley with a spade. Graley, thou.2ll progressing favourably, was not able to attend the court.
THEFT OF OLD IRON.

At St. Helens on Saturday, Margaret Kearns, Elizabeth Heslin, and Elizabeth* Davock, three young women of Greenbank, were charged with stealing a quantity of old iron from the Gre,mbank Alkali Works on Thursday, and were each fined us., or fourteen days.

div.head: THROWING BOILING WATER ON A WOMAN.
div.p: THROWING BOILING WATER ON A WOMAN.

On Wednesday, in consequence of some misunder- standing between them, it is alleged a woman named Catherine Burns, of Wpperas-street, tnrew a can of boiling water on a widow named Catherine Ford, of the same street, while standing at her own door. The water got into one of Ford's eyes, aid otherwise she was seriously injured. She appeared at the police court on Thursday morning swathed in bandages,and a summons w as granted against the accused woman.

div.head: SERIOUS ACCIDENT AT A COLLIERY.
div.p: SERIOUS ACCIDENT AT A COLLIERY.

Richard Price, aged fourteen, son et a collier living at 139, Peasley Cross-lane, St. Helens, was on Tuesday afternoon run over by an engine and two waggons on the railway siding at, the Peaslev Cross Colliery, where he had gone to look for work. The injured youth was taken to the Cottage Hospital, where it was found necessary to amputate the left leg below the knee He also sustained a compound fracture of the right leg. ST. HELENS MIINICIPAL ELECTIONS.

Councillor J. B. Rose, presiden t of the St. Helens and District Cottage Prmperty Owners' Association, who was elected as a Liberal last November for North Eccleston Ward, has publicly announced that he is no longer a member of the Liberal organisation of St. Helens, or of any other political organisation in Sr. Helens, for the present, but an independent, or, in other words, a non- political, member of the Town Council, claiming the right to vote for whom he likes, how he likes, and for what he likes.

div.head: SUSPICIOUS CHARACTER.
div.p: A SUSPICIOUS CHARACTER.

On Monday, before Alderman Harrison and Mr. T. Glover, a middle-aged man, whf4 gave the name of William Adamson, of Bolton, was charged with being on the enclosed premises of the Mersey Loan Company, Hamer-street, for an unlawful purpose. Police-constable John Hall said he met the prisoner in Tontine-street,and suspeAing him, followed hini through several streets,and eventually saw him force an entrance into the back pre- mises of the company. When taken into custody he said "You won't allow us to beg or sleep out, and we are obliged to do something."—Chief Constable Wood asked for a remand to make inquiries into his character, and this was agreed to. SCENE IN THE POLICE COURT.

At St. Helens on Monday, Robert Wynne, of Liverpool who gave himself up at Wigan for the murder of a publican, but whose statement was found to be devoid of truth, was charged with doing wilful damage to the Shakespeare Vaults, Bridge-street. About nine 'o'clock on Sunday night prisoner went into the house,and when ordered out he loitered about a little, and then dashed thedoor so violently that an engraved sheet of glass in it. valued £3. was broken. Prisoner, who was in a state of excitement, suddenly fell in the dock, and struggled violently. He was, however, after some trouble, got an to his legs, and, having been previously convicted several times, was committed for two months with hard labour.

div.head: CHARGS OF ASSAULTING A FARM BAILIFF.
div.p: CHARGS OF ASSAULTING A FARM BAILIFF.

At the St. Helens County Petty Sessions on Tuesday. George Harrison, Daniel Casson,James Burns, and Rich. Kerwick, four youths, of St. Helens,were summoned for wilfully damaging turnips belonging to Colonel Gamble, C.B. ; and Casson, Burns, and Kerwick were also sum- moned for assaulting a farm bailiff named Robert M`Kennell. Mr. Swift, who prosecuted, said the most serious part of the business was that when M'Kennelt had secured the defendant Harrison. the latter called upon a number of of lads who were with him to assist him to get away. The other three defendants were charged with throwing stones and otherwise assaulting the (arm bailiff.—They pleaded not guilty, and as there was only ono magistrate (Alderman Cook) present, the cases were adjourned to September 11th.

div.head: RAILWAY TRESPASSING.
div.p: RAILWAY TRESPASSING.

Mr. William J. Bland, of the solicitor's department, Lime-street Station, appeared at St. Helens police court on Monday, to prosecute twelve working men for tres- passing unon the lines of the London and North Western Railway Company. Mr. Bland said that although there had been numeroos prosecutions, and people had been kited while trespaF-sing, it did not prevent the trespass- ing going on. Detective Ede gave evidence in each case and the following defendants were fined ss. including coats :—Patrick Gaffney, Owen's-row Rainhill ; Patrick Doyle, Owen's-row- Rainhill • Henry Taylor, Rainhill ; William Routledge, 46, Whittle-street, St. Helens; Harry Travis, 4, South-street, St. Helens; Thomas Heves, 6, Sandon-street, St. Helens; Thomas Highcock, 12 Phy- thian-street, St. Helens ; John Tynan, 16, Edward-street St. Helens; William Hiughton, 44, Paul-street, St. Helens; John Murphy, 11, Eccleston-street, St. Helens ; Anthon Smith, 46, Corporation-street, St. Henens ; and James Owen, Ravenhead. The magistrates expressed the hope that others we uld take warning and keep of the railway lines.

div.head: HAYDOCK.
div.p: HAYDOCK.

ST. JAMES' CHURCH SCHOOLS.—The annual treat to the ehildren attending the above schools, and St. Alban's Miisicn Schools took place on Saturday. The children mustered at the Church schools about three o'clock, and after forming in procession they walked, headed by the Haydock brass band, as far as Clipsley-row, where they were joined by the St. Albans scholars. They then re- traced their steps, as far as the Ram's Head, and returned to the schoolroom where tea was served. A move was afterwards made to a field kindly lent by Mr. Harrision, where racing and games of various kinds were indulged in until dusk, the older portion tripping it merrily to the strains of the band.

div.head: STOCKroN HEATH.
div.p: STOCKroN HEATH.

DRINKING WATER FROM THE RIVER MERSEY AND THE RESULT.-At the fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority held on Tuesday afternoon, at Dutton Workhouse, Mr. John Mel ntyre, presiding, the nuisance inspector (MT. J. Farrington) reported that he had received a notification of tvphoid fever in Green Bank Terrace, Wiidespool. He visited the house to which he was directed and found on enquiry that the pltient, who was a man, hid, whilst working on the River Mersey Diversion work, drank some of the im- pure water in the river. This the patient admitted. Mr. Farrington tLI him he had been very foolish for having done so as that had undoubtedly been the cause of his present illness.

div.head: HALTON.
div.p: HALTON.

BOWLING.—An interesting main of bowls was played off on the green adj,ining the Norton Arms Hotel on Saturday afternoon last. There were 22 entries, and at intervals some very good play was to be seen. The fol- lowing were the. winners :-1, H. Fogg, Warrington ; 2, S. Dawson, H titon ; 3.8. Hughes. Halton ; 4, W. Snape, Halton; 5, It, Jones, Runcorn ; 6, W. Dugdale, Halton.
NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

For farmers, and indeed for everybody, the weather of the past week or two has been as bad ag could possibly be expected, at least that is our ex- perience in this part of the globe. Even the sea- side and watering place weather chroniclers have been torced to admit that there has daily been a slight tall of rain, and in their reports of the amount of sunshine recorded they very carefully avoid the stereotyped "brilliant sunshine,"and sub- stitute "sky overcast." Of course this is a mild way of putting it, but they have not made anY I mention of the cold wind which has blown stronglY from the N.W. for nearly a fortnight. The reports this week are much more favourable, and at the time of writing there is every prospect of finer weather.

I seethe Newton-le-Willows Horticultural Societ, intend holding their annual exhibition of fruit. vegetables and flowers to-day (Saturday). Appear.- ances are not all in their favour so far, because must be admitted, to secure any measure of succes°, they must have a tine day. With a balmy day, and the sun shining brilliantly overhead, nothing coull be more enjoyable than a well laid out and we.ll stocked horticultural show, but with plenty of rain in evidence, the surroundings are of a fairly miser- able character. However the Committee have made strenuous efforts to attract the public, by encourag- ing a large number of exhibitors this year, which naturally means an enhanced display of floral and fruit growths. They have engaged an efficieht band, which, with a fine day, wilt tend to make things more enjoyable.

The Ashton Freemasons had a very pleasant jaunt to Bettws-y-coed last week, and from what I can hear they got as much enjoyment out of their trip in the short time at their disposal, as it was possible to squeeze, Although the lodge is an Ash- ton one, yet a very large number of the members bail from Earleeown and Newton. They had a beautiful day in Wales,and the natives of Bettws-y. coed had a practical exhibition of Lancashire exu- berance of spirits. The greater portion of their outing consisted in driving about in conveyances, but on arrival at the various places, which are set down in the guide books as planes which should be visited, they alighted, and duly inspected them, as a matter of duty, combined of course with pleasure.

If one may judge from the report of the Com' missioners meeting last week, we have obtained s short respite on .the Post Offi se question. The Commissioners received a deputation from Newton and patiently listened to their explanation, the upshot. after some acrimonious personalities, wse that the question should stand over until November. What will be done then of course lam not is. a
position to state, but I think something should be done to improve the present condition of the postai arrangements at both places.
A New York newspaper gives currency to a report tl?a,t President Cleveland is suffering from a maiadv wble,u must eventually disable him, if it does not Cause bis death.

div.head: MCCORQUODALR AND CO.'S EXCURSION.
div.p: MCCORQUODALR AND CO.'S EXCURSION.

The annual' excursion of the employ& of Messrs. McCorquodale and Co., .of Newton, took place an Saturday. The places chosen were Blackpool and Liverpool,about 1,300 being conveyed to the former place in a couple of trains, the first leaving at seven o'clock and the second five minutes later. Blackpool was reached about 9.20 and 9.30, and the excursion- ists at once dispersed to enjoy themselves in their own particular way. About 600 were taken to Liverpool where they landed about nine o'clock,and although a good number remained in the city, the majority betlok themselves to the Cheshire side of the river, and the weather being fine a very enjoy- able day was spent. The trippers returned home at various times, the last train being from Black- pool, which reached Newton about one o'clock on Sunday morning.

div.head: I.O.G.T._(EBENEZER LODGE):
div.p: I.O.G.T._(EBENEZER LODGE):

The usual weekly session of the Earlestown Ebere-zer Lodge No. 752 was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall on Tuesday. The "Gleam of Sunshine" temple officered the Lodge at seven o'clock and Bro. E. Mullins presided. A Rood number of bros. and sisters gave songs, recitations &c., about 90 being present bet-ides a good number of adults. The meeting, which was of a very interesting chatacter, closed at 8 30. A vote of thanks were tendered to the juveniles from the adult lodge for their excellent programme. The adult lodge was called to order at 830. Bro. W. J. Taylor, C.T„ presiding. The roll of officers was called after which the usual business was gone through. Tnree candidates were 'admitted to membership. Bro. T. Marsh was welcomed as a visitor from the Hope of Earlestown Lodge. Brother Rolfe of St. :Helens was also present. In the programme of the evening the following Bros. took part :—Bro. John Singleton, J. Lane, V. Brown, Sister Haden and others.
